items.articleBody:
# Repräsentative Umfrage: Das sagen Lehrer zur Arbeitszeiterfassung

Seit den Urteilen des Europäischen Gerichtshofs und des Bundesarbeitsgerichts ist gerichtlich bestätigt, dass eine Arbeitszeiterfassung zum Gesundheitsschutz vorgeschrieben ist. Wird sie bald auch für Lehrkräfte eingeführt? © Getty Was für die meisten Arbeitnehmerinnen und Arbeitnehmer in Deutschland eine Selbstverständlichkeit ist, gilt für Lehrkräfte als umstritten. Seit einem Urteil des Europäischen Gerichtshofs aus dem Jahr 2019 und einer Entscheidung des Bundesarbeitsgerichts aus dem Jahr 2022 ist auch gerichtlich bestätigt, dass die Erfassung der gesamten tatsächlichen Arbeitszeit zum Gesundheitsschutz zwingend vorgeschrieben ist. Die KMK pochte auf eine Sonderregelung für Schulen, das Bundesarbeitsministerium bekräftigte, dass es keine Ausnahmen für den Schulbereich geben würde. Wie stehen aber die Lehrkräfte selbst zu einer verpflichtenden Erfassung ihrer Arbeitszeit?

Neue Daten, die dem Deutschen Schulportal exklusiv vorliegen, zeigen nun erstmals, dass eine Mehrheit der Lehrkräfte in Deutschland die Einführung einer verpflichtenden Arbeitszeiterfassung befürwortet. 55 Prozent sind dafür, 34 Prozent dagegen. Weitere 11 Prozent sind bei dem Thema noch unentschlossen. Zu diesem Ergebnis kommt eine Umfrage, die das Meinungsforschungsinstitut Forsa im Auftrag der Robert Bosch Stiftung für das Deutsche Schulportal durchgeführt hat. Im September 2026 wurden insgesamt 1.056 Lehrkräfte an allgemeinbildenden und berufsbildenden Schulen in ganz Deutschland befragt. Die statistische Fehlermarge für die gesamte Lehrerschaft beträgt bis zu drei Prozentpunkte.

© Henriette Anders Infografik herunterladen Eine Zustimmung zur Arbeitszeiterfassung gibt es in fast allen befragten Gruppen. Besonders hoch ist sie bei Lehrkräften an Gymnasien, von denen 60 Prozent eine verpflichtende Erfassung befürworten. An Haupt-, Real- und Gesamtschulen liegt der Wert bei 56 Prozent, an Grundschulen bei 51 Prozent und an beruflichen Schulen bei 49 Prozent. Auch unter Schulleitungen und stellvertretenden Schulleitungen befürwortet eine Mehrheit die Arbeitszeiterfassung: 56 Prozent sind dafür, 35 Prozent lehnen sie ab.

## Warum viele Lehrkräfte eine Erfassung ihrer Arbeitszeiten wünschen

Doch was erhoffen sich Lehrkräfte von der Arbeitszeiterfassung? Die mit Abstand häufigste Antwort auf die offen gestellte Frage lautet: mehr Transparenz über die tatsächliche Arbeitsbelastung. Unter den Befürworterinnen und Befürwortern nennen 70 Prozent die Sichtbarmachung ihrer Arbeitszeiten und ihrer Arbeitsbelastung als wichtigstes Argument für die Einführung einer verpflichtenden Erfassung.

23 Prozent der Befürworterinnen und der Befürworter hoffen auf mehr Gerechtigkeit und Vergleichbarkeit zwischen Lehrkräften und Fächern. Weitere 15 Prozent nennen den Gesundheitsschutz und die Prävention von Überlastung, während 14 Prozent eine angemessene Vergütung oder Entschädigung für Überstunden als wichtigsten Grund anführen. 9 Prozent hoffen, dass die Erfassung der Arbeitszeiten dazu beiträgt, gesellschaftlichen Vorurteilen gegenüber dem Lehrerberuf entgegenzuwirken. Die Gründe für die Befürwortung oder die Ablehnung einer verpflichtenden Arbeitszeiterfassung wurden ohne vorgegebene Antwortoptionen anhand offener Fragen erhoben, wobei Mehrfachnennungen zulässig waren.

> Seit ich meine Arbeitsbelastung in der App erfasse, plane ich meine Woche deutlich bewusster.

Der Bremer Lehrer Björn Wolf erlebt bereits, wie die Arbeitszeiterfassung den Schulalltag verändern kann. Bremen ist in diesem Schuljahr als erstes Bundesland mit einem Pilotprojekt zur Arbeitszeiterfassung an Schulen gestartet. Wolf unterrichtet an der Oberschule an der Lerchenstraße, einer der teilnehmenden Schulen.

Auf der Fachtagung „Lehrkräftearbeitszeit als Hebel für gute Schule” am 4. November 2026 in Bremen schilderte er seine Erfahrungen: „Seit ich meine Arbeitsbelastung in der App erfasse, plane ich meine Woche deutlich bewusster“, berichtet Wolf. „Ich sehe, wie viele Stunden mir zur Verfügung stehen, und kann dann gezielt entscheiden: An welchen Tagen habe ich Unterricht? Wann bleibt Zeit zum Vorbereiten? Und wann passen die übrigen Aufgaben hinein?“ Die Tagung wurde vom Senator für Kinder und Bildung der Freien Hansestadt Bremen, der Telekom Stiftung, die das Bremer Pilotprojekt fachlich begleitet , der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Bildungsverwaltung und dem Netzwerk Schulentwicklung veranstaltet.

Auch der Leiter der Oberschule an der Lerchenstraße, Jonathan Dauber, sieht Chancen für einen besseren Arbeitsschutz. Vor allem jüngere Lehrkräfte an seiner Schule seien oft ständig erreichbar und täten sich schwer, Grenzen zwischen Arbeit und Privatleben zu ziehen. „Die Arbeitszeiterfassung kann helfen, ohne schlechtes Gewissen zu sagen: Jetzt bin ich nicht erreichbar.“

## Jede dritte Lehrkraft lehnt eine verpflichtende Arbeitszeiterfassung ab

Dennoch stößt die verpflichtende Arbeitszeiterfassung auch auf erheblichen Widerstand. Laut der Umfrage lehnen 34 Prozent der Lehrkräfte sie ab. Ihr häufigstes Argument ist, dass sich die tatsächlichen Arbeitszeiten im Lehrerberuf nur schwer zuverlässig erfassen lassen.

Unter den Gegnerinnen und Gegnern geben 40 Prozent als wichtigsten Grund an, dass die Arbeitszeiten von Lehrkräften praktisch nicht erfassbar, messbar oder kontrollierbar seien. Weitere 23 Prozent befürchten bürokratischen Mehraufwand, während 21 Prozent Bedenken haben, an Flexibilität einzubüßen oder eine Atmosphäre wachsenden Misstrauens zu schaffen. Seltener genannt werden die Vermischung von Privat- und Berufsleben (11 Prozent), Zweifel am grundsätzlichen Nutzen (8 Prozent) und die Gefahr eines Missbrauchs (7 Prozent).

Bedenken gegenüber der Arbeitszeiterfassung wurden auch auf der Fachtagung in Bremen deutlich. Sven Räther, stellvertretender Schulleiter des Hamburger Gymnasiums Ohmoor, stellte infrage, ob eine minutengenaue Erfassung mit den Realitäten des Lehrberufs vereinbar ist. „In der Theorie klingt das gut“, so Räther. „Aber eine Lehrkraft kann nicht sagen: ‚Die Arbeitszeit ist jetzt vorbei, lieber Schüler, ich habe keine Zeit mehr für dich.‘ Das ist entscheidend, denn genau dieser Teil macht unseren Beruf so besonders.“

Auch Jan Riedel, Bildungsminister des Landes Sachsen-Anhalt, äußert sich auf der Konferenz skeptisch. Er argumentierte, der Debatte fehle ein klar definiertes Ziel. Gehe es darum, die Schulen zu verbessern, eine gerechtere Verteilung der Arbeitsbelastung zu erreichen oder eine übermäßige Arbeitsbelastung sichtbar zu machen? „Ich befürchte, dass wir Erwartungen wecken, aber nicht klar definieren, was unser eigentliches Ziel ist“, sagt er.

## Bremen erprobt als erstes Bundesland die Arbeitszeiterfassung

Seit August 2026 erfassen in Bremen und Bremerhaven rund 700 Beschäftigte an neun Schulen ihre Arbeitszeiten digital mithilfe der App „Untis Arbeitszeit“. Erste Erkenntnisse deuten darauf hin, dass der Zeitaufwand für die einzelnen Einträge relativ gering ist. Laut Projektkoordinator an der Bremer Schulbehörde Kolja Buß sind 50 Prozent der Einträge innerhalb von 32 Sekunden erledigt, während 90 Prozent nicht länger als 82 Sekunden dauern. Ein besonderer Schwerpunkt des Pilotprojektes liegt auf dem Arbeitsschutz. Untersucht wird zudem, wie gesetzliche Ruhezeiten im Schulalltag eingehalten werden können.

Dies kann insbesondere für Lehrkräfte mit kleinen Kindern eine Herausforderung darstellen, die möglicherweise erst spät am Abend Zeit finden, Unterricht vorzubereiten oder Aufgaben zu benoten. „Die Einhaltung der elfstündigen Ruhezeit ist ein Thema, das uns aus den Schulen bisher am häufigsten zurückgemeldet wurde“, berichtet Buß auf der Fachtagung.

## Rackles: Arbeitszeiterfassung könnte zu einer gerechteren Aufgabenverteilung führen

Für den Bremer Bildungssenator Mark Rackles (SPD) stellt die Einführung der Arbeitszeiterfassung einen großen kulturellen Wandel dar. In einem Interview mit dem Deutschen Schulportal im Juli 2026 erklärte er, dass Lehrkräfte bisher nur einen Teil ihrer Arbeitszeit nachweisen mussten. Künftig werde viel transparenter werden, wer wie viele Stunden arbeite.

Er erwartet, dass das System erhebliche Unterschiede in der Arbeitsbelastung zwischen einzelnen Lehrkräften aufzeigen wird. Dies könnte auch unangenehme Konsequenzen haben. Während Lehrkräfte mit besonders hoher Arbeitsbelastung Entlastung benötigen würden, könnte von anderen erwartet werden, zusätzliche Aufgaben zu übernehmen. „Die, die unterhalb des Arbeitssolls sind, müssen mehr arbeiten – das ist völlig klar“, so Rackles im Interview. Das würde jedoch nicht unbedingt mehr Unterrichtsstunden bedeuten. Stattdessen könnten zusätzliche Aufgaben gerechter auf das Kollegium verteilt werden.

## Was geschieht, sobald die Arbeitszeiten erfasst sind?

Doch selbst wenn eine Arbeitszeiterfassung eingeführt wird, bleibt eine entscheidende Frage offen: Was geschieht mit den gesammelten Daten? Rackles sieht die Chance, mit Hilfe der Daten, Aufgaben innerhalb der Schulen gerechter zu verteilen und übermäßige Arbeitsbelastungen abzubauen. Gleichzeitig könnten sie eine Grundlage dafür bieten, zusätzlichen Personalbedarf zu ermitteln und zu begründen.

Auf der Konferenz in Bremen betonte er, dass zusätzliche Mittel in Zeiten knapper öffentlicher Haushalte sorgfältig begründet werden müssen: „Mehr Ressourcen für Bildung geht immer“, sagt Rackles. „In der heutigen Zeit muss man aber sehr präzise sagen, wofür wir mehr Ressourcen brauchen. Wir brauchen konkrete Zahlen statt eines Bauchgefühls. Dieser Debatte muss man sich 2027 stellen.“ Ob eine verpflichtende Arbeitszeiterfassung tatsächlich zur Entlastung der Lehrkräfte führt, wird daher weitgehend davon abhängen, wie Schulen und Bildungsbehörden die erhobenen Daten nutzen.

Die repräsentative Forsa-Umfrage macht erstmals deutlich, dass eine Mehrheit der Lehrkräfte eine verpflichtende Arbeitszeiterfassung grundsätzlich befürwortet.

Mitarbeit: Jasmin Shamsi

items.articleBody:
“So che voglio e non ho cosa io voglia” (I know that I desire, and I don’t have anything I desire) Carlo Michelstaedter (1913)

Is All Ages Lorenzo Senni‘s midlife crisis album? Six years after Scacco Matto, the Italian electronic musician appears to be taking stock, revisiting the hardcore punk, straight-edge and skateboarding cultures that shaped his youth while questioning some of the musical conventions he has since made his own. Where Scacco Matto seemed content to defer gratification indefinitely — “Dance Tonight, Revolution Tomorrow” — All Ages feels more like a moment of reckoning. There is also a narrative drive that was less immediately apparent in his earlier albums, which were more concerned with mood, anticipation and the mechanics of euphoria. Senni’s trademark pointillistic trance is still recognisable, as are the euphoric excesses of bubblegum bass and deconstructed club music, but the compositions have become more expansive, playful and unexpectedly personal.

The album opens with “Art Life & Skateboarding”, featuring legendary American skateboarders Chad Muska and Jamie Thomas, whose contrasting attitudes towards partying and straight-edge discipline reflect the opposing worlds Senni has long inhabited. “Skateboarding and music were the glue that connected our crew”, recalls one of them, before the track concludes with a curt renunciation: “Goodbye, I’m out.” What follows is an extraordinary succession of hyperactive rhythms, elastic basslines, cartoonish synthesiser flourishes and intricate keyboard passages that occasionally veer towards jazz-funk and fusion. The ebullient “Smile Through Tears” almost seems to embody the album’s emotional contradictions, while “Jealous Of Michelangelo” brings a mischievous irreverence to the question of artistic ambition.

Yet beneath the exuberance runs a more troubled current. “Your Favourite DJ” samples Brainiac’s “1 Am a Cracked Machin3”, transplanting Tim Taylor’s manic vocals into an electronic environment where the distinction between human performer and malfunctioning machine becomes increasingly blurred. On “La Persuasione e la Rettorica”, Xiu Xiu’s Jamie Stewart recalls childhood experiences of vulnerability and exclusion, including being pushed off a bicycle and finding no way back up. The title refers to Carlo Michelstaedter’s 1910 philosophical thesis, which contrasts the possibility of fully inhabiting one’s existence with the illusions through which we continually defer fulfilment. Stewart’s repeated “down” acquires a peculiar resonance with Michelstaedter’s image of a weight endlessly seeking a lower point without ever finding satisfaction.

Memory returns on “Self eXamined Endurance”, which samples Smokescreen’s “Tabula Rasa”, its reflections on experiences that made one feel alive and the tendency to romanticise suffering introducing a more ambivalent note beneath Senni’s deliriously playful electronics. There is something revealing about an artist revisiting the music of his youth through lyrics that question the very act of mythologising the past. Elsewhere, “Orpheus In the Underground (Who are the Brutes!?)” plunges from a deceptively gentle opening into a riot of percussion and synthesiser figures, its title playfully collapsing the distance between classical mythology and the rave underground. The unexpectedly tender piano miniature “Purely Coincidental” offers a rare display of intimacy.

The album ends with a zipper cut, and an urgent appeal to put an end to one’s selfish ways, right now. The closing “KILL LIES ALL” urges one to break the chain, act insane and hold on to the truth. After so much reflection on memory, vulnerability and endurance, the track makes one final sprint up the court, as though determined to break free of everything holding it back.

For all its restless energy and humour, All Ages is ultimately concerned with the difficulty of letting go of the past without losing the experiences that made us who we are. Moving beyond the carefully suspended anticipation of his earlier work towards something more immediate, unpredictable and emotionally exposed, Senni seems to have found a new freedom in revisiting his old obsessions. Who knew a midlife crisis could be so much fun? (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.title: Straße von Kertsch - Neue Angriffe auf die Krim-Brücke
items.subtitle: Die ukrainischen Streitkräfte haben nach russischen Angaben erneut die Krim-Brücke attackiert.
items.feedText: Krim-Brücke wurde bereits vor zwei Tagen schwer beschädigt. (AFP/HANDOUT) Der Zugverkehr über die Brücke sei vorerst eingestellt worden, der entstandene Schaden werde derzeit ermittelt, teilte der von Moskau eingesetzte Verwaltungschef Aksjonow auf Telegram mit. Erst in der Nacht zum Dienstag hatte ein massiver ukrainischer Angriff mit Marschflugkörpern einen Stahlbogen des etwa 19 Kilometer langen Bauwerks zerstört. Die Krim-Brücke gilt als Prestigeprojekt des russischen Präsidenten Putin und verbindet die 2014 annektierte Schwarzmeer-Halbinsel mit dem russischen Festland. Die russische Armee transportiert über die Brücke unter anderem militärische Ausrüstung auf die Krim. Die Ukraine hat das strategisch wichtige Bauwerk über die Straße von Kertsch darum in den vergangenen Jahren immer wieder angegriffen.

# Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb

November 18, 2026

## Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb

edited by Robert Egan

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

peer-reviewed publication

trusted source

proofread

When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance.

And when the scientists took a closer look, they found something even more surprising.

"Remarkably, the atoms were flashing in two very different kinds of light at once—microwaves and infrared light—in perfect step with each other. That had not been observed before," says Faraon (BS '04), Caltech's William L. Valentine Professor of Applied Physics and Electrical Engineering and the Fletcher Jones Foundation Director of the Kavli Nanoscience Institute.

Now, working with researchers at Stanford University led by Joonhee Choi, Faraon's team has figured out what causes this synchronized flashing. They used the mechanism to create a new type of specialized laser called a superradiant frequency comb that could be more stable than other lasers.

Unlike conventional lasers that emit a single color of light, frequency combs act like a ruler for light across a range of frequencies, or colors; the spacing between neighboring colors is exactly the same, like the teeth of a comb. Frequency combs have been used to improve precise measurements of time and distance, leading to improvements in atomic clocks, ultrafast science and the identification of chemicals. The discovered superradiant frequency comb would simultaneously produce microwave and optical light, and thus could help enable links between quantum devices.

The scientists describe the superradiant frequency comb in a paper in the journal Nature . The paper's lead author, Tian Xie (Ph.D. '25), completed the work as a graduate student in Faraon's lab and is now a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford University.

## Atoms synchronize without mirrors

Superradiance itself is not new. Scientists have known about the emission for more than 50 years. To understand the quantum phenomenon, first consider laser light. In a laser, atoms in a material such as a gas or a crystal are excited to higher energy levels. Then light bouncing between mirrors prompts the excited atoms to release that energy in step with it, adding more light to the beam with every bounce.

This process builds up coherent light—light waves with crests and troughs that are aligned with one another. The distance between the mirrors helps determine the frequency of the light. If the mirrors move even a minuscule amount, the frequency will also change.

Something different happens with superradiance: There are no mirrors to coordinate the light. Instead, the individual atoms lock into step on their own through a shared electromagnetic field and then radiate together. Previous work has shown that clouds of such synchronized atoms can emit a quick superradiant flash or a steady beam at a frequency determined by the atoms themselves rather than the distance between mirrors.

The Caltech and Stanford researchers were surprised to see that instead of a single flash or a steady beam, the synchronized atoms could be made to fire in a repeated regular rhythm to produce a frequency comb.

"Imagine a crowd suddenly starting to clap in perfect rhythm without anyone leading them. That's essentially what these atoms are doing when they produce repeated flashes of light, and it's remarkable that they can organize themselves this way," says Choi, now an assistant professor at Stanford University and formerly a postdoctoral scholar at Caltech.

Discover the latest in science, tech, and space with over 100,000 subscribers who rely on Phys.org for daily insights. Sign up for our free newsletter and get updates on breakthroughs, innovations, and research that matter— daily or weekly .

## A crystal sets the pulse

The researchers embedded billions of ytterbium ions, charged atoms, within a yttrium orthovanadate crystal located beneath a tiny microwave resonator—in this case, a layer of superconducting material that trapped the microwaves. When a laser energized the ions, they emitted microwaves. Since all the ytterbium ions experienced the same microwave field, they influenced one another and became synchronized, emitting light steadily. But past a certain laser power, the ions switched from emitting steadily to pulsing in rhythm.

"Other mode-locked frequency combs depend on bouncing light off mirrors in a cavity, and those cavity lengths can fluctuate due to things like temperature," Xie says. "Because superradiance comes from atom–atom interference, it's absolutely frequency-stable, and therefore it can, in principle, be a much better platform than previous frequency combs."

The researchers would like to learn how to adjust and shape the rhythm of the superradiant pulsing at will, "so that the atoms become a kind of programmable light source," Faraon says. By tuning the properties of the atoms with the laser light, the team should be able to naturally change the emission properties of the resulting frequency comb. "Being able to tune each emission strength, pulse separation, and emission format would be very useful to suit each specific application," he says.

## Linking microwave and optical devices

Beyond improved frequency combs, the work holds promise for linking quantum devices. One common strategy for quantum computers uses superconducting circuits that work with microwaves. But microwaves lose their quantum information easily if they are not kept at ultralow temperatures, near absolute zero (about minus 460 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 273 degrees Celsius). Optical light, by contrast, can carry information over long distances through fiber cables, but superconducting circuits cannot directly send or receive optical light.

Ytterbium ions, though, can interact with both microwave and optical light. The ions, Xie explains, have three discrete energy levels; there is a small gap, or transition, between two of the energy levels, and a larger gap between another pairing. The energy required to jump across the small gap corresponds to the emission or absorption of microwave light, while the jump across the larger gap involves optical light. Since the same ion has both gaps, it can interact with both frequencies of light.

"Whenever these ions generate a microwave field, there is a process that naturally generates a corresponding optical field at the same time," Xie says. "That's why in the experiment, you send a laser light to pump the atoms and you see two emissions coming out at very different frequencies."

This suggests it might be possible to use the microwave emission to interface with superconducting hardware and the optical emission to enable information to be carried long distances.

Publication details

Tian Xie et al., Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs, Nature (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11289-7 . On arXiv : arxiv.org/abs/2604.14601

Journal information: arXiv , Nature

items.feedText:
The elements that bind you together were born in the earliest moments of the universe and forged in faraway stars. The sugars that permit your muscles to move were all made by plants devouring light from a fiery orb. The oxygen that fills your lungs is borrowed from forests and oceans, and the water that makes up most of your body once fell from the sky as drops of rain. You are constructed of wonder, which is to say nature. all images photographed by Jacques Brun for Atmos

items.articleBody:
- ## WE ARE MADE OF WONDER

The atoms that shiver throughout your being are older than organic life. The elements that bind you together were born in the earliest moments of the universe and forged in faraway stars. The sugars that permit your muscles to move were all made by plants devouring light from a fiery orb. The oxygen that fills your lungs is borrowed from forests and oceans, and the water that makes up most of your body once fell from the sky as drops of rain.

You are constructed of wonder, which is to say nature.

all images photographed by [Jacques Brun](https://jacquesbrun.com/) for [Atmos](https://atmos.earth/)

- ## THE MYTH OF SEPARATION

And yet, much of human existence on this planet has been separated from it. The very word we use to describe the sum totality of life is defined by the exclusion of our species. Nature is a learned way of seeing the world as everything that isn’t us. To other anything is the first step to allowing harm, paving the road for extraction and catastrophe. We have bowed out of belonging to the revelry of biological exuberance that is the Earth, and then wonder why we feel lonely.

We can trace the roots of this divide to the Scientific Revolution of 16th- and 17th-century Europe, in which anatomy mapped the body, microscopic life revealed itself, the heavens no longer revolved around us, and gravity was demystified. Alongside these revelations, a new view took shape: nature as a series of mechanical processes, governed by laws that could be observed, understood, and harnessed. And humans, with our uniquely rational minds, were set apart.

- ## THE CARTESIAN DIVIDE

Few did more to articulate this perspective than René Descartes. In *Discourse on the Method* (1637), he described the bodies of animals as machines. He believed that scientific knowledge could allow humans to become “the lords and possessors of nature.” Cartesian dualism was a fissure that cleaved the world in two: mind and matter, thinking subject and physical object. In order to understand the rest of life, we had to observe it from afar.

While Descartes’s *cogito ergo sum* (“I think, therefore I am”) is widely known, the context is less so. He tied rationalism to doubt: “from the very circumstance that I thought to doubt of the truth of other things, it most clearly and certainly followed that I was.” Doubt, a verb that is so close to wonder, though one houses worry and the other awe. Perhaps rather than doubt leading to thinking to existing, wonder can lead us to feeling to belonging.

- ## FROM KNOWLEDGE TO WISDOM

Science has taught us extraordinary things about the workings of this world. But to learn how to live within it, we need wisdom.

In the long memory of our planet and the thousands of years in which our species has been living on it, this way of seeing nature as separate from us is a recent phenomenon. The idea that we are separate from nature has never been universal. Many Indigenous cultures have maintained traditions that recognize us as part of the living world, rooted in reciprocity and stewardship. Seeing ourselves as one strand in the web of life is not a new worldview. It’s a very old one.

- ## LEARNING TO BELONG

In *Braiding Sweetgrass* (2013), botanist and enrolled member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation Robin Wall Kimmerer advocates for a weaving of Indigenous knowledge and Western science. Through stories about plants that plait the personal, cultural, and biological, she illuminates a world in which every growing thing is a guide beckoning us into deeper relationship with the Earth and all of the beings it houses. This is the fertile ground of ecological wisdom.

If knowledge is a collection of facts, wisdom is what we do with it. While science helps us gather knowledge in order to better understand the world we live in, sapience—the possession of wisdom—helps us discern how to move through it. For example, scientific knowledge can reveal that forests exchange nutrients through fungal networks. Ecological wisdom asks what those relationships might teach us about reciprocity, cooperation, and collective well-being.

- ## THE ECOLOGICAL DISCONNECT

It’s telling that, while many of us were raised on the importance of science and studied it in school, few of us are taught sapience. Shouldn’t we let everything we have learned about life on Earth guide us in our individual and collective lives? Climate change, biodiversity loss, and ecocide are the evidence of this disconnect, and the wider chasm between us and nature.

Ecological wisdom bridges this divide.

- ## RE-ENCHANTING OUR WORLD

This is core to our work at [Atmos](https://atmos.earth), a multimedia ecosystem weaving nature into public consciousness. Our mission is to inspire cultural transformation by re-enchanting people with nature. We reveal the ways that human life is interwoven with the Earth, and believe that this connection leads to the solutions that preserve and protect our planet. Our vision is a society in sync with nature’s efficiencies, reciprocities, and beauty. What we offer is proof of wonder.

I have spent the last six years gathering this in the form of a newsletter called [The Overview](https://atmos.earth/topic/climate-culture-newsletter-overview/). Rather than liquify in a chrysalis, dragonflies metamorphose incompletely across many moltings. Can we adopt their patience for transformation? Long before humans invented agriculture, ants were farming fungi for food in a way that benefited both. What if our modern agricultural systems could be similarly symbiotic? Hummingbirds can hover, drawing nectar from flowers without ever needing to land on them. Can we learn to live as lightly, leaving so little trace?

- ## LESSONS FROM OTHER LIVES

In this time, it has become a continuous practice for me to turn to nature for wisdom about how to live. In moving through grief, I turned to ravens and crows, who have been seen holding funerals for the fallen. When struggling with vulnerability, I looked to frogs, who partly breathe through their sensitive skin. Seeking advice on how to navigate the unknown, I found comfort in bats, who make maps of the dark by listening.

In every life form, crawling or winged, scaled or soaring, there are lessons to be found.

- ## NATURE AS BLUEPRINT

At the scale of systems, one of the most direct ways ecological wisdom can guide the way we design our lives is through biomimicry. As Janine Benyus, who popularized the term with her 1997 book, once told me: Every species that is alive today is an example of life having gotten it right—and elegantly so. In [our conversation](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/janine-benyus-on-biomimicry-and-designing-with/id1800758497?i=1000704408393) for [The Nature Of podcast,](https://atmos.earth/podcast/) she pointed out that our species has a massive design challenge on our hands, but life’s intelligence is all around us.

Bullet trains that take cues from kingfishers, structural color that mirrors the brilliant blue of morpho butterflies rather than synthetic dyes, shark skin-inspired antimicrobial surfaces, temperature regulation modeled after termite mounds—biomimicry provides the blueprints for a designed society that is not separate from, but functionally intertwined with the wonders of the more than human world. It sees every species as a schematic written with possibilities.

- ## DESIGNING FOR LIFE

Biomimicry is more than taking inspiration from nature or borrowing its aesthetics: it’s about emulating nature’s artistry in both form and function, in a way that gives back to life. As Benyus told me: “Life creates conditions conducive to life.” And we are part of that creative genius. We can design a society that works with nature as we simultaneously remember our place within it.

In *World as Lover, World as Self* (1991), the late Buddhist and deep ecologist Joanna Macy describes three movements in the story of our species. The first she labeled participation mystique, the state in which one does not distinguish oneself from surrounding objects and the environment. The second was when we left that state and began to see the world as separate, which gave us science but also alienation. The third movement is the one we must now make: back to an awareness of ourselves as part of nature, bringing with us all we have learned.

- ## RETURNING HOME

As Macy put it, “Now it can dawn on us: we are our world knowing itself.”

The root of “eco” is the Greek *oikos* meaning “home.” We can return to a way of living with this understanding as the foundation already laid, one that reconnects us to the resplendent, abundant aliveness in the garden of life. Our species is standing at the threshold, and ecological wisdom is the key. Outside the house of isolation that we have constructed, home awaits: a circle of belonging as wide as the world. And the architecture of the world is wonder.

[Willow Defebaugh](https://www.instagram.com/willowonearth/?hl=en) is the cofounder and editor-in-chief of [Atmos](https://atmos.earth/), a climate and culture publication exploring humanity’s relationship with the natural world. Defebaugh is also the author of *The Overview*, a deep ecology newsletter and book, and the host of *The Nature Of* podcast.

*This article is part of designboom’s* *POSTHUMAN UTOPIAS* *chapter, exploring what happens when humans are no longer the measure of all things. These* *stories rethink our relationship with the planet through interspecies architecture, living materials, regenerative landscapes and emerging technologies – learn more* *[↗ designboom.com](https://www.designboom.com/tag/chapter-posthuman-utopias/)* *!* The chapter is presented in partnership with [INDX|GLOBAL](http://www.indxglobal.vision/) – a global cultural platform placing Indian architecture, design, and creative intelligence in conversation with the world.

# Xi, Trump und Putin: Drei Perspektiven, viele Differenzen

Treffen von Xi, Trump und Putin Drei Mächte, drei Perspektiven und viele Differenzen Stand: 19.11.2026 • 00:33 Uhr

Es gilt schon vorab als historisch - das erste Dreier-Treffen von Xi, Trump und Putin auf dem APEC-Gipfel in Shenzhen. Doch die Positionen der drei Präsidenten bei den Themen atomare Abrüstung, Iran oder Ukraine klaffen teils auseinander.

Es ist die erste Zusammenkunft dieser Art, bislang gab es nur bilaterale Gespräche: Chinas Staatschef Xi Jinping, US-Präsident Donald Trump und Kremlchef Wladimir Putin sind zu Gesprächen in China. Heute soll es ein Treffen zu dritt geben - am Rande des zweitägigen Forums der Asiatisch-Pazifischen Wirtschaftskooperation (APEC) in Shenzhen.

Putin und Trump sind bereits am Mittwoch in der südchinesischen Industriemetropole eingetroffen und wurden von Xi warm empfangen. Bei einem ersten Treffen mit Putin erklärte Xi, die Beziehungen ihrer Länder seien felsenfest. Wenig später wurde Trump ungewöhnlicherweise direkt am Flughafen per Umarmung von Xi begrüßt. Das Dreiergespräch wird international mit Spannung erwartet. Worum geht's?

## Nukleare Abrüstung

Trump will trilaterale Gespräche über die Reduzierung der Atomwaffenarsenale und die Eindämmung der Proliferation, also der Weiterverbreitung von Nuklearwaffen. Die USA möchten China in künftige Rüstungskontrollvereinbarungen einbinden. Das Auslaufen des New-Start-Vertrags im Februar, des letzten Abkommens zwischen den führenden Atommächten USA und Russland, eröffnete laut Washington die Möglichkeit, ein "besseres Abkommen" zusammen mit Peking zu schließen.

Peking lehnt verbindliche trilaterale Abrüstungsverhandlungen derzeit ab, solange die USA und Russland ihre deutlich größeren Arsenale nicht zuerst reduzieren. China verweist auf seinen vergleichsweise kleineren Bestand und will nicht unter Bedingungen teilnehmen, die seine strategische Position schwächen. Nach einem Bericht des Stockholmer Friedensforschungsinstituts SIPRI verfügte China im Januar dieses Jahres über 620 Atomsprengköpfe.

Moskau ist grundsätzlich an Rüstungskontrolle interessiert, insbesondere nachdem das bilaterale US-russische Atomabkommen im Februar ausgelaufen ist. Ein konkreter, verbindlicher Dreierdeal gilt aber als unwahrscheinlich. Russland dürfte Abrüstung auch als Hebel für breitere geopolitische Zugeständnisse nutzen - sprich dafür Gegenleistungen verlangen.

## Krieg in Iran

Donald Trump will mit Xi Jinping und Wladimir Putin über ein Ende des Kriegs in Iran sprechen. Die USA stehen nach der gemeinsamen Offensive mit Israel im Februar unter Druck. Nachdem Beobachter die Niederlage der US-Republikaner bei den Midterm-Wahlen maßgeblich auf den Krieg in Iran zurückführen , steht Trump noch mehr unter Druck. Langfristig kann er an einer weiteren Eskalation kaum interessiert sein, wenn auch er regelmäßig Bereitschaft signalisiert, weitere Schritte gehen zu wollen.

China verurteilt den Krieg als Angriffskrieg und fordert eine Rückkehr zu Verhandlungen. Als wichtiger wirtschaftlicher Partner Irans stellt sich China selbst als Friedensvermittler dar. Peking will eine erneute Eskalation vermeiden, lehnt Sanktionen und ein Militäreinsatz als Mittel aber grundsätzlich ab.

Russland hat ein Interesse an einer Beendigung des Kriegs, ohne die iranische Seite offen zu isolieren. Auch hat der Kreml kein Interesse an einer weiteren Eskalation zwischen Iran und den arabischen Staaten am Persischen Golf. Iran wurde nach dem Einmarsch Russlands in die Ukraine zu einem wichtigen Waffenlieferanten. Andererseits deuten Beobachter das beharrliche Schweigen des Kreml gegenüber Trump in Bezug auf den Krieg in Iran als Schwäche Putins. Dennoch tritt Russland als Partner Teherans auf.

Allen drei Parteien gemein ist wohl das Interesse daran, den Schiffsverkehr in der Straße von Hormus wieder zum Laufen zu bringen. Seit Beginn des Iran-Krieges hält Teheran die Meerenge weitgehend blockiert. Die USA verhängten im Gegenzug eine Blockade iranischer Häfen.

Analyse 23.04.2026

### China An der Seite Irans - aber nicht zu offensichtlich

Wie verhält sich China im Iran-Krieg? Peking versucht es mit einer Doppelstrategie. mehr

## Verhandlungen mit der Ukraine

Ob das Thema Ukraine bei der Begegnung eine größere Rolle spielen wird, darf bezweifelt werden. Das stärkste Interesse daran dürfte Russlands Präsident Putin haben. Der Kreml will zurück zu den Einflusszonen des Kalten Krieges und den Krieg gegen die Ukraine auf dieser Basis beilegen - möglichst unter Ausschluss der Ukraine und der Europäer.

Dazu passt das Treffen in Shenzhen zumindest auf der symbolischen Ebene - dass die Ukraine deshalb vor einem "Jalta 2, 3 oder 4" warnte, dürfte Putin gefallen haben. Aus seinem Umfeld kommen Signale in alle Richtungen. Außenminister Sergej Lawrow erinnerte an Putins Vorstoß in Richtung einer "Sicherheitsstruktur für Eurasien", sein außenpolitischer Berater Juri Uschakow betonte, es sei "vereinbart worden, die Zusammenkunft im Geiste des gegenseitigen Verständnisses und der Allianz unserer drei Staaten im Zweiten Weltkrieg zu gestalten", und sein Sprecher Peskow erklärte, Russlands Weltordnung bestehe "gerade darin, niemandem eine bestimmte Ordnung aufzuzwingen".

China wiederum spricht zwar nicht von einer Neuordnung der Sicherheitsarchitektur, sondern von einer multipolaren Welt, steht im Ukraine-Krieg aber fest an Russlands Seite - politisch und militärisch, auch wenn China sich selbst nicht als Partei im Krieg bezeichnet. Zugleich betont Xi aber auch, die Europäer müssten Teil einer Lösung sein und sollten nicht übergangen werden.

Die USA schließlich sehen China nicht als Teil des Verhandlungsprozesses. US-Offizielle betonten vor dem Gipfel, man betrachte die Bemühungen um ein Kriegsende als separaten Verhandlungsstrang, an dem China nicht beteiligt sein sollte. Trump dürfte demnach wenig Interesse daran haben, dem Thema Ukraine größeren Raum zu geben.

20.10.2026

### Nach Gesprächen in Norwegen Selenskyj fordert Teilnahme an Putin-Xi-Trump-Treffen

Trump hatte Interesse an einem Gespräch mit den Präsidenten Russlands und Chinas über die Ukraine gezeigt. mehr

items.articleBody:
As of iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, and macOS 27, there is now a WebKit API to enable [Global Privacy Control (GPC)](https://www.w3.org/TR/gpc/), an emerging web standard. As a developer using WebKit APIs like WKWebView, or WebPage for SwiftUI, you can add your own user setting to control it.

The [specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/gpc/) as of November 10, 2026, says:

> “Global Privacy Control is designed to allow users to express a preference to opt out of sharing and cross-context targeted advertising”

According to the California Office of the Attorney General’s [webpage](https://www.oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa) for the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) as of November 10, 2026:

> “This landmark law secures new privacy rights for California consumers, including: (…) The right to opt-out of the sale or sharing of their personal information including via the [GPC](https://www.oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa/gpc)”

## API

There is a new WKWebpagePreferences property, globalPrivacyControlEnabled. Setting it to YES on the preferences object handed back from the navigation-policy delegate opts that navigation into GPC. This applies to the whole document tree produced by the navigation. Once enabled, both navigator.globalPrivacyControl and the Sec-GPC: 1 request header are active for the main frame, its subframes, and their subresources.

The Swift WebPage API exposes the same capability through a WebPage.NavigationPreferences property, isGlobalPrivacyControlEnabled.

### Apple Developer Documentation Links

- [WKWebpagePreferences / globalPrivacyControlEnabled](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/webkit/wkwebpagepreferences/globalprivacycontrolenabled)
- [WebPage.NavigationPreferences / isGlobalPrivacyControlEnabled](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/webkit/webpage/navigationpreferences/isglobalprivacycontrolenabled)

## Example Usage

### Swift (WKWebView)

func webView(
_ webView: WKWebView,
decidePolicyFor navigationAction: WKNavigationAction,
preferences: WKWebpagePreferences
) async - > (WKNavigationActionPolicy, WKWebpagePreferences) {
preferences.globalPrivacyControlEnabled = userPrefersGlobalPrivacyControl
return (.allow, preferences)
}

### Swift (WebPage)

func decidePolicy(
for action: WebPage.NavigationAction,
preferences: inout WebPage.NavigationPreferences
) async - > ### Objective-C

- (void)webView:(WKWebView *)webView
decidePolicyForNavigationAction:(WKNavigationAction *)navigationAction
preferences:(WKWebpagePreferences *)preferences
decisionHandler:(void (^)(WKNavigationActionPolicy, WKWebpagePreferences *))

items.articleBody:
A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) [voted today](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/press/rep/release/commerce-republicans-advance-slate-of-bipartisan-bills-and-nominations/) to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote.

All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee's 13 Democrats were absent. "We're going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs," Cruz said at today's hearing.

Nominees are vetted in committees first, and then seek require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/11/ted-cruz-led-committee-approves-trump-fcc-nominee-15-0-as-democrats-boycott-vote/)

items.articleBody:
Did 3,330 "solid red" Republican counties vote Democrat in the 2026 midterms? No, that's not true: There are not that many counties in the United States. According to the National Association of Counties, 3,069 counties administer elections at the local level. The claim also confuses counties that administer elections with counties that vote as a single political bloc. Within the same county or state, election results can vary among congressional districts, other voting jurisdictions and communities.

The claim appeared in [a post](https://x.com/political_rock/status/2122653353024819440) by the @political_rock account on X on Nov. 17, 2026. It read:

> The mathematical probability of 3,330 solid red counties across the US turning blue is 1 in 1 Trillion.

This is what the post looked like on X at the time of writing:

*(Image source: post by @political_rock on X.)*

The meme appears to be a reaction to the blue wave in the 2026 midterm elections, when Democrats flipped control of the U.S. House. Republicans held a 220-215 majority before the election, while Democrats emerged with a 257-171 advantage afterward, with some races still undecided as of Nov. 18, 2026.

The premise of the meme is flawed from the start. There are not 3,330 counties in the United States. According to the [National Association of Counties](https://www.naco.org/page/what-are-counties), 3,069 counties administer elections at the local level.

The meme also treats counties as if they vote as single political blocs. In reality, voters cast individual ballots, and election results can vary among congressional districts and other voting jurisdictions within the same county. A county's overall results do not necessarily reflect how every voter or congressional district within it voted.

In the [2026 midterms](https://www.cookpolitical.com/vote-tracker/2026/house), the electorate dramatically shifted toward the Democratic Party, but Republicans still tallied more than 42% of the vote, compared to 56% for Democrats in House races. In the [2024 House vote](https://www.cookpolitical.com/vote-tracker/2024/house), Republicans held 51% of the vote to 48% for Democrats. Neither was a winner-take-all situation.

#### 2026 House vote

Although these maps break down results by congressional district rather than county, they show Republicans retaining large areas of the country while winning by narrower margins in many of the districts they carried. At the same time, Democrats strengthened their overall position.

[The first map](https://www.cookpolitical.com/vote-tracker/2026/house) shows Democrats with a 257-to-171 advantage over Republicans, with seven seats still undecided.

*(Image source: The Cook Political Report.)*

[The second map](https://www.cookpolitical.com/vote-tracker/2026/house) shows how voting margins shifted between the 2024 presidential election and the 2026 midterms. Even in states and congressional districts won by Republicans (see above), the margin shifted toward Democrats in all but a small number of cases:

*(Image source: The Cook Political Report.)*

#### News searches

Lead Stories searched [Google News](https://news.google.com/search?q=%22solid%20red%2C%22%20%22counties%2C%22%20%22Democrat%2C%22%20and%20%22midterms.%22&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) and [Yahoo News](https://news.search.yahoo.com/search;_ylt=A2RRBbVwIP5qvgIAM_LQtDMD;_?fr=uh3_news_web&.tsrc=uh3_news_web&fr2=sb-top&p=%22solid+red%2C%22+%22counties%2C%22+%22Democrat%2C%22+and+%22midterms.%22) and found no matching reports about the claim from established news outlets using the search terms: "solid red," "counties," "Democrat" and "midterms."

items.articleBody:
Unlike most surviving Cham towers that crown dramatic hilltops, Binh Lam Tower rises almost unexpectedly from the flat, verdant plains of a quiet lowland village.

Constructed around the late tenth to early eleventh century, this 20-meter brick sanctuary serves as a vital architectural bridge, catching the art form mid-evolution between the delicate, lyrical features of the My Son A1 style and the grand, spear-like forms of classic Binh Dinh towers.

Its weathered facade features slender vertical pilasters, mini-temple false doors, and faint relief carvings of the mythical bird-god Garuda. Beyond its standing brickwork, Binh Lam hides deep subterranean secrets: archaeological digs uncovered vast foundations of a once-extensive religious complex, alongside stone Nagas and relief sculptures.

Furthermore, the tower once formed the eastern heart of ancient Thi Nai Citadel, positioned along river channels leading to the historical port—making this lowland monument a crucial physical anchor to Champa's lost naval and architectural empire.

items.articleBody:
# The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search

- News
- Policy
## The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search

Google is trying to force Gemini on schools, and they’re not thrilled.

Google is trying to force Gemini on schools, and they’re not thrilled.

New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times . Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times , New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to The Verge , Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills , and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests . There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age . But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

- Terrence O'Brien
- Google

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times , New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to The Verge , Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills , and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests . There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age . But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

- Terrence O'Brien

items.articleBody:
Asked at a Wednesday confirmation hearing whether the law allowed people to give the president a $1 million bribe in exchange for a pardon, a White House attorney up for a major intelligence job said it was a “complicated legal question.”

Gary Lawkowski, who advised President Donald Trump in office and on the campaign trail, faced tough questioning from Democrats during his Wednesday hearing to serve as general counsel to the Office of Director of National Intelligence.

> “You were just the lawyer. But so many times, ‘I was just the lawyer’ kind of becomes the default answer.”

The hearing came as Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., sought to rush Lawkowski’s confirmation to the top intelligence posting before the end of the year, when Democrats take over Congress.

Although Lawkowski drew no hostile questions from Republicans, Democratic senators were concerned about Lawkowski’s role in Trump’s pardon spree, as well as his involvement in controversial executive orders that directed federal law enforcement to crack down on the left and [designate antifa](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/03/antifa-prairieland-protests-terrorism-conspiracy/) as a domestic terror organization.

“We’re looking for judgment here,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “And I understand: You were just the lawyer. But so many times, ‘I was just the lawyer’ kind of becomes the default answer.”

[Related Trump Taps Campaign Lawyer and Pardon Adviser for Top U.S. Intel Agency](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/trump-lawyer-lawkowski-pardons-odni/)

Lawkowski’s current position is deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president. He was little known outside the White House before Trump [nominated](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/trump-lawyer-lawkowski-pardons-odni/) him earlier this month to serve at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, a Cabinet-level department where he would coordinate legal advice for the 18 different agencies making up the intelligence community.

According to a questionnaire, Lawkowski has not held jobs at intelligence agencies before. His prior national security experience involves advising Trump on classified matters over the past two years.

He also has a long-standing relationship with Trump. During Trump’s time out of the White House, he helped provided legal advice to the president’s reelection campaign and defended him from [lawsuits](https://clearinghouse.net/case/48067/)brought by people harmed during the January 6 insurrection.

## Questioning His Record

During the Senate hearing, Warner criticized Trump’s pardons for [January 6 rioters](https://theintercept.com/2025/02/04/jan-6-prosecutions-ed-martin-reparations/) and for crypto mogul [Changpeng Zhao](https://theintercept.com/2025/10/24/trump-pardon-crypto-binance-cz/). The crypto tycoon’s company Binance was involved in a transaction that benefited one of the Trump family’s crypto ventures.

[Related Trump Is Rewriting History to Justify His Sketchy Pardon of a Crypto King](https://theintercept.com/2025/10/24/trump-pardon-crypto-binance-cz/)

Lawkowski suggested that prior reporting in the [New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/08/us/politics/trump-pardons-clemency.html?eafs_enabled=false) had exaggerated his role in the pardon process.

“My main focus was litigation and policy,” he said. “I’m actually not our primary pardon counsel. I have worked on some pardon issues.”

Sen. Angus King, an independent from Maine who caucuses with the Democrats, pressed Lawkowski on whether it would be illegal for someone to walk into the Oval Office and hand the president a $1 million bribe for a pardon.

“That’s OK?” King said.

“Well, bribery itself would be a separate statutory crime. How that would interact with presidential immunity would be a complicated legal question that I think the court kind of reserved in that case,” he said, referring to a [2024 Supreme Court decision](https://theintercept.com/2024/07/01/supreme-court-trump-presidential-immunity/) that granted the president broad immunity from prosecution for official acts.

Another senator zeroed in on Lawkowski’s role in crafting National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, commonly known as [NSPM-7](https://theintercept.com/2026/02/12/pam-bondi-domestic-terror-list-nspm-7/), the executive order directing federal law enforcement agencies to target “antifa” and other [boogeymen of the far right](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/03/antifa-prairieland-protests-terrorism-conspiracy/).

In the written questionnaire, Lawkowski said he was involved in “communications” regarding that order and another that purported to [designate antifa](https://theintercept.com/2025/09/18/trump-antifa-domestic-terrorism/)— the [loose-knit](https://theintercept.com/2025/12/11/fbi-antifa-terrorist-location/) anti-fascist movement — as a domestic [terror group](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/28/trump-antifa-terrorist-websites-free-speech/). He declined to explain further, citing the confidentiality of his legal conversations with the president.

> “There is no basis in law to designate a domestic terrorist organization, but you have claimed the president can just do it.”

“There is no basis in law to designate a domestic terrorist organization, but you have claimed the president can just do it anyways based on some magical constitutional authority,” said Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. “Once he’s operating outside the law, are there any limits to how Donald Trump can persecute Americans?”

“I don’t agree with the premise that the president is acting outside of the law,” Lawkowski said. “Of course, the president is constrained by the limits of the Constitution.”

# IG-Metall Tarifrunde: Kämpfen oder kapitulieren

(Bild: Mahmoud Mahdi Photo, shutterstock )

Warnungen alleine werden wohl nicht reichen – die Arbeitgeber mauern, Beschäftige murren: Was in der aktuellen Tarifrunde auf dem Spiel steht. Eine Analyse.

Aufruhr in den Werken: Nach Ablauf der Friedenspflicht Anfang November und indiskutablen Arbeitgeberangeboten machte die IG Metall den Weg für 24-Stunden-Warnstreiks frei. Eine solche Eskalation gab es erst einmal : 2018.

Zuvor war die dritte Verhandlungsrunde gescheitert , nahezu eine halbe Million Beschäftigte in Warnstreiks getreten und Hunderttausend bei DGB-Kundgebungen auf die Straße gegangen . Bei den Entgelten klaffen die Positionen extrem auseinander: Die IG Metall fordert rund fünf Prozent, die Arbeitgeber bieten 1,3 (tabellenwirksam aber erst nach 20 Monaten).

Gestritten wird somit um die Verteilung der Krisen-, Inflations- und indirekt auch der Aufrüstungslasten.

### Klassenkampf von oben?

Der einstimmige Gewerkschaftsbeschluss kam dennoch überraschen. Denn zunächst hatte die IG Metall bedeutende Zugeständnisse angeboten , jedoch verbindliche Investitionsgarantien gefordert. Lohnverzicht sollte es nur gegen Standortsicherung geben. All dies blieb bisher ohne Erfolg.

Dies könnte auch so bleiben, denn Mercedes schaltete in den Angriffsmodus: Der Konzern stoppte alle Investitionen an deutschen Standorten. Arbeitsdirektorin Britta Seeger kündigte an zu prüfen , welche Standorte sich der Konzern noch leisten könne. Intern würden Standorte in Osteuropa geprüft.

Ein Nachahmereffekt bleibt bisher aus, doch das Vorgehen passt zum Branchenkurs: Schaeffler streicht 3400 Stellen, Volkswagen verhandelt über einen umfassenden Abbau. Die Arbeitgeberseite nutzt die Krise nicht nur zur Rechtfertigung von Einschnitten, sondern um die Kräfteverhältnisse in den Betrieben zu verschieben.

items.articleBody:
One of [the most important things I have learned about life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/10/22/marginalian-18/) is that joy is a choice, an orientation, a practice of bending the mind in the direction of gladness — a choice increasingly countercultural in our age of competitive complaint, and yet all the more urgent precisely because our world gives us so many valid reasons for despair. “Experience of conflict and a load of suffering has taught me that what matters above all is to celebrate joy… Life is wasted when we make it more terrifying, precisely because it is so easy to do so,” the artist René Magritte wrote in [his timeless manifesto for the courage of joy](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/05/31/rene-magritte-enchantment/) in the wake of the second World War of his life. “We’ve all had too much sorrow — now is the time for joy,” Nick Cave sang an epoch later as he contemplated [the paradox of joy](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/09/05/joy/) against the backdrop of unimaginable loss.

Joy is not difficult to find, but it can be difficult to trust — partly because the merchants of pseudo-morality have sold us the dangerous myth that, in an unjust world, despair is an emblem of our solidarity with justice, and partly because in this age of grandiosity, we have forgotten that joy is a plurality of smallnesses: a function of what Hermann Hesse called [“the little joys”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/03/06/hermann-hesse-little-joys-my-belief/) that light up a life with presence.

We need them, these reminders that joy is not a denial of suffering but the fulcrum of our resilience in its midst; that it comes to us not with horns and cymbals but as a distant whisper from the birthplace of the ordinary, not like a bouquet of roses offered with champagne but like the lovely little weed blooming through a crack in the sidewalk of the quotidian. And that is precisely what artist-philosopher [Maira Kalman](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/maira-kalman/) offers in her book [Joy](https://www.amazon.com/Joy-Maira-Kalman/dp/0063447452/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](https://www.worldcat.org/title/1347490011)) — a love letter to the sweet strangeness of life, to its unboastful wonderland of small miracles, to the way it expands and expands and expands the moment we contract the aperture of attention onto a single unit of gladness.

It begins where we must begin:

> Don’t I know
> that you know
> that suffering and sorrow
> envelop our planet
> and our little lives.

And then it goes where we, short-termists of the present, rarely go: into the lives of some of her heroes who lived through times and turmoils far more unimaginable than ours: She paints Alfred Dreyfus sitting in his prison cell on Devil’s Island; she paints the bedroom in which Beethoven, fully deaf, [wrote “Ode to Joy”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/05/17/beethoven-ode-to-joy/); she paints Virginia Woolf and her “surprisingly colorful” sitting room just before she filled her coat pockets with stones and waded into the River Ouse; she paints Kafka under the black hat he wore as a helmet of despair, his hand rested tenderly on his beloved dog.

As if to remind us that we are always in relationship with those whose lives have touched ours, whether living or dead, whether or not we have ever met them, she paints her imaginary conversations with Gertrude Stein, with James Baldwin, with Vladimir Nabokov.

[Dog](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/29/beloved-dog-maira-kalman/) punctuate this love letter to joy, cradled in arms and curled in corners, peeking from the pages with their searching eyes and their uncomplicated sweetness: “Isn’t that the answer to everything,” she writes with an eye to a friend who tends to her four dogs “with unlimited care and love.”

And people, of course, so many people with their strange and soulful faces, each a universe of feeling conjured up with just a few brush strokes.

> What might happen
> if you could leave gloom (pervasive)
> and perils (lurking)
> for just a little bit?
> Where might you go?
> What solace might you find
> if you turned your gaze
> to a thing of beauty.

She reverences trees, “kind and strong and loving,” and a medieval painting of “a saint with a terrific hairdo” at the Met, and a beautiful man with a porkpie hat at the bookstore, and the fig tree in a friend’s backyard, and people singing, and a young man playing Bach on his violin under the cherry tree, and [Pablo Casals](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/12/03/pablo-casals-work-age/) playing Bach on his cello while smoking a pipe.

> And isn’t it true
> we are lost without music?

> Do children not give us our reason?

Page by page of these small reveries — birdsong, a summer breeze, books and libraries, a woman “lost in thought basking in the morning sun with her little dog by her side,” the bowl of fresh berries on a dying friend’s table, the way a garden, any garden, “can fill you with elation,” the way sitting by the ocean, any ocean, is “enough to make your spirits soar,” the way holding a child’s gaze can make you “forget all the sorrows of the world” — you discover that any moment of joy contains “the essence of what it means to be alive.”

> And don’t I know,
> and don’t you know,
> how one sublime instant,
> one sublime,
> fleeting instant,
> changes everything
> and makes the world right?
> Just for an instant.

It isn’t nothing, that instant — this atom of time, this unit of eternity, the only thing we ever have that is ours for the keeping. “Time is a reality confined to the instant and suspended between two voids,” philosopher Gaston Bachelard [wrote](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/01/18/intuition-of-the-instant-gaston-bachelard/). Because [attention is what fills the instant with reality](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/05/10/iain-mcgilchrist-the-matter-with-things/), how we spend our attention is how we spend our lives. Emerging from these painted pages is a beckoning to train our attention on joy in all its variousness, its unassuming abundance, its sacred smallness.

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

items.articleBody:
## Long-Lost Georgia O’Keeffe Painting Found Hidden in a Closet Sells for $4.8M

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/georgia-okeeffe-closet-painting-discovery-christies/)

Georgia O'Keeffe, “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I,” 1930. (Photo: [Christie’s Images Ltd.](https://press.christies.com/long-lost-georgia-okeeffe-painting-recently-discovered-in-an-east-village-closet-to-be-offered-and-exhibited-at-christies-new-york/))

You never know what could be hiding in someone’s closet. Earlier this year, a long-lost [Georgia O’Keeffe](https://mymodernmet.com/georgia-okeeffe-great-american-modern-painter/) painting was discovered in the closet of a woman’s Manhattan apartment, and was recently presented as part of [Christie’s](https://www.christies.com/en) 20th Century Evening Sale in New York.

The 1930 painting, *Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I*, was estimated to be worth between $3 million and $5 million. On Nov. 17, it sold at auction for $4.8 million. It depicts the tan, green, and brown rolling mountains of New Mexico, using O’Keeffe’s signature sweeping curves that bring the viewer’s eye across the landscape. O’Keeffe first visited New Mexico in 1929 and it would continue to inspire her to paint throughout her career.

“This is a wonderful painting, a remarkable story, and extraordinary opportunity for collectors and the general public alike,” said Tylee Abbott, senior specialist and international director of American Art at Christie’s.

The discovery of the painting itself was just as remarkable. The owner of the work, who wished to remain anonymous, had invited her niece to her East Village apartment earlier this year to help go through her belongings. While the niece knew that her aunt was an art collector, she was shocked when the woman casually mentioned that she had an O’Keeffe in her front closet.

After digging through the closet, her niece found an old wooden box tucked behind dozens of coats. Inside was the 10-inch by 24-inch painting, complete with O’Keeffe’s signature on the original backboard. The painting had been a graduation gift to the owner when she earned her master’s degree in the 1960s. It was purchased by her mother for just $3,800 from O’Keeffe’s art dealer in Manhattan.

The painting hung on the wall of her apartment for over 20 years, until the owner grew worried after noticing that a guest was paying a little too much attention to it. She decided to tuck it away in its original box in the closet, where it remained hidden for decades.

Now, after spending decades out of sight, the painting is finally getting to see the light of day. The work was on public display at Christie’s New York, November 7-17, ahead of its appearance at the auction house’s 20th Century Evening Sale.

## A long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting was found in a Manhattan art-collector’s closet, intact in it’s original box.

The original wooden box that held Georgia O'Keeffe's “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” in a Manhattan closet for decades. (Photo: [Christie’s Images Ltd.](https://press.christies.com/long-lost-georgia-okeeffe-painting-recently-discovered-in-an-east-village-closet-to-be-offered-and-exhibited-at-christies-new-york/))

## The 1930 painting titled Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I marks the beginning of O’Keeffe’s artistic fascination with the desert landscape of New Mexico.
