items.articleBody:
This month, fed-up, stressed-out Americans headed to the ballot box and tacked hard to the left, supporting the party that is promising to restore billions of dollars in federal spending and billions of dollars in federal tax revenue. Democrats won in blue states. They won in purple states, such as Georgia, Michigan, Maine, and North Carolina. They flipped seats in Trump-hat-red Nebraska, Indiana, Kentucky, Texas, Iowa, and Montana. Voters in South Carolina sent a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1998; in Mississippi, since 1982.

At the same time, fed-up, stressed-out Americans headed to the ballot box and curved to the right, supporting a bevy of measures to [restrain government spending](https://www.ncsl.org/news/details/landmark-tax-decisions-feature-in-2026-midterm-elections). Some revenue-raising initiatives won; Coloradans created a graduated state income tax, for instance. But in Florida, voters gutted the property-tax system. In Louisiana, they sheltered seniors from taxation. In Arizona, they limited levies on groceries and banned them on vehicle-miles traveled. In progressive California, they turned down a onetime wealth tax on billionaires and made it harder for the state to impose one in the future.

The midterm landslide was another instance of the electorate rejecting incumbents and revolting against the establishment. It was another example of American voters raging against the country’s brutal cost-of-living crisis. It was also a triumph of what I have come to think of as “no take, only throw” politics, a reference to an old Tumblr meme, itself a reference to a common experience among dog people: Fido demands that his human servant throw the ball, but won’t drop it. That’s politics today, more or less. Voters want big-government budgets and small-government taxes. Politicians act like they can give it to them.

cupcakelogic / Tumblr

But you can’t throw without taking unless you have a pocket full of tennis balls, which the United States Treasury, at the moment, does not. Americans can turn the tax code into Swiss cheese and keep levies on middle-class and upper-middle-class families low. They can spend trillions on initiatives to bolster the spending power of working households. They cannot do both of those things while keeping politically and societally destabilizing inflation in check.

Inflation hasn’t been [in check](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FPCPITOTLZGUSA) since the arrival of the coronavirus pandemic. Prices are increasing nearly [twice as fast](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm) as the Federal Reserve wants them to, and the costs of many essential goods and services are spiking even faster. Gas prices shot up nearly 60 percent from January to May. Employer-sponsored insurance premiums jumped 5 percent this year and are expected to increase another 8 percent to 11 percent next year. (The premiums on marketplace plans will rise as much as 13 percent come 2027.) The price of electricity has risen 11 percent year over year in Idaho, 14 percent in Maine, and 23 percent in Hawaii. The price of home insurance is up 9 percent around the country. Even coffee costs 41 percent more than it did two years ago, if you buy ground beans to brew at home.

These isolated bumps add up, compound, and bleed families dry. If prices had increased at the central bank’s target rate since Donald Trump was reelected, the typical middle-class family would have $1,800 more in its bank account than it does right now—cash to spend on Christmas presents or invest in a retirement fund. If inflation had been subdued since Joe Biden’s election, that same family would have saved more than $36,000 on everyday expenses. That’s enough to buy a used car. It’s a big chunk of a down payment on a typical apartment.

The post-COVID bout of inflation is not in and of itself responsible for the country’s cost-of-living crisis, which has been decades in the making. Land-use restrictions have throttled the housing supply, pushing up prices in dense cities and remote towns. A surfeit of subsidies, lack of cost controls, and consolidation in the health-care market has spurred insurers to jack up the price of coverage.

Still, not only has Washington failed to fix the housing shortage and rationalize the health-care system; it has stoked price increases across the whole economy. This year, it is spending $2 trillion more than it is receiving in revenue, a budget deficit equivalent to 6.2 percent of GDP. That’s almost as big a stimulus as the government was running in 2012, during the miserable jobless recovery from the Great Recession. Back then, the country desperately needed the deficit spending: The unemployment rate was four percentage points higher and the GDP growth rate markedly lower. Now Washington’s largesse is pumping up prices, forcing up interest rates, and making the rich richer. Indeed, Trump’s signature tax bill slashed federal tax revenue by $460 billion this year alone, with much of the relief going to wealthy households and wealthy corporations. (I should be fair: He did soak up some of the red ink by defunding HIV-prevention programs and taking food stamps away from kids.)

On top of that, Trump has engaged in a foolish trade war, driving up the cost of imported goods. He has engaged in a foolish war on immigration, shrinking the labor pool and increasing the cost of child care and construction. He has engaged in a foolish *actual* war, pushing up the cost of oil and gas. He has also promoted the AI build-out, which has pumped up borrowing costs and utility bills.

Democrats have regained power promising to undo Trump’s policies, in particular his cuts to Medicaid, SNAP, and health-insurance subsidies. It’s a priority for affordability reasons and moral reasons as well. The SNAP cuts are already stoking widespread food insecurity in Arizona, Florida, Georgia, and Nevada, among other states. The Medicaid-coverage losses are expected to spur dozens of safety-net hospitals to close and are projected to cause 51,000 [unnecessary deaths](https://ysph.yale.edu/news-article/proposed-federal-budget-could-lead-to-over-51000-preventable-deaths-researchers-warn-in-letter-to-senate-leaders/). If Democrats regain the White House, they want to do a lot more: universal child care, prescription-drug-price controls, lowering the [Medicare-eligibility](https://x.com/SenatorBaldwin/status/2121994242260119963) age, maybe even Medicare for All.

These policies come with costs: $90 billion a year for restoring Medicaid, $20 billion for SNAP, $35 billion for the Obamacare subsidies. To cover them, Democrats are planning on reversing Trump’s tax cuts for rich families and corporations. Yet they are torn on whether and how to pay for new proposals going forward. (Lowering the Medicare-eligibility age to 60 would cost [something like](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/57918) $25 billion annually; universal child care, $80 billion; single-payer health care, $2 trillion, offset by the evaporation of private-insurance premiums.) They are also torn on whether to make winnowing the deficit a goal unto itself. In an interview with [The Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/politics/democrats-torn-over-floating-new-taxes-to-cover-multitrillion-dollar-agenda-0d3293fa)[,](https://www.wsj.com/politics/democrats-torn-over-floating-new-taxes-to-cover-multitrillion-dollar-agenda-0d3293fa)Brian Schatz, a Democratic senator from Hawaii, objected to the idea that Democrats should have to worry about the budget when Republicans didn’t: “I don’t think we should play this game where the things we want have to be paid for and the things they want can be put on a credit card.”

On the revenue side, Democrats have vowed not to raise taxes on the 97 percent of American households earning less than $400,000 a year. (Trump’s tax cuts have made that vow a lot more expensive.) Democrats are considering further reducing the burden on working-class and middle-income households by expanding the earned-income and child tax credits. They’re also joining in the American public’s rollicking tax revolt, pushing carve-outs for seniors, tipped workers, hourly workers, police officers, public-school teachers, and homeowners.

Democrats are promising a whole lot of throw and not asking for a lot of take, in other words. This kind of budgetary posture would have worked when the economy was limping out of the global financial crisis in 2012, or when it screeched to a halt in 2020 because of COVID. It doesn’t really work now that deficits are contributing to excess inflation—as voters let Joe Biden and Kamala Harris know in 2024, and as they informed [132 Republican incumbents](https://www.multistate.us/elections/primary-losses) earlier this month.

Still, Democrats are not totally out of tennis balls. Ending the Iran war, easing immigration restrictions, and eliminating tariffs would blunt price increases or even *lower* prices without running up the debt, as would requiring the AI hyperscalers to pay for their own water and electricity and land, as would implementing cost controls for utilities, as would [continuing to fast-track](https://bipartisanpolicy.org/issue-brief/inside-the-deal-whats-in-the-final-21st-century-road-to-housing-act/) homebuilding in high-priced communities, as would breaking up corporate monopolies, as would having Washington negotiate prescription-drug prices for the American consumer market. (Heck, why not have it set payment rates for medical procedures and doctor visits too?) Getting the IRS to collect the taxes it is statutorily owed would reduce the deficit without harming the 97 percent. Pulling shut loopholes for and raising marginal tax rates on millionaires and billionaires would do the same.

In time, borrowing costs would ease, inflation would cool down, and the affordability crisis would let up, as Americans so desperately want. Maybe then we could finally have the conversation about how important *drop it* is to *fetch*.

items.articleBody:
NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 24 mission launched Saturday, April 11, 2026, aboard the company’s Cygnus XL spacecraft atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will deliver approximately 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station.

NASA, Northrop Grumman, and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 10:47 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, for the next launch delivering science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. The agency also will hold a prelaunch media teleconference on Monday, Nov. 23.

Filled with approximately 11,000 pounds of cargo, the Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, will launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25.

After arriving at the International Space Station, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, who are living and working aboard the space station, will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture the Cygnus XL on Tuesday, Dec. 1. Ground controllers then will install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading.

NASA’s live launch and docking coverage will stream through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online:

[https://www.nasa.gov/live](https://www.nasa.gov/live)

Highlights of space station research and technology demonstrations being delivered aboard this Cygnus XL spacecraft include experiments to improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, predict cancer spread, and advance treatments for muscle loss, as well as improve radiation sensing and advance food production for future long-duration missions.

The spacecraft is scheduled to remain at the orbiting laboratory until May 2027, then depart with several thousand pounds of disposal items and other unneeded cargo, burning up harmlessly during re-entry.

Northrop Grumman named the spacecraft the S.S. James “Jim” A. Lovell in honor of the former NASA astronaut. Lovell flew four missions, including Gemini VII, Gemini XII, Apollo 8, and the Apollo 13 mission around the Moon.

**Monday, Nov. 23**

12 p.m.: Prelaunch teleconference will stream on NASA’s [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@NASAgovVideo/streams) channel with the following participants:

- Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager, NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program
- Jennifer Buchli, chief scientist, NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program
- Dave Schiller, vice president, civil space and sciences, Northrop Grumman
- Jared Metter, director, flight reliability, SpaceX

To participate in the teleconference, media must contact the NASA Johnson Space Center newsroom for call details by 11 a.m., Nov. 23, at: jsccommu@mail.nasa.gov or 281-483-5111. To ask questions, media must dial in no later than 10 minutes before the start of the call. The agency’s [media credentialing policy](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/nasa-agencywide-media-accreditation-policy/) is available online.

Additional prelaunch updates will be available on NASA’s space station [blog](http://nasa.gov/blogs/spacestation).

**Sunday, Nov. 29**

10:25 a.m.: Launch coverage begins

10:47 a.m.: Launch

**Tuesday, Dec. 1**

1:10 a.m.: Arrival coverage begins

2:35 a.m.: Capture

**NASA website launch coverage**

Launch day coverage of the mission will be available on the NASA [website](https://www.nasa.gov/live/). Coverage will include live streaming and blog updates beginning no earlier than 10 a.m. on Nov. 29, as the countdown milestones occur. On-demand streaming video on NASA+ and photos of the launch will be available shortly after liftoff. For questions about countdown coverage, contact the NASA Kennedy Space Center newsroom at 321-867-2468. Follow countdown coverage on our International Space Station blog for updates.

**Attend launch virtually**

Members of the public can [register](https://www.eventbrite.com/e/nasas-northrop-grumman-crs-25-launch-registration-2003421595924?aff=oddtdtcreator) to attend this launch virtually. NASA’s virtual guest program for this mission also includes curated launch resources, notifications about related opportunities or changes, and a stamp for the NASA virtual guest passport following launch.

**Watch, engage on social media**

Let people know you’re watching the mission on X, Facebook, and Instagram by following and tagging these accounts:

items.feedText:

items.articleBody:
Alderperson Pat Dowell, center, chair of the Finance Committee, speaks to reporters following a Chicago City Council meeting on Wednesday. Dowell called for an outside review of the city’s finances. Victor Hilitski/WTTW News

The debate over Chicago’s financial struggles — out in the open as never before — took a new turn on Wednesday as the City Council added to the scrutiny.

The City Council voted 45-5 in a special meeting to give a leading alderperson the authority to hire an outside firm to independently review Chicago’s finances.

It’s unclear if an audit would be complete in time for the City Council to consider its findings before the Dec. 29 deadline mandated by state law to pass a 2027 budget, in what likely will be contentious negotiations with Mayor Brandon Johnson. Later in the day came another sign of distress: S&P Global put the city [on credit watch with a warning](https://news.wttw.com/sites/default/files/article/file-attachments/RatingsDirect_ResearchUpdate_ChicagoGORatingAndSalesTaxSecuritizationCorp.%2CILDebtRatingPlacedOnCreditWatchNegative_3663295_Nov-18-2026.pdf) that the budget wrangling is likely to result in a credit downgrade within 90 days.

The intense council debate over the city’s financial future comes in the wake of a [package of stories](https://news.wttw.com/2026/11/16/chicago-debt-burden-public-health-safety) published Monday by WTTW News and ProPublica that examined how a $55 billion debt burden, decades in the making, was hampering efforts to service Chicagoans and how the Johnson administration was turning to more borrowing to plug holes, such as large police settlements.

Alderperson Pat Dowell had called for the outside review after former Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch abruptly resigned Friday over what she described as a political environment that forced her to downplay certain facts about the city’s financial situation. Gabrysch argued that her integrity would be compromised if she stayed on.

Just as Gabrysch had once been a trusted part of Johnson’s team, Dowell was once thought to be a mayoral ally. Johnson tapped Dowell, who endorsed him during the 2023 mayoral election, to lead the City Council’s Finance Committee soon after he took office.

But since then Dowell has proven to be a thorn in the mayor’s side, refusing last year to support his proposal to impose a $25 per month per employee tax on most firms that have more than 125 employees and hike the city’s personal property lease tax. (Johnson continues to push for that idea.)

The ordinance gives Dowell the authority to spend whatever is necessary “to determine whether any material or intentional misstatements of the city’s financial condition to investors, the City Council and the public have been made in any public document, presentation, offering or financial reporting within the prior three years.”

The firm, or firms, hired to conduct the review will have access to all city documents and records, and all city officials must cooperate with the probe, according to the ordinance.

“We must ensure that our math is correct,” Dowell said, vowing to act quickly. “The discrepancies over the past few weeks have been particularly disturbing to me. As my mother used to say, where there’s smoke, there’s fire.”

Johnson said he welcomed the review and will not veto the ordinance.

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson presides over a special City Council meeting on Wednesday. Victor Hilitski/WTTW News

Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said he wasn’t certain an audit was warranted while acknowledging its importance in another way. He noted that the audit vote coupled with the inability of the council and the mayor to agree on a budget plan already may have done damage with credit rating agencies.

“The way cities make their budgets matter,” Marlowe said. “It matters that for the third year in a row that there are disagreements over basic facts.”

In short, Marlowe said, “Investors don’t like uncertainty, and this is creating a lot of uncertainty.”

Alderperson Matt Martin said Wednesday that the analysis by ProPublica and WTTW was “sobering.” He is questioning some of Johnson’s borrowing strategies.

Over the years, Chicago alderpersons have generally acquiesced to mayoral directives on finances. But that has changed under Johnson, in part due to his preference for a head tax but also because of the growing realization that the city’s finances have been undermined [by a series of decisions from previous mayors](https://news.wttw.com/2026/11/16/three-financial-sins-left-chicago-55-billion-debt-and-counting).

Similarly, top administration officials generally choose to leave City Hall either quietly or with words of praise for the current mayor. That’s not how Gabrysch handled her exit.

The statement she released Friday made it clear she had severe doubts about the way Johnson was portraying the city’s debt problem. And she reiterated those concerns in a [commentary in the Chicago Tribune](https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/11/15/opinion-chicago-cfo-financial-truth-ashlee-gabrysch/) over the weekend that also laid out her suggestions for how the city can more responsibly handle its budgeting (for example, “Don’t borrow to pay everyday bills, even if we’ve done so in the past”).

Then, in a brief [interview with the Chicago Sun-Times](https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/11/16/outside-audit-city-hall-finances-cfo-resignation-ashlee-gabrysch) on Monday, she said she supported calls for a financial audit.

“If this makes it easier for residents to see that Chicago actually is in a fairly dire fiscal situation where hard decisions … and shared sacrifices have to be made, that can be helpful,” Gabrysch said. “Shining some light on the city’s finances — whether or not they discover wrongdoing, but rather showing the nuances of how dire some things have become — could be worthwhile.”

Chicago’s credit rating has been plummeting, adding to the cost of borrowing and leaving the city just two or three levels above junk status among leading Wall Street rating agencies. Gabrysch had been hired just three months ago from Fitch Ratings, with an eye toward shoring up the city’s reputation.

S&P Global, one of a handful of major ratings agencies, released a statement on Wednesday about its “CreditWatch” for Chicago. It cited the intense battle over the budget and an increased likelihood that “the city will resort to significant one-time measures to balance the fiscal 2027 budget.”

That means analysts see at least a 1-in-2 chance of issuing a rating cut in the next three months.

Johnson’s administration has sought to portray Gabrysch as someone who fell short in her duties and mismanaged a major transfer of funds — characterizations she has disputed.

### Read More

[Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.](https://www.propublica.org/article/chicago-debt-burden-public-health-safety)

[Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting](https://www.propublica.org/article/chicago-debt-crisis-pensions-parking-meters-police-misconduct)

The mayor has dismissed the conflict that led to Gabrysch’s resignation as a “technical dispute.” When he unveiled his 2027 budget, Johnson and administration officials said 76% of the budget gap would be closed with “structural fixes” — long-term or permanent solutions — that would bring expenses in line with revenues. That could help the city avoid another credit downgrade.

But Gabrysch told the City Council on Oct. 26 that the decision to borrow $481 million to cover the cost of resolving police misconduct lawsuits in 2027 and 2028 changed that calculation, reducing the amount the gap closed with revenue the city can count on in future years to just 56%.

As recently as September, Johnson told reporters the city would not borrow to cover those costs.

If the City Council approves Johnson’s proposal to borrow $481 million, the city’s massive debt burden — which now tops $55 billion — is set to grow for the second straight year to cover the cost of running the city, a sign of financial trouble.

That distress, Johnson has argued, is largely due to the decisions of previous administrations. “It’s no secret: Our city finds itself in a precarious financial situation due to decades of mismanagement,” he said Tuesday.

items.title: Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This
items.subtitle: WIRED is tallying up how many times Nvidia’s interim CEO has assured everyone that the company has everything under control.
items.feedText: Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era. Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO Colette Kress has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ‘24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.” By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it:
items.articleBody:
# Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This

Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era.

Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO Colette Kress has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’s public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce . And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ‘24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.”

Tuesday’s earnings call:

“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”

Wednesday’s all-hands meeting:

“Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we've got this.”

Wednesday’s all-hands meeting, again:

Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together.

“It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song… Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.”

Kress’s new catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got…what?)

Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and said, “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment.

Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’s mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase , adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post.

And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot.

Which means that Kress, for the moment, has … got this.

Paresh Dave contributed to this article.

items.articleBody:
# Did Hakeem Jeffries say Jerusalem is '6th borough' of NYC?

About this rating

On Nov. 18, Democrats nominated New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker of the House, pushing him closer to leading the Democratic majority and becoming the first Black lawmaker to hold the position.

Amid the closed-door vote — which he won with an overwhelming 251-11 majority — people claimed Jeffries once said during a speech at an American Israel Public Affairs Committee event that Jerusalem is the "sixth borough" of New York City. AIPAC is a pro-Israel lobby group.

For example, one X user wrote ( archived ): " Hakeem Jeffries says in a past speech at AIPAC that Jerusalem is the 'sixth borough' of New York City and says he visits there 'to catch up with my constituents.'"

Jeffries has reportedly received upward of $1.74 million from AIPAC over the years. Recent polls show that voters, particularly younger constituents , increasingly oppose U.S. support for Israel amid its war on Gaza, which the U.N. has declared a genocide .

Clips purportedly showing Jeffries producing the quote in question spread on TikTok , Bluesky and Reddit , together amassing millions of views.

The footage is authentic, meaning not the product of an artificial intelligence tool or digital fakery. Jeffries did say the comment about Jerusalem being a borough of New York City while speaking at an AIPAC conference in March 2020. Therefore, the quote has been correctly attributed to him.

As of this writing, AIPAC's official YouTube account still publicly lists the video , from which the clips above originate ( archived ). While being interviewed, Jeffries said (at minute 2:30 ):

> Someone said to me, they said, "Hakeem, you're going to Israel a fifth time?" I said listen, I'm from New York City. And back home, back home in New York City, we consider Jerusalem to be the sixth borough. And so I'm just trying to catch up with my constituents.

It is unclear whether his comments were meant to be taken seriously. The interviewer and members of the audience can be heard laughing in response to his remark.

Snopes contacted Jeffries' office seeking comment. We will update this article if we receive a response.

Although a petition calling for House Democrats to choose a different speaker gained more than 1.2 million signatures, Jeffries ran unopposed.

items.articleBody:
Enormous trees dominate dreamlike wooded landscapes in the mixed-media paintings of [Sylvain Lefebvre](https://www.instagram.com/sylvainlefebvre_artist/). A spectral form with dense, gnarly branches shelters a lounging woman in “The Quercus Corallium,” and a table alive with conversation nests beneath the canopy in “A Debat at Tea Time.”

The French artist’s *Journeys Into the Unseen Forest* at [Rebecca Hossack Art Gallery](https://www.rebeccahossack.com/) comprises a series of almost fairytale-like tableaux. Collaged, hand-marbled papers beneath the delicate layers of oil paint represent the barely visible or unknown. And trees group closely in the background darken in the distance, while diminutive figures climb around and relax at the base of monumental trunks.

“The Polyphane Pachidermus” (2026), oil, acrylic, and ink on hand-painted marbled paper, on canvas, 120 x 160 centimeters

Summer 2026 marked France’s [hottest ever documented](https://apnews.com/article/france-climate-hottest-summer-fires-f8cb2b86f839ccab7ae06676ab29b99a) since records began, during which rainfall was low and unprecedented wildfires raged. Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, where the effects of the climate crisis are dramatic and impossible to ignore. In *Journeys Into the Unseen Forest,* Lefebvre delves into an imaginary realm where humans coexist harmoniously with flora and fauna, and old-growth sentinels harbor a wide range of life.

The artist says, “I wanted to put myself in the place of a forest and its trees by asking myself the following question: How is it that when we look at nature, whatever form it takes, it always appears balanced, while the trees that make it up can grow in such unbalanced ways… twisted, diagonally or horizontally, struggling to find their way towards the light?”

In “The Quercus Corallium,” a white tree glows like a sacred spirit, and in “The Polyphane Pachidermus,” one can imagine the canopy extending forever into the blue distance. “In the unseen forest, [Lefebvre] discovers species of trees that have never been seen before,” the gallery says. “They are completely plausible species that may exist somewhere in the few corners of the world that have not yet been discovered. Perhaps they are trees of the future.”

*Journey Into the Unseen Forest* continues through December 23 in London. See more on Lefebvre’s [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/sylvainlefebvre_artist/).

items.feedText: Magerit's Laniakea Pro combines five digital synthesis engines, five sound-shaping algorithms and three reverbs in an eight-voice instrument that operates as either a 20HP Eurorack module or a battery-powered standalone synthesizer.… Read More Magerit Introduces Laniakea Pro Eight-Voice Synthesizer For Eurorack & Standalone Use
items.articleBody:
# Magerit Introduces Laniakea Pro Eight-Voice Synthesizer For Eurorack & Standalone Use

Magerit has introduced Laniakea Pro , an eight-voice digital synthesizer that can operate as a 20HP Eurorack module or as a portable standalone instrument using an optional battery-powered enclosure.

The new instrument is a substantial redesign of the original Laniakea, with five synthesis engines, five sound-shaping algorithms and three reverb types.

The synthesis engines include wavetable, virtual analog and chiptune, two-operator FM, Infinite Keys and Karplus-Strong physical modeling. The wavetable engine uses a 16 × 16 matrix of interpolated waves and supports up to 16 user-loaded wavetables. Infinite Keys models six keyboard instruments, including piano and church organ, with sustained notes that can ring indefinitely.

The instrument provides up to eight voices of polyphony over MIDI, with individual low-pass gates for each voice. Its CLUSTER and CHORD functions provide additional ways to organize notes, while DENSITY and LIFE introduce granular behavior.

Features:

- Five synthesis engines: Wavetable, Analog & Chiptune, FM, Infinite Keys and Strings.
- Five sound-shaping algorithms: Multifilter, Waveshaper, Modal Resonator, Lo-Fi and Tape Delay.
- Three reverbs: Hall, FDN and Shimmer, with a FREEZE function.
- SPACE! modulation macro with independently adjustable modulation depths and an internal attack-decay envelope.
- Up to eight-voice MIDI polyphony, with one low-pass gate per voice.
- 35 chords, 35 scales, quantization and custom chord and scale configuration.
- Eleven dedicated parameter CV inputs, plus V/OCT, EXCITE and assignable CV inputs.
- USB-C connectivity for 48 kHz audio and MIDI, without requiring additional drivers.
- Free companion application and VST3/AU plugins for Windows, macOS and Linux, with 128 factory presets.
Pricing & Availability:

Magerit Laniakea Pro is available directly from Magerit . The module-only version costs €379, the module and battery-powered enclosure bundle costs €469, and the enclosure alone is €149. The companion software and plugins are free downloads.

items.articleBody:
# Störung am Nürnberger Hauptbahnhof behoben

Eine Stellwerksstörung hat am Abend den Nürnberger Hauptbahnhof stundenlang lahmgelegt und den Nah- und Fernverkehr weiträumig zum Erliegen gebracht. Erst nach 20.00 Uhr konnte die Bahn Entwarnung geben. "Die Störung in Nürnberg ist behoben, der Zugverkehr läuft wieder an", sagte ein Sprecher. Züge könnten die Strecken im Raum Nürnberg wieder regulär befahren. Während sich der Verkehr normalisiere, sei allerdings weiter mit Verspätungen und einzelnen Ausfällen zu rechnen, erklärte er.

## Ursache der Störung noch unklar

Grund für den stundenlangen Stillstand war nach den neuesten Angaben ein Ausfall der Kommunikationsanlage des Stellwerks Nürnberg Hauptbahnhof. Die genaue Ursache für den Ausfall werde derzeit ermittelt, hieß es weiter. Als Erstes hatte die Bahn bereits eine Stellwerksstörung als Grund für den Stillstand angegeben, dann zeitweise eine lokale Störung des Bahnfunksystems GSM-R .

Wegen der Störung waren keine Zugfahrten von und nach Nürnberg Hauptbahnhof möglich. Sicherheitshalber seien alle Züge an Bahnhöfen zurückgehalten worden, hieß es. Betroffen waren sämtliche Züge und S-Bahnen, auch der Fernverkehr. Wie viele Züge und wie viele Fahrgäste davon in Bayern und darüber hinaus betroffen waren, war am Abend zunächst unklar.

## Bahn entschuldigt sich

Nürnberg ist einer der zentralen Bahn-Knotenpunkte in Bayern und liegt unter anderem auf der für den Fernverkehr wichtigen Achse Berlin - München.

Die Bahn bat nach Ende der Störung alle Fahrgäste, sich vor Reiseantritt im Internet unter bahn.de oder über den DB-Navigator zu informieren. "Die DB unterstützt die Reisenden am Nürnberger Hauptbahnhof mit zusätzlichen Servicekräften", sagte der Sprecher. "Wir bedauern die entstandenen Unannehmlichkeiten und bitten unsere Reisenden um Entschuldigung."

Zusätzlich verschärft wurde die Lage wegen einer Streckensperrung: Der Abschnitt zwischen Nürnberg und Ansbach war gesperrt, wie es bei der Bahn hieß. Hier wurde als Grund eine Reparatur an der Oberleitung genannt.

## Was ist das Bahnfunksystem GSM-R?

GSM-R steht für "Global System for Mobile Communications - Railway". "Das GSM-R Mobilfunknetz ersetzt nahezu alle analogen Funksysteme der Deutschen Bahn AG", heißt es auf der Webseite der DB InfraGo, der Betreiberin der Infrastruktur der Deutschen Bahn. Demnach bietet es Vorteile wie etwa hohe Sicherheit in der betrieblichen Kommunikation, die Möglichkeit spezieller Gruppenanrufe und die Option zur gezielten Kontaktaufnahme mit den Fahrdienstleitern.

Im Juni hatte eine deutschlandweite Störung des Bahnfunksystems bundesweit für rund zwei Stunden Stillstand gesorgt.

items.articleBody:
# The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning

The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning October 27, 2026

Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni, Google Research

We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs.

Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.

While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting , a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.

Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a sleep framework in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous periodic lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning.

## Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases

Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information.

Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states:

- Active (wake) phase : The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components.
- Sleep phase : The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement.
While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged.

## Key components of the sleep process

The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming.

### 1. Memory consolidation

In the human brain, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) slow-wave sleep consolidates fragile memories into long-term structures via abstraction and distillation. Our proposed sleep framework mirrors this natural phenomenon through two key technical mechanisms:

- Parameter expansion & continuum memory hierarchy: To prevent catastrophic forgetting, the model dynamically scales its capacity during sleep. Using a Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Hope architecture , newly unlocked, low-rank experts are integrated into stable, lower-frequency memory blocks to store incoming knowledge without disrupting older parameters.
- Knowledge seeding (upward distillation): Fragile short-term memories stored in high-frequency layers (e.g., in-context memory) are transferred into the newly expanded long-term parameters. This is achieved through Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) combined with reinforcement learning (RL)-based imitation learning : On-policy distillation: The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences.
- Learning to imitate (LTI): The student model is rewarded based on semantic and absolute similarity ( Levenshtein distance ) when completing prefixes of teacher-generated text.
- Synaptic pruning: Once the memory consolidation into lower-frequency modules is complete, the high-frequency temporary parameters are reset, freeing up capacity for future active sessions.
Overview of our sleep framework: Input streams from the active phase are stored in short-term memory before entering the sleep cycle, which bifurcates into Consolidation (transferring fragile short-term tokens into expanded long-term parametric memory using low-rank structures and MoE) and Dreaming (autonomous self-improvement via synthetic routing with random experts and RL refinement).

### 2. Dreaming for self-improvement

During REM sleep , the human brain actively simulates scenarios, consolidates emotional/semantic connections, and explores novel neural pathways. Mirroring this, during the “dreaming stage”, the sleep framework implements an autonomous self-improvement loop:

- Random expert selection: During synthetic data generation, the MoE router randomly activates non-standard experts. This forces the model to mix disparate domains of knowledge and uncover latent patterns.
- Curated rehearsal: The model generates synthetic training samples ("dreams") and filters them using gradient-based data selection to prioritize samples with the highest potential to boost overall model capability.
- RL refinement: The model performs supervised fine-tuning on top-rated dream samples and evaluates whether the generation improves performance on downstream tasks.
## Theoretical foundations

Beyond the empirical results, our sleep paradigm is grounded in a theory that clarifies why its two stages (memory consolidation and dreaming) can support continual learning without simply trading new knowledge for old capabilities.

For memory consolidation, the analysis shows that knowledge seeding can be understood as a structured, low-rank compression problem. The model is not asked to copy every detail of its short-term traces into its parameters. Instead, it identifies a compact set of directions that best preserve both the model’s own on-policy behavior and the semantic qualities rewarded by the learning objective.

This perspective explains the complementary roles of the two signals: on-policy distillation aligns consolidation with the trajectories the model will actually produce at inference time, reducing the mismatch that can arise when training only on teacher-generated distributions; meanwhile, the semantic reward changes what is worth retaining, prioritizing directions that preserve meaning and task-relevant behavior rather than merely matching token probabilities. Parameter expansion then provides the capacity needed to write these selected memories without overwriting previously consolidated knowledge.

For dreaming, the theory characterizes random expert activation and reward-based sample selection as mechanisms for improving the geometry of learning. Injecting different MoEs broadens the set of gradient directions explored during synthetic generation, exposing the model to a richer collection of updates than those induced by its ordinary wake-time data alone. Gradient-based filtering then emphasizes the synthetic experiences that carry the most useful learning signal, strengthening informative directions while preserving the structure of the underlying gradient space.

Together, these steps yield a more balanced optimization landscape: learning is less dominated by a small number of directions, gradients are better conditioned, and the model can make more stable progress when refining its capabilities. In this view, dreaming is not simply self-generated data augmentation; it is a deliberate process for diversifying, selecting, and consolidating the updates through which the model improves itself.

Comparative performance of our sleep framework against baseline approaches (such as in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning) across major evaluation axes, including Class-Incremental Learning, continual translation, long-context scaling up to 10M tokens, factual knowledge incorporation, and mathematical reasoning.

For continual translation , in unseen languages, such as Manchu and Kalamang, the sleep framework maintained a near-zero performance drop in multi-stage evaluations, whereas standard baselines like ICL, Cartridges , and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) suffered severe catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning.

In long-context understanding on the BABILong benchmark, our sleep method demonstrated near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens, outperforming strong baselines like GPT-4 , and Titans by using sleep-time consolidation to compress long-context information directly into parametric memory.

For factual knowledge incorporation evaluated on SQuAD and continued pre-training (CPT), our sleep method achieved 48.9% on single-task and 46.2% on CPT evaluations, outperforming baseline methods including the base model, SFT, and Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL) by successfully integrating new factual information without degrading existing model representations.

Finally, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks including AIME 24/25 and HMMT 25 , sleep-enhanced base-model achieved accuracy scores of 79.2%, 69.0%, and 46.1%, respectively. This outperformed baselines like SFT, group relative policy optimization (GRPO), and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), showing that pairing memory consolidation with imitation learning drives superior reasoning performance.

## Conclusion

Our sleep paradigm provides a path toward autonomous, continually learning AI systems. By moving beyond static pre-training and fragile context windows, alternating between active learning and offline rest empowers LLMs to retain short-term memories, abstract new skills into long-term parameter structures, and continuously self-improve without catastrophic forgetting.

## Acknowledgements

This research was conducted by Ali Behrouz (Google and Cornell University), Farnoosh Hashemi (Cornell University), Adel Javanmard (Google and University of Southern California), and Vahab Mirrokni. We thank Yuan Deng and Corinna Cortes for reviewing the work and their valuable suggestions. We also thank Mark Simborg, Kimberly Schwede, and Tim Herrmann for their help in crafting this blog post.

# The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning

The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning October 27, 2026

We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs.

Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.

While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting , a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.

items.articleBody:
President Donald Trump falsely claimed that former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden “did nothing” in terms of funding for historically Black colleges and universities that Trump said he “saved” from bankruptcy.

During his first presidential term, Trump signed a bipartisan bill in late 2019 that made mandatory federal funding for HBCUs permanent. That was after the funding briefly lapsed earlier that year amid negotiations in Congress.

But HBCUs also received that same mandatory funding each year under Obama and Biden, and Obama and Biden also authorized additional money for HBCUs during their presidencies. The mandatory money is a fraction of all federal funding for HBCUs.

Trump made those and other claims about HBCUs in an [interview](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-interview-stephen-a-smith-online-show-november-12-2026/) with sports media personality Stephen A. Smith that aired Nov. 12. Smith is an [alumnus](https://www.wssu.edu/about/news/articles/2025/09/wssu-alumnus-stephen-a-smith-to-be-inducted-into-national-black-college-alumni-hall-of-fame.html) of Winston-Salem State University in North Carolina, one of about 100 HBCUs [recognized](https://nces.ed.gov/COLLEGENAVIGATOR/?s=all&sp=4&pg=6) by the Department of Education, and he is [an ambassador](https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/stephen-smith-makes-money-move-045839964.html) for the HBCU Week Foundation. About 289,000 students were attending HBCUs as of 2022, [according to](https://nces.ed.gov/fastfacts/display.asp?id=667) the National Center for Education Statistics.

Trump was talking about what he has done for “the Black community” when he said, “I saved the historically Black colleges and universities. They were out of business.” When Smith brought up the fact that HBCUs also received federal funding during the Obama and Biden administrations, Trump said, “They were going bankrupt during my administration. The money that they gave was stolen and it didn’t fund. They were going bankrupt.”

The president added later: “I got them financed, and I got them more than they wanted. Barack Obama did nothing for it, and Biden did nothing for it.”

Trump has been [claiming](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2020/01/23/trumps-claim-about-saving-hbcus-was-false-his-administration-has-largely-backed) to have “saved” HBCUs since his 2020 presidential campaign. But his analysis is a combination of false, misleading and exaggerated claims, and the White House did not provide an explanation for them when we asked. We also don’t know what Trump meant when he said funding from Obama and Biden “was stolen.”

## What Trump Did

Trump later said that he got “10-year financing” for HBCUs, an apparent reference to the Fostering Undergraduate Talent by Unlocking Resources for Education Act, or [FUTURE Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/5363), which he signed in December 2019.

Among other things, the legislation, which [passed](https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/5363/all-actions) with bipartisan support, amended Title III of the 1965 Higher Education Act to [provide](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R46400) permanent mandatory grant funding for HBCUs and other minority-serving institutions. The bill made $255 million available in total each year, and about $85 million of it was specifically for HBCUs, [according](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/nbcblk/congress-finalizes-bill-restoring-funding-black-colleges-n1099676) [to](https://apnews.com/article/c4834e48841d97c5a93312b1bf75302a) breakdowns of the funding. The law [says](https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/5363/text) the funding is available for “fiscal year 2020 and each fiscal year thereafter” – not just for 10 years.

But the FUTURE Act reinstated annual funding that was first [approved](https://www.congress.gov/bill/110th-congress/house-bill/2669) in 2007 by Congress and then President George W. Bush. The authority to grant that funding was [extended](https://www.congress.gov/bill/111th-congress/house-bill/4872/text/statute?format=txt) through fiscal year 2019, when Obama signed a 2010 healthcare and education bill. The funding then [lapsed](https://www.insidehighered.com/quicktakes/2019/10/15/hbcus-plan-cuts-after-congress-misses-funding-deadline) in 2019, when Congress initially could not agree on an extension before the Sept. 30 deadline.

The compromise legislation that was enacted under Trump was negotiated for months by a bipartisan group of lawmakers. While one Republican involved in the negotiations gave Trump [some credit](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2020/08/31/some-hbcus-bristle-being-held-sign-trumps-concern-race) for the legislation becoming law, some Democrats said he played a minor role, if any.

Students walk past a building on the campus of Howard University in Washington, D.C., in August 2024. Photo by Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images.

It’s true that some HBCUs were preparing to make staff and program cuts if the funding was not renewed, [according to](https://www.insidehighered.com/sites/default/files/media/Post-Deadline%20FUTURE%20Act%20-TMCF.pdf) a letter sent to Congress in October 2019 by [Harry L. Williams](https://tmcf.org/wp-content/uploads/Dr.-Harry-L.-Williams-1.pdf), president and CEO of the Thurgood Marshall College Fund, a nonprofit organization that represents dozens of HBCUs. But it’s an exaggeration to claim that the colleges and universities were “saved” from “going bankrupt,” as Trump said.

While the mandatory funding is a significant funding source for the schools, it is not their only source of funding. It’s not even the only source of funding from the federal government, as [Education Department records](https://web.archive.org/web/20240528221741/https://www.ed.gov/programs/iduestitle3b/funding.html#top#top) show that Congress has regularly appropriated three times as much in discretionary funding for HBCUs than the required mandatory funding.

Discretionary funding authorized during the Obama administration ranged from a low of about $216 million in fiscal year 2013 to a high of almost $266 million in fiscal year 2010. Those discretionary funding amounts then increased in Trump’s first term and again under Biden.

Furthermore, the discretionary and mandatory funding totals do not include other grants and contracts that HBCUs can be awarded by federal departments and agencies.

In the interview, Trump also mentioned $612 million in discretionary money awarded to HBCUs during his current term and said that “Democrats fought me on” that funding. Democratic lawmakers, including the chairs of the Black, Hispanic and Asian Pacific American congressional caucuses, [objected](https://capac.house.gov/press-release/joint-statement-tri-caucus-chairs-trump-administration-diverting-235-million-grants) [to](https://capac.house.gov/press-release/joint-statement-tri-caucus-chairs-trumps-termination-grants-minority-serving) the money being diverted from other minority-serving institutions. They said that redirecting the funding would “pit minority communities against each other.”

## What Biden Did

We previously [wrote](https://www.factcheck.org/2023/08/post-retreads-false-claim-about-bidens-funding-for-historically-black-colleges/) in 2023 that the mandatory funding reauthorized by the FUTURE Act continued during the Biden administration, contrary to false online claims that Biden “revoked the 250 million … fund that Trump pledged to give historical black colleges for the next 10 years.”

Discretionary funding also [increased](https://web.archive.org/web/20240528221741/https://www.ed.gov/programs/iduestitle3b/funding.html#top#top) yearly during the Biden administration, and we noted in our 2023 story that there was also [$2.7 billion](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/fact-sheet-state-state-analysis-record-27-billion-american-rescue-plan-investment) for HBCUs included in the American Rescue Plan Act that Biden signed in March 2021, during the recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic. That was in addition to the nearly $363 million in discretionary funding, and more than $80 million in mandatory funding, for HBCUs in fiscal year 2022, which began on Sept. 1, 2021.

When Smith said in the Trump interview that Biden “did over $17 billion when you take everything into account,” he was referring to a [figure](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/fact-sheet-biden-harris-administration-announces-13-billion-additional-funding-and-record) put out by the Biden White House in September 2024. That funding total [includes](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/fact-sheet-biden-harris-administration-announces-record-over-16-billion-support-for) federal grants, contracting awards, debt relief for HBCUs, and financial aid and educational benefits, such as Pell grants, for students attending HBCUs, according to a White House press release.

Editor’s note: FactCheck.org does not accept advertising. We rely on grants and individual donations from people like you. Please consider a donation. Credit card donations may be made through [our “Donate” page](https://giving.aws.cloud.upenn.edu/?fastStart=simpleForm&program=ANS&fund=602014). If you prefer to give by check, send to: FactCheck.org, Annenberg Public Policy Center, P.O. Box 58100, Philadelphia, PA 19102.

# Introducing Gemini 4 Neon

## Introducing Gemini 4 Neon

Nov 18, 2026

- x.com
- Facebook
- LinkedIn
- Mail
- Copy link
Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

Koray Kavukcuoglu

SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google

- x.com
- Facebook
- LinkedIn
- Mail
- Copy link
Your browser does not support the audio element.

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing.

The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window.

Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app .

## Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work

Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench .

Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.

On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%).

## Built for production-ready code

Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions.

Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks.

Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon.

In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets.

Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk.

In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes.

## Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows

We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs.

Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting.

## Built for fast, efficient, frontier-level cyber defense

As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%).

Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models.

To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models.

- Finding code vulnerabilities: Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge.
- Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon.
- Patching vulnerabilities: Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2 , driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon.
Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program .

## Designed for safe, dependable execution

Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack — maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on:

- Mitigating frontier misuse safety risks: Because Neon brings frontier-level capabilities to a faster, lower-cost model, we paired it with strong real-time safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse comparable to our Carbon protections, while declining far less legitimate work in these areas, refusing for instance just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science.
- Advancing alignment and disciplined model behavior: In internal coding use, alert rates from our chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor remained below the already low baselines set by Carbon, suggesting improved alignment propensity for Neon — and that same monitor is deployed to protect Neon across external surfaces. Neon is trained to complete multi-step work without cutting corners, fabricating results, or overstepping user boundaries — continuing to improve the balance between following through on requests and staying within scope. It matched Carbon with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and took shortcuts on just 2.45% of tasks on our coding cheating evaluation (the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model). It also achieved a 0.09% misaligned action rate on our agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on our agent honesty evaluation. On our agentic behavior evaluation, Neon builds on Carbon’s strong baseline by further reducing under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels.
- Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark, Neon is more resilient than other models in its class when malicious instructions are planted in the web pages, emails, documents, or code it accesses. We found that with real-time safeguards at its highest thinking level, Neon resisted every attack within this Gray Swan benchmark, matching the 0.0% attack success rate reached only by other Gemini models.
For more details, see the Gemini 4 Neon model card .

## Built for deeper analysis

In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses.

- Higher-quality writing and knowledge work: Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs.
- Reliable research and analysis: Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data.
- Faster help for tougher tasks: Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund.
## Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family

Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.

## Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today

Gemini 4 Neon begins rolling out today:

- For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in Google AI Studio and Android Studio , if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try Neon in Google Antigravity and all Pro and Ultra subscribers can try it in AI Studio.
- For enterprises: Use Gemini 4 Neon in Gemini for business (via the API or model drop-down) and Google Antigravity.
- For consumers: If you’re a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can select Gemini 4 Neon from the model drop-down in the Gemini app .
- For cybersecurity defenders: Eligible Fairwind Program members will begin receiving access over the next few days. To request access to the Fairwind Program, contact your Cloud account team.
## Get the latest news from Google in your inbox

Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more.

Done. Just one step more.

Check your inbox to confirm your subscription.

You can also subscribe with a different email address .

Your information will be used in accordance with Google's privacy policy. You may opt out at any time.

items.articleBody:
Ever since the Huang/Nvidia scandal erupted, I’ve been thinking about a short post I wrote back in March, under the headline “[Jensen Huang Doesn’t Smell Anything](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/03/31/jensen-huang)”:

> Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, during an on-stage interview at The Hill
> & Valley Forum last week, was asked “What do you see as America’s
> unique advantages that other countries don’t have?”
> His answer, after taking a moment to think, “America’s unique
> advantage that no country could possibly have is President Trump.”
> Huang, newly appointed to the [aforelinked](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/03/31/presidents-council-of-advisors-on-science-and-technology) President’s Council
> of Advisors on Science and Technology, seemingly [doesn’t smell the growing stink](https://politicalwire.com/2026/03/30/can-trumps-approval-fall-even-further/).

The stink was the historically low (and sinking) popularity to which Trump’s 2.0 presidency had sunk. Undeniable to anyone in touch with reality. Huang’s obsequious Trump-fellating answer to that question would have been eye-catching even a year prior, when Trump first rolled back into office with an aggressive agenda and a surplus of political capital from a clear election victory — but it was, frankly, a startling thing to say in March 2026. It makes a lot more sense, though, [given what’s come to light in the last 10 days](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/18/huang-tweets).

[Update: This event was [in July 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9WkGNe27r_Q), not March 2026, but while I regret that error, my points stand.]

If you’re not paying close attention you might think Huang’s was the sort of answer any major tech CEO might have given. But it’s not. That was a really unusual thing for Huang to say, way out of line with how corporate leaders typically approach politics. The typical approach for large publicly held corporations is to avoid partisan politics. Advocate only for policies directly related to the company’s business, and otherwise stay out. The political winds change direction every few years. George Bush senior in 1988 was the last new president elected from the same party as the outgoing incumbent, and he only lasted one term. It makes no sense for a corporation that intends to continue thriving for more than the next few years to closely align itself with one party — unless they believe that party will remain in power for the foreseeable future, à la the FDR/Truman Democrats, who won five consecutive presidential elections from 1932 to 1948 (and seven out of nine through 1968).

One metaphor I use for politics is a football field. Democrats on the left, Republicans on the right. CEOs typically stay as close as they can to the 50-yard line in the middle of the field. That way, when an election puts the other party in power, they don’t have to move — they just need to turn around. That’s how someone like Tim Cook could maintain good relations with the White House from Obama to Trump to Biden back to Trump again. He just stayed close to midfield and turned around after each election.

Remaining as close as possible to political midfield under Trump required unseemly obsequious tribute, unprecedented in modern U.S. history. [Million-dollar tickets](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2025/01/03/allen-tim-cook-1m-trump-inauguration) to his inauguration. [That ridiculous gold trophy](https://daringfireball.net/2025/08/gold_frankincense_and_silicon). Embarrassing stuff. But that’s ultimately [a reflection of Trump’s avarice](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2025/01/04/consider-cook-as-a-tragic-figure), not the politics of Cook personally or Apple as a company. That was the price to stay on the 50-yard line. Cook has often repeated that his two personal heroes are [Martin Luther King Jr. and Bobby Kennedy](https://www.cultofmac.com/news/klan-mlk-bobby-kennedy-inspired-apple-ceo-tim-cook) (senior, to be clear). He keeps portraits of both of them [in his office](https://www.vanityfair.com/news/tim-cook-apple-vision-pro). He never swapped them out for portraits of, say, Ronald Reagan. Apple never changed its internal policies or language regarding racial and LGBT equality. The Apple homepage never stopped celebrating Martin Luther King Jr. Day — [even when it coincided with Trump’s second inauguration](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2025/01/20/apple-homepage-mlk).

And yet Trump remains so enamored of Cook that he [floated his name](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/12/trump-weighs-in) to succeed Huang at Nvidia. [Tim Apple](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/04/21/trump-praises-tim-cook-tim-apple/89717408007/) remains the apple of Trump’s eye. Yet Apple had nothing to change or apologize for when Biden came into office, nor will they again if, as now [seems likely](https://polymarket.com/event/which-party-wins-2028-us-presidential-election), Trump is succeeded in 2029 by a Democrat elected to clean up his kakistocratic kleptomaniacal mess. (Presumably Apple will gladly pony up at least [another $25 million](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/10/15/trump-ballroom-donor-list) to restore the East Wing after Trump’s [architecturally ungodly ballroom edifice](https://x.com/HillaryClinton/status/2121291689231032754) is torn down.) And Apple certainly won’t need lawyers to defend them from charges of corruption and/or breaches of national security. Nvidia, not so much.

This is what we should want: business leaders who endeavor to stay out of partisan politics, not hopelessly enmesh themselves in it. Industry and politics cannot operate in isolation, but they should avoid intertwinement except where necessary. Great companies stand the test of time. That’s not feasible if you hitch your corporate wagon to one party or the other, no matter the political moment. We don’t think of Procter & Gamble, Coca-Cola, or Berkshire Hathaway as being Democratic or Republican companies. You cannot chart their fortunes over time based on which party was in power in any given decade. You may well have strong political opinions that are far from the 50-yard line, on one side or the other. I do. But you shouldn’t look for those opinions to be validated by industry executives, any more than you should look for business and product-design decisions to be made by elected government officials. True American values put country over party when it comes to business. And, as Calvin Coolidge aptly put it, “The chief business of the American people is business.”

America does possess unique advantages that other countries don’t have. Personal liberties enshrined in our Bill of Rights. A vibrant, diverse, ever-changing melting pot of a citizenry. A strong tradition of the rule of law, placing no man above it. Competitive markets that allow new entrants to supplant entrenched incumbents. Any CEO worth their salt should have an answer to the question of America’s unique advantages that holds true no matter who, from which party, is currently president. And they should *believe* it.

What makes Huang’s answer so off-putting isn’t that it was so abjectly partisan — politically tone-deaf to the inevitability of Democrats coming back into power, and perversely obsequious to Trump personally — but that Donald Trump is the antithesis to the entire above list of things that actually give America unique advantages other countries don’t have. Trump and the MAGA movement are also decidedly American and uniquely so, but they represent what’s *worst* about America.

But I give Huang credit for honesty. Clearly, he believed what he said. Huang didn’t just stray from the 50-yard line — he broke for Trump’s end zone.
