# How we can prepare for future cyberattacks on critical infrastructure

November 18, 2026

## How we can prepare for future cyberattacks on critical infrastructure

edited by Robert Egan

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

trusted source

written by researcher(s)

proofread

A new day, a new cyberattack. The most recent is an attack that impacted 178 major websites, including those of the BBC, CNN, Zoom, HSBC, Salesforce and Equifax .

This follows a series of cyberattacks and disruptions over the last two months—most notably on supermarkets throughout Europe. A series of attacks in France during October raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures to 50 C (122 degrees Fahrenheit) in more than 350 supermarkets. Overnight, large amounts of food spoiled, equipment overheated and fires were reported. Affected stores had to discard food and temporarily close.

Similar attacks and disruptions were then reported across several countries in November, including Ireland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg.

In all of these cases, hackers remotely reprogrammed internet-connected temperature controls. They switched evaporators to defrost mode, raising temperatures beyond safety limits. These simple changes impacted physical equipment, businesses and people.

How will the next cyberattack unfold, and where? Our industrial critical infrastructure offers many targets—from blood banks to chemical manufacturing plants , nuclear reactors , aviation and other transportation systems and wastewater treatment facilities . The potential consequences are vast.

Our team at the Cyber Security Evaluation and Assurance (CyberSEA) research lab at Carleton University has simulated cyberattacks on a Canadian municipal wastewater treatment facility to identify the most serious consequences. We have also mapped out seven dimensions for understanding cyberattack impacts .

## The vulnerability of critical infrastructure

Critical infrastructure refers to 10 broad sectors, including energy and utilities, water, health, transportation and food. Systems in these sectors provide essential services. Connecting the systems to the internet improves efficiency but can also expose such services to modern cybersecurity threats.

Cybersecurity analysis tends to focus on attacks and how they could have been prevented. Cyberattack impact analysis , on the other hand, looks at what happens after a system is compromised—which operations are disrupted, how the effects spread and who or what might be harmed.

A supermarket is more than its refrigerator temperature controls. It's a system involving food, equipment, employees, customers, business continuity and public confidence. Similarly, a water utility contains pumps and software but also protects a wider system of treatment processes, public health, the environment and access to safe water.

Cyberattacks on critical infrastructure radiate impact through all of our lives.

## Learning from wastewater systems

Wastewater treatment provides a good example of the far-reaching consequences of a cyberattack.

When we simulated cyberattacks on a Canadian municipal wastewater treatment facility , we found this could force equipment to operate excessively or near safety limits. It could also increase chemical consumption, push the plant into costly contingency modes or interfere with chemical dosing.

The most serious scenario involved discharging undertreated wastewater into the city's river.

This might seem extreme, but something similar has already happened. In 2000, a former employee attacked the Maroochy Shire wastewater system in Australia . He remotely interfered with sewage pumping stations, preventing pumps and alarms from operating properly. Over three months, millions of gallons of untreated sewage entered waterways and local parks.

## 7 dimensions of impact

Our recent research identifies seven dimensions for understanding the consequences of cyberattacks. The supermarket attacks across Europe illustrate all seven.

Operational impacts occur when a system cannot perform its intended function, while physical impacts involve changes or damage to equipment and materials. In the supermarkets, altered temperature controls disrupted food preservation, equipment overheated and food spoiled.

The consequences can then spread beyond the system. Safety impacts expose people to hazards, such as fires or unsafe food. Environmental impacts harm air, water, land or ecosystems—such as discarded food creating additional waste. Economic impacts include lost products, equipment repairs, downtime and lost customers.

Broader consequences may also emerge. Societal impacts disrupt communities or their access to important goods and services, such as fresh food. Reputational impacts arise when people lose confidence in an organization or service, for example, due to concerns about food safety.

These dimensions are connected. One disrupted operation can produce several impacts at once, some continuing after the technical problem has been resolved.

## Preparing for consequences

We may not know how the next cyberattack will unfold. But we can prepare for unsafe water, damaged equipment, environmental harm, interrupted services, financial losses and diminished public trust.

Impact analysis helps decision-makers ask practical questions: Which consequences are unacceptable? Where are additional safeguards needed? Who must respond when safety or environmental harm occurs? Which services must be restored first?

The goal is not merely to keep attackers out of computer systems. It is to keep essential services working when cyberdefenses fail.

More information

Alvi Jawad et al., Exploring dimensions and metrics of cyber-to-physical impact: A systematic review, International Journal of Critical Infrastructure Protection (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.ijcip.2026.100910 Key concepts Cybersecurity frameworks Provided by The Conversation Who's behind this story? Robert Egan Bachelor's in mathematical biology, Master's in creative writing. Well-traveled with unique perspectives on science and language. Full profile →

items.articleBody:
A [table lamp](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/type/table-lamps/) comprising a [plastic](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/plastic/) base topped with five [magnetically](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/magnets/) attached glowing orbs is among the products recently published on our Showroom section.

**[Bubbly lamp by Canalside Studio](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/bubbly-lamp-canalside-studio-dezeen-showroom/)**

Magnetic connector points are placed inside the five globe-like bulbs that light this table lamp by Hong Kong-based [Canalside Studio](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/brand/canalside-studio/).

The [Bubbly lamp](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/bubbly-lamp-canalside-studio-dezeen-showroom/) comprises a statuesque base with five bulbs attached, which can be removed and positioned around a room – including attached to metal surfaces – to spread out its ambient glow.

Other products published last week include a tile collection by [Ceramiche Keop](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/ceramiche-keope/)e, acoustic pods by [Actiu](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/brand/actiu/) and an outdoor rug range by [Rima Dain](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/brand/rima-dain/).

Read on to find out about some of our latest products:

**[Grace Lithos tiles by Ceramiche Keope](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/grace-lithos-tiles-ceramiche-keope-dezeen-showroom/)**

[Grace Lithos tiles](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/grace-lithos-tiles-ceramiche-keope-dezeen-showroom/) by [Ceramiche Keop](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/ceramiche-keope/)e are intended to mimic the striated appearance of natural Villeneuve quartzite quarried in Italy.

As well as being striped with differently coloured striations, the tiles feature the stone's abundance of mineral inclusions and the glinting mica microcrystals that it is studded with.

[Find out more about Grace Lithos](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/grace-lithos-tiles-ceramiche-keope-dezeen-showroom/)

**[Blueroots marble by Antolini](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/blueroots-marble-antolini-dezeen-showroom/)**

items.title: Outage Chaos: When Tech is too Big to Fail
items.subtitle: Outages happen, but we deserve a resilient internet where no one outage at one company can put people at risk and disrupt the global economy.
items.feedText: We can only get there by addressing an over-reliance on a few cloud monopolists through effective antitrust laws and interoperability requirements. items.articleBody:
Outages happen, but we deserve a resilient internet where no one outage at one company can put people at risk and disrupt the global economy. We can only get there by addressing an over-reliance on a few cloud monopolists through effective antitrust laws and interoperability requirements.

Service outages, like we’ve seen recently at Microsoft, Apple*, banks, courts, airlines, and elsewhere, can be more than an annoying hurdle. Losing a vital service due to an error can cause the same impacts as a government-ordered internet shutdown—people losing access to vital information and lines of communication.  As usual, the greatest harms are faced by people on the margins globally.

There’s not much hope in companies out-nerding these issues either. Technical errors will always exist, whether it’s a bug, negligence from an administrator, or a malicious attack. The problem is an over-reliance on any one company or system when these inevitable outages occur. It’s a matter of public safety and economic stability that policymakers mitigate the impact of these disruptions before they occur.

In order to do so, we must ensure antitrust prevents providers of key technical systems from becoming too big to fail.

The harms inflicted by tech monopolies go beyond monetary costs to the end user. In fact, monopolists can often offer lower prices, or even offer free services, thanks to their greater scale and incentive to shut out competitors using free-flowing investment capital. The problem is this puts a few tech companies in a position of incredible influence. The true cost is a loss of control when our private data, access to knowledge, and free expression all become mediated by tools owned by a handful of billionaires.

Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone.

This isn’t just a bad deal for us as individuals. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. When everything from daily tasks to national security is reliant on a few digital monocultures, one mistake or exploit can cascade into an explosive impact. The risks multiply in the current investment climate, where financial markets reward companies that strip-mine redundancy and resiliency from critical systems. Even if you see the problem coming, an outage that hits clients, suppliers, collaborators or loved ones proves just as disruptive. We need to remove these chokepoints for good, which means a digital sovereignty movement that makes the web more free by design—not just importing existing levers of control into another nation's borders.

Central to this effort must be undercutting platform control by fostering interoperability, i.e. when tools are made to be compatible among competitors. When this is done carefully, it’s not only easier to switch to better alternatives, we wind up with more alternatives as it becomes more viable to compete or offer complementary tools alongside existing systems.

This is what made systems like email great. You could choose your own apps and services, even using several simultaneously, and never lose touch with a contact. Early architects of the internet did not take reliable hosting for granted. Services were often on a machine a few rooms over, and needed to be prepared for the occasional interruption of service.

But in the age of hyperscalers and massive data centers, the infrastructure underlying the web isn’t owned by many scattered IT departments, it’s rented from a handful of “cloud” providers. These providers managed to scale up quickly and replace interoperability with walled gardens, enticing customers with lower costs while making it costly to leave and tightly controlling how services behave. Once in control, these platforms have every incentive to enshittify their services and devalue their workers, delivering an increasingly shoddy and restrictive service.

This context makes building interoperability an act of defiance—often coming from the sweat of open source developers. These projects may be tolerated by monopolists in the short term, but can be one boardroom decision away from being broken entirely. A better internet means championing these creators through funding, liability protections, and requiring big players to cooperate. Here is what lawmakers should do:

Federal and state legislators should—

Defend competitive compatibility. Developers merely providing alternative interfaces for tools should be shielded from liability. In the U.S., that means explicit protections under DMCA, CFAA, and corporate Terms of Service agreements. These protections should cover shared protocols and APIs as well as automated content retrieval through scraping.

Encourage interoperability. Lawmakers should force open key aspects of platform infrastructure by requiring big tech to support: (1) data portability, so users can move to a new service (2) back-end interoperability, to support more tools with competitive compatibility and (3) delegability, so people are not prevented from having code act on their behalf. So far, the Digital Markets Act in the EU has provided some positive examples of such legislation

Fund open source. In order to be sustainable, interoperable tools and standards cannot rely solely on corporate interest and volunteer labor. Programs like the EU Sovereign Tech Fund could help create viable alternatives within and beyond the borders of the EU.

Municipalities and institutions should—

Buy interoperable services. At any level, government agencies should set minimum interoperability requirements in procurement and hold a competitive bidding process to evaluate vendors’ privacy, security and lock-in risks. Agencies dependent on a sole provider, including through cooperative purchase agreements, are stuck with corporate price-gouging and even higher switching costs.

Fund Departments of Information Technology. Cloud services are often adopted to offset spending on IT professionals but, when these departments atrophy, institutions become even more reliant on the cloud providers. Maintaining in-house talent prevents this cycle of dependency and improves emergency responses to outages.

Adopt a plus-one approach to public communications. Institutions shouldn’t force citizens into walled gardens just to access public communications. In addition to posts to corporate social media, government agencies should share the same information on an open protocol—whether it’s bluesky, the fediverse, or just an RSS feed.  By putting these in the open, more people will have access to urgent alerts and can create new useful tools.

Building a more resilient and democratic internet is possible, and many people are already hard at work doing just that. Above are some necessary steps to get corporate and government interests out of the way of rewilding the net with greater community and individual controls. The dream of the internet as a digital commons operating for the public good is not dead yet, and is worth fighting for.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

items.articleBody:
Apple added a dedicated Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app with iOS 27, which you can read more about in [Federico’s annual review](https://www.macstories.net/stories/ios-and-ipados-27-review/7/). Now that same feature is set to come to the iPad.

Earlier this week, Apple released developer beta two for the 27.3 OSes. [I wrote about many of those upcoming changes](https://www.macstories.net/news/apples-latest-second-27-3-developer-beta-adds-face-unlock-for-iphone-duo-new-mac-privacy-controls-and-more/) earlier this week but missed the changes to the iPad’s Camera app. As with iOS, when you open the Camera app in iPadOS 27.3, there will be a dedicated Siri mode. Switch to the new mode and the shutter button becomes a Siri icon. Tap it, and Siri will analyze the scene, describing what it sees. From there, you can use your finger or an Apple Pencil to circle or scrub over individual items, activating Visual Intelligence to search Google, Amazon, and other Visual Intelligence-enabled apps. Here’s a quick demo of it on the latest iPad mini that [I recently reviewed](https://www.macstories.net/reviews/ipad-mini-2026-review-pushing-the-boundaries-with-apples-smallest-ipad/):

Visual Intelligence is one of those iOS and iPadOS features that I’ve had trouble remembering to use. However, as you can tell from the video, it works really well for things like recognizable products. I’m glad to see this coming to the iPad, especially the mini, which I’m much more likely to use as a camera for capturing my surroundings.

items.articleBody:
David Lehman at *The Hudson Review*:

For poets who associate poetry with freedom, a release from obligations, a holiday, writing is “play for mortal stakes,” a wager made by persons who know they will never learn the outcome of their bet. They write for the posthumous fame or glory that is nowhere conferred but may be recorded someday in an official-sounding anthology. Reputation is fickle. Emily Dickinson, who dismissed “publication” as the “Auction / Of the Mind of Man,” died unknown; Emma Lazarus did not live long enough to know that her sonnet “The New Colossus” would come to articulate the meaning of the Statue of Liberty. Nor do the prizes a poet receives while alive guarantee a lasting readership. Edmund Wilson, aged seventy-one, got worried when he received an honor, because “an accepted reputation can be derived from no real merit whatever.”

A commonly used metaphor for literary reputation is that of the gyrations of the stock market. Shares of Shelley reached new highs through most of the nineteenth century but crashed in the 1920s when first T. S. Eliot and then F. R. Leavis and others put out “sell” recommendations on the English Romantic poets in general and Shelley in particular. At the same time, and for overlapping reasons, every English department across America took a strong position in such “metaphysical” poets of the seventeenth century as John Donne, Andrew Marvell, and George Herbert. It was the equivalent of a peaceable revolution, a nonviolent overthrow of the existing order.

items.articleBody:
“It seems that philosophers have started to make substantial use of AI in their papers, and it’s not uncommon for AI-generated text to make it into philosophy published in decent journals.”

Not uncommon. How much are we talking here?

That’s the question [Maximillian Noichl](https://maxnoichl.eu/) (Utrecht) recently took up.

His answer? An estimated “12% of published philosophy in 2026 [involves] some AI assistance,” though he notes that the figure will vary depending on the AI detection software used and how the false-positive threshold is set.

So AI writing in philosophy articles is not yet normal. But, he notes, it is increasing.

In the following guest post, Noichl explains how he investigated the issue.

(A version of this post [first appeared at Noichl’s site](https://maxnoichl.eu/blog/2026/ai-in-philosophy-publishing/).)

## How Much AI-Generated Text Is In Today’s Philosophy Journals? by Max Noichl

When reading philosophy in the last few months, I’ve often had the nagging feeling that what I’m reading had a distinct AI smell. I thus wanted to investigate the prevalence of AI usage in philosophy in a data-driven way. This post outlines the results of that investigation. Long story short, it seems that philosophers have started to make substantial use of AI in their papers, and it’s not uncommon for AI-generated text to make it into philosophy published in decent journals. It also appears that preprint servers in philosophy are increasingly clogged up by AI-generated content.

Here’s what the results look like, at a glance:

AI usage in a sample of published philosophy papers (n=11957). Click the figure to view it at full size.

### Methods and Data

AI detection is funny in that, around three years ago, it was extremely bad and unreliable. Many people thought it might even be impossible to detect AI-generated content at all. This changed sometime over the last year, as more reliable AI detectors like [Pangram](https://www.pangram.com/) ([Emi & Spero, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14873)) came on the market. Now the best AI detection systems appear to be pretty reliable ([Jabarian & Imas, 2025](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34223)) at least under decent conditions (enough text, English language, etc.). This means that for some time now, many people have been heavily underestimating how detectable AI writing is in practice. This doesn’t mean that it’s a fully solved problem. For one, it remains tricky to distinguish between AI-based editing, translation, and full generation, especially for very short texts, and there is the danger that new large language models might, at least temporarily, get ahead of the detectors. But right now AI detection with reasonable confidence is possible.

For this project, I will be using an open-source AI detector called MELD, published by [Li et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06903). MELD is based on a transformer model, Ettin-1B, from the ModernBERT family.

Transformer models (very) roughly work such that text is split into small subword units called tokens. These tokens get individual numerical representations called embeddings, and as text is pushed through the model, in a process called *attention*, the embeddings of individual tokens change based on the tokens around them, encoding contextual semantics, grammar and so on. In LLMs these embeddings are usually randomly initialized at the beginning of the training process and then iteratively updated, so that the embeddings that drop out at the end of the model become more useful for specific tasks, for example, predicting the next token for text generation in GPTs or predicting a token from its surroundings (in BERT-style models). For an interactive walkthrough of these steps, I like to recommend the [Transformer Explainer](https://poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer/).

In the case of MELD, a model pre-trained on general text tasks is trained further. To make it work for the task of AI detection, a small additional neural network, which projects the large token embeddings coming out of it to a much lower, 48-dimensional space, is added on top of it, as well as two small sets of anchor vectors, one which contains vectors meant for different AI-model families and one for humans. The model is then trained further, now on a mixture of texts for which we know whether they are AI-generated or human. As the model is trained, each token in each incoming text is compared to all anchors, and its similarity to the most AI and the most human-like prototype is scored. These scores are used for a general prediction on the text, and depending on how it gets its predictions right, the prototypes used in each training step, as well as the whole network leading up to them, get updated ([Li et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06903)). MELD can, in principle, try to distinguish between different types of AI usage (raw generation, polishing, etc.), but for our current investigation we are looking for any content that appears to have come out of, or gone through, an AI model in *any form*.

In my experience so far, MELD performs pretty well. I suspect it is not quite as good as Pangram, especially with regard to the most recent state-of-the-art models. It has the big advantage, though, that it is open source, so we can check how it works under the hood, what it was and wasn’t trained on, and how it performs on our specific datasets. It also means that we can run it ourselves if we acquire a strong enough GPU, which costs a little bit of money, but is far less expensive than running a large number of philosophy papers through Pangram, which would charge around 5 dollars per paper. This also means that potentially copyrighted material can stay on machines that we control. I couldn’t get access to the canonical weights of MELD, so I have been using this [mirror](https://huggingface.co/odeveloper/meld).

MELD uses a threshold approach. When using the frozen weights after training is done, each token gets its own AI score, and we can decide ourselves at what threshold we want to assume that the text is actually AI-generated. The MELD authors recommend setting the threshold on material that we know is not AI-generated, which we do for each individual dataset in this project based on the papers from 2021 and 2022, as ChatGPT in its earliest version was introduced in November 2022. For the presented results, we set the threshold so that we accept a 1% false positive rate in those pre-AI years, which is the more strict of the thresholds suggested by the authors of MELD for the results reported in their paper. On their own evaluation dataset, at a 1% false positive rate, they detect 99.7% of AI texts successfully.

I should note that this is significantly less strict than Pangram’s reported overall false positive rate of one in 10,000 ([Emi, 2025](https://www.pangram.com/blog/all-about-false-positives-in-ai-detectors)). As I am not trying to judge individual authors’ work for potentially life-changing decisions, but to get a general sense of how things are going in philosophy, I am just as worried about the model missing more subtle cues of AI writing (false negatives), as I am about false positive judgements.

For the data, we are considering four publicly available sources of philosophical articles, namely the journals *Philosophers’ Imprint* and *Ergo*, which are, to my mind, well-respected venues that have the big advantage of being fully and freely available on the internet. I have gently scraped these two publications, as well as all the preprints on the [PhilSci-Archive](https://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/). I also downloaded all preprints available from PhilPapers’ PhilArchive via the [CORE collection](https://core.ac.uk/data-providers/160/). After restricting to papers from 2021 onwards with at least 1,500 words of text (and, for PhilPapers, to English-language articles of at most 30,000 words), this leaves full texts of 197 papers from *Philosophers’ Imprint*, 374 from *Ergo*, 4723 from the PhilSci-Archive and 29954 from PhilPapers. For the final year 2026, CORE had about a third of the records available, compared to around 78% available for the earlier years, so we have a still somewhat incomplete dataset to work with right now. I noticed that many preprints were backdated (posted in 2025/26 but claimed to be from 21/22) and therefore could not reliably be considered AI free. I thus removed them from the dataset, and used only articles actually uploaded in those early years for calibration of the threshold.

For the PhilSci-Archive and PhilArchive, I linked the records to OpenAlex, which allows us to check the publication status of each paper. For this, I consider all papers that appear in a journal with an ISSN listed on the [PhilPapers journal list](https://philpapers.org/journals) as published in philosophy. While these papers ended up being published in some form, we should keep in mind that their deposited version is not always fully identical to the final published one. Because different genre compositions and text sources will be treated differently by MELD, I calculated separate thresholds for (1) the two open access journals, (2,3) published and only preprinted works in the PhilSci-Archive, and (4,5) published and preprinted work from PhilPapers.

All of these papers were converted from their various HTML/PDF formats into a uniform text format using BeautifulSoup (for the journals’ HTML pages) and PyMuPDF (for the PhilSci-Archive PDFs). For PhilPapers, I use the text that CORE had already extracted. The papers were then parsed with MELD using GPUs rented on Google Colab. MELD read the texts in windows of 2,046 tokens (around 1,500 words) at a time and scored every token; these token scores were then summarised in passages of 256 tokens (around 190 words). Following the procedure in the MELD paper, the MELD scores were then calculated by taking the similarity to the human prototypes as opposed to the AI prototypes, and by taking the average of the top 25% of token scores as the AI score for the whole passage.

I usually post all code and data for the analyses I do, and I believe it’s crucially important to do so for published work. In this case, however, I will not be sharing the data and code (not even privately), at least in the immediate future. AI use is a highly sensitive topic, and accusing authors of it could have implications for their careers. The idea of doing so wrongly is mortifying to me, and I don’t trust the current workflow enough to be sure that this would not happen.

I’m further not convinced that all the AI usage I find with this method is equally problematic. I think there is, for example, a big difference between AI use for translation as opposed to spamming journals with one-shot prompted slop. For these reasons, I will only be reporting aggregate values in this post and won’t be quoting from any of the AI-generated texts. I know that this is somewhat unsatisfying and makes the whole project less convincing, but for now, it seems to me to be the most responsible way of going about this.

### Results

So, what do we find? First, we can look at the AI use detected in the two specific journals we have gathered: *Philosophers’ Imprint* and *Ergo*. In the graphic below, each paper’s passages are stacked from bottom to top, from the lowest detected AI use (very unlikely to be AI-generated, shown in gray) to the highest detected AI use (very likely to be AI-generated, shown in red). Each narrow column therefore represents the distribution within one paper. This shows how prevalent AI use is overall, as well as its distribution in the papers in which it occurs. Within each year, columns are arranged by the amount of AI use above the threshold, which we set based on the years 2021 and 2022.

Philosophers’ Imprint (197 papers) and Ergo (374 papers). Click the figure to view it at full size.

As we can see, the values before 2023 are around 1%, which corresponds to the expected false positive rate we set. After 2023, we see a slow increase in AI use in *Ergo*, which continues into 2026: some passages get flagged, but there are few papers with marked AI use. In *Philosophers’ Imprint*, usage stays low until 2025 and then seems to rise considerably in 2026. In both journals, we now see papers that contain at least sizable chunks of material that likely passed through a large language model in some way. I haven’t been able to find an AI policy for *Philosophers’ Imprint*, but *Ergo* considers AI-generated content to be usually inappropriate, and in any case, such use has to be disclosed ([Ergo, 2026](https://journals.publishing.umich.edu/media/journals/24/publication_ethics_ergo_2026.pdf)).

At this point, I feel like I should reiterate that I included these two journals because they are fully open access. They are the only way I could study the full run of individual philosophy journals without worrying about the issues around bulk-downloading licensed material. There is no indication that these journals are particularly full of AI material: To the contrary, as we will see, they appear to be around, or even below average.

Turning to the PhilSci-Archive, which in the study period yielded 4723 papers in total, I’ve split these into papers that have been published in philosophy journals, according to the PhilPapers journal list and OpenAlex, and papers that have remained preprints or were published in other venues that are either not considered philosophy by PhilPapers or are book reviews, contributions to collected volumes, and so on. Here we seem to find much higher shares of AI content in 2026, with 18% of material published in philosophy journals showing evidence of AI generation and a number of the papers scoring uniformly quite high. An even higher share, 27% of the textual material uploaded to the PhilSci-Archive as preprints, is considered as AI-generated by MELD. It also appears that most papers that make use of AI are by no means fully AI-generated, but have more or less extended passages in them that get flagged. But there are a few largely AI-generated papers that appear to have made it into publication.

PhilSci-Archive: papers published in philosophy journals (2223) and preprints and other papers (2500). Click the figure to view it at full size.

We find a somewhat similar preprint/published split for papers that have come online via PhilPapers’ PhilArchive. Around 11% of published material seemed to be AI-generated in 2026, and a stunning 62% of the material that was uploaded to PhilPapers in 2026 and has not yet gone on to be published in philosophy journals appears to be AI-generated. Manually checking these results, it appears that much of this material is actually barely related to philosophy. This is in contrast to the PhilSci-Archive, which doesn’t have a pronounced rise from 2025 to 2026. One explanation may be that the new moderation policies the PhilSci-Archive put into place in June 2026 are working.

PhilPapers: papers published in philosophy journals (9898) and preprints and other papers (20056). Click the figure to view it at full size.

If we combine (and deduplicate) all samples that got published in philosophy journals from PhilPapers, the PhilSci-Archive, *Ergo* and *Philosophers’ Imprint*, and score them according to their own thresholds, we arrive at [the figure at the top of this post](https://maxnoichl.eu/blog/2026/ai-in-philosophy-publishing/#published-philosophy), an estimate of 12% of published philosophy in 2026 involving some AI assistance.

### Qualifications and Summary

I have checked a few dozen of the highest-scoring passages from all of these datasets, both manually and using Pangram. Many of them do hold up, and I will say that I have been surprised, and a little shocked, to find extended passages of writing in decent journals, where my intuitive reading, the MELD scoring, and the Pangram spot checks have all agreed on AI use. So one conclusion of this project is that AI use in philosophy is *here*. I think it is prevalent, even in well-respected journals.

I should also note that, as should be expected from their different accepted false-positive rates, MELD seems to be much more aggressive than Pangram in flagging text as AI. What I’ve often seen during manual checking is that MELD flags long stretches as AI-involved writing, whereas Pangram flags only smaller chunks within those texts. But, when something does get flagged highly by MELD, Pangram usually is also at least suspicious, giving non-zero AI-use scores or indications of AI-assistance.

If we want to be more careful in our estimates (which might also mean letting a big chunk of AI content slide), we can make our threshold more severe. Lowering the accepted false positive rate in 2021/2022, e.g. to one in a thousand, we would get 6% of material flagged in papers published in journals in 2026, and 37% in preprints. The plot below shows how results change with the threshold. That being said, I lean towards accepting that MELD is currently giving less reliable, and likely higher, estimates than Pangram would. A more thorough study than this one might very well be worth the effort, and show a different picture.

Share of a paper’s text above the threshold in 2026, as the accepted false positive rate is lowered from one in a hundred to one in a thousand. Thick lines: published papers and preprints, with 95% bootstrap intervals. Thin lines: individual sources. Click the figure to view it at full size.

I have also seen a number of clear failure modes of this approach. The first is that some papers fully marked as AI-generated are, after reading into them, likely to be papers where people used AI translation. These papers have a distinct “AI smell” in their phrasing but seem well thought out and were published by people that I assume might not be native speakers of English. While I personally would caution against doing this as an author, I don’t think this is a particularly problematic use of AI (especially in view of recent work on linguistic inequality in philosophy, see [Marsili & Rehren (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s41073-026-00252-9), [Peters et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13164-025-00779-8)), even if I would prefer to see that disclosed.

Another failure mode I have observed is when authors are writing *about* AI and put long, correctly marked quotations from ChatGPT or Claude into their papers. It’s nice to see that MELD catches these instances, but of course these results should be considered spurious as well.

Finally, I have observed a small number of cases where material on Asian philosophy that made use of many Chinese characters in the text was flagged as AI-generated. One notable case of this was flagged only by MELD and not by Pangram, which makes me think this might be a problem area where MELD may need some additional improvement.

So, to summarize our findings: Most philosophy published in 2026 probably was not generated with AI. But AI-generated material appears to be increasingly prevalent in philosophical writing. Most papers that get flagged for AI usage seem to take the form of localized editing, where people intersperse AI-generated or AI-assisted passages with their own writing. Fully AI-generated, “slop” papers, do occur but are still relatively rare, although they drive a lot of the total AI volume. And finally, it appears that the preprint archives in philosophy, which I think are very good for the discipline, have an increasingly big AI problem, as they are getting swamped with large numbers of likely AI-generated papers. Some forms of automated AI checking might become necessary here in the near future.

It seems that AI-assisted writing has fully arrived in philosophy and is unlikely to go away any time soon. I think it is important that we have an honest and open discussion about the ways in which it is, and is not, acceptable.

*I’m grateful to Hein Duijf, Dominik Klein and Erik Stei for discussing these results with me.*

**AI usage statement:** This blog post was largely dictated via MacWhisper. The dictation was cleaned up using Fable 5.1, and edited by me. Fable 5.2 assisted me in editing the citations, fact-checking, setting up an automated process to put in the numbers, as well as layout and typo checking. I have applied MELD to the text of the post itself, and it hasn’t flagged anything, at any of the thresholds used. The code for the underlying analysis was generated using Fable 5.2, under my close supervision.

items.subtitle: Over the past decade, MIT researchers have developed aerial microrobots with bumblebee-like speed, agility, and durability, for tasks like precisio…
items.feedText: But these featherweight microrobots couldn’t carry the electronics needed for navigation, forcing them to remain connected to a motion-capture system in the lab. items.articleBody:
Over the past decade, MIT researchers have developed aerial microrobots with bumblebee-like speed, agility, and durability, for tasks like precision agriculture or search-and-rescue. But these featherweight microrobots couldn’t carry the electronics needed for navigation, forcing them to remain connected to a motion-capture system in the lab.

Now, the researchers have designed a flapping-wing microrobot with onboard sensors and computation, which can follow a complex trajectory and land precisely on a sunflower outside the lab’s motion capture environment.

While the robot is still connected to an offboard power source, this demonstration highlights the potential of aerial microrobots to be used for precision agriculture in the future.

For instance, flying microrobots could weave through a field of almond trees or blueberry bushes to carefully pollinate delicate blossoms in regions where natural pollinator populations have been decimated by habitat loss. They could also hover near plants without causing damage, monitoring crop health and spotting pests before they become widespread.

To enable onboard sensing and computation, the researchers developed a method to expand the artificial muscles that power the robot’s wings, increasing the net payload so the tiny robot could carry the necessary electronics.

They also designed a sensor suite that can rapidly estimate the robot’s position and orientation without relying on an offboard motion capture system, and a miniature electronics package to securely hold the tiny computational components on the nimble vehicle.

“This is a really important milestone for the research community. This is the first demonstration of an aerial microrobot that is sensory and compute autonomous. There are many situations, like pollination or industrial surveillance, where you can’t use a larger robot. Small-scale robots are uniquely positioned for these types of tasks, and if this thread of technology becomes successful in the future, it could be very promising,” says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-corresponding author of a [paper on the robot](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scirobotics.aeg6618).

He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Yi-Hsuan (Nemo) Hsiao, Quang Phuc Kieu, and Zhongtao Guan; co-corresponding authors Jonathan P. How, a Ford Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) and the Aerospace Controls Laboratory (ACL) at MIT; Elizabeth Farrell Helbling, an assistant professor at Cornell University; and others at MIT. The research [appears today in Science Robotics](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scirobotics.aeg6618).

**Increasing the payload**

The MIT researchers previously developed a [swift, agile aerial microrobot](https://news.mit.edu/2025/mit-engineers-design-aerial-microrobot-fly-like-bumblebee-1203) with four wings, each powered by a set of soft actuators, or artificial muscles, that flap the wings rapidly so the bot can perform detailed maneuvers.

The robot, roughly the same size and shape as a microcassette, weighs less than a paperclip.

To bring this tiny robot closer to real-world applications, the researchers need it to carry the additional weight from electronics for onboard sensing and computation, while still being fast, maneuverable, and robust to collisions.

In this research, they developed a method to scale up the artificial muscles without hampering the robot’s performance. They carefully tuned the radius and length of the soft actuators, increasing their size by 50 percent while boosting the robot’s net lift forces by 46 percent.

“It is very difficult to scale up the actuators without causing the output power of the system to go down, which reduces the lift forces. We tuned the geometry of the robot very precisely so lift proportionally increases with the additional actuator weight,” Chen explains.

They were able to achieve a lift-to-weight ratio of 1.9, giving the robot more than enough lift force to carry the onboard electronics package they developed, which weighs only 244 milligrams.

The tiny electronics package contains the sensors, and microcontroller needed for onboard sensing and computation.

The researchers incorporated an inertial measurement unit to estimate attitude, an optical flow sensor to estimate lateral flight speed and position, and a time-of-flight sensor to measure height.

But without the precision of the attached motion capture system, the robot does not know its absolute position, causing it to drift off course.

**Speedy sensing**

To overcome this challenge, the team designed a sensing algorithm to calculate the robot orientation, angular velocity, and position extremely quickly, simplifying the calculations to reduce the computational cost.

They found that estimating position continuously at a faster rate yielded higher performance than a more accurate, slower estimation.

“We spent a lot of time optimizing the selection of the sensors and position estimators so the robot would have very low drift. Our robot can now fly with positional accuracy that is comparable to flying with offboard cameras,” says Hsiao.

They integrated the sensors and computing components into a tiny electronics package, which they attached to a fiberglass substrate so it wouldn’t be thrown off by vibrations of the robot.

“When you are talking about a computer which is that small, everything must be thought through carefully. There are so many factors to consider; it must do both perception and control, while fitting onto the robot and running fast enough that the vehicle will remain stable during flight,” How says.

They tested the offboard computation capabilities of the aerial microrobot through a series of flight demonstrations, including hovering at different heights and following point-to-point trajectories. The robot maneuvered quickly and precisely, with positional errors of only a few centimeters.

In addition, they demonstrated the robot’s potential for artificial pollination by using a joystick to send high-level position setpoints, guiding the aerial vehicle around several plants before carefully landing on a sunflower.

“This is quite difficult to do, even if you do have a motion-capture system,” Hsiao says.

The researchers analyzed the vehicle’s power expenditures and found the electronics only consume about 6 percent of the total power, with the rest fueling the robot’s artificial muscles and wings.

They identified ways to further reduce power consumption from the electronics. This would allow for the addition of more components, like a camera that would enable the robot to recognize objects.

The researchers are now working toward two goals: putting a camera onboard for autonomous object recognition and obstacle avoidance; and integrating power electronics and batteries onto the tiny robot, which would enable untethered flight in an outdoor environment.

This research was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), U.S. Office of Naval Research, U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and a Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

items.articleBody:
** The latest on Trump’s approval rating**

**Updated November 18, 2026**

After rebounding slightly to 38 percent, Donald Trump’s approval rating is back on the downswing. **Today, 37 percent of Americans approve of the job he’s doing, while 60 percent disapprove**.

Show more Show less

Just 18.9 percent of Americans *strongly* approve of Trump, dangerously close to the 18.3 percent who *weakly* approve. If the president continues to get less popular, those figures could flip in the not too distant future. **-EMD** **, 11/17/26**

**See also: [Iran War support dashboard](https://www.natesilver.net/p/iran-war-polls-popularity-approval).**

This is the landing page for Silver Bulletin presidential approval ratings. We’ll regularly update the charts below as new polls about Donald Trump’s approval rating come in.1 This page is designed to be [viewed on the web](https://tinyurl.com/3fzxm9wc) rather than in our email client or in the Substack app.

[Click here for more information on how the average works](https://www.natesilver.net/p/silver-bulletin-polling-average-methodology). The Silver Bulletin average weights more reliable polls heavily — you can **[find our latest pollster ratings here](https://www.natesilver.net/p/pollster-ratings-silver-bulletin)**.

### The topline: So, just how popular is Trump?

Our default average reflects a combination of all polls, whether conducted among adults, registered voters or likely voters. If a pollster releases multiple versions of the same survey, we use the all-adult version of the poll before the registered voter version.2 This is because all Americans have a say in how popular the president is — whether or not they vote.

### The polls: What do the surveys say?

Each poll gets an “influence” score based on its pollster rating, its sample size, its recency, and how often a pollster is publishing numbers.3 Sometimes, surveys with mediocre pollster ratings have more weight in the model just because they were conducted very recently or polled more people.

items.articleBody:
**Apple hat die Leitung von Apple Pay und Wallet neu besetzt. Neuer Chef des Bereichs, zu dem auch die Apple Card gehört, ist Corey Fugman. Er folgt auf Jennifer Bailey, deren Ruhestand Apple bereits im August intern angekündigt hatte. Wir haben die Details.**

Wie [Bloomberg-Journalist Mark Gurman](http://26 Jahre im Unternehmen Wie Bloomberg-Journalist Mark Gurman berichtet, ist Fugman seit 26 Jahren bei Apple. Im September 2000 fing er direkt nach seinem Studium in Stanford als Merchandising-Manager im Einzelhandel an. Von 2019 bis 2021 war er für die Apple Card und Apple Cash zuständig. Seit November 2021 leitet er als Senior Director den Bereich Apple Pay und Wallet. In der neuen Rolle berichtet er direkt an Services-Chef Eddy Cue. Apple selbst wollte sich zu der Personalie nicht äußern. Baileys Erbe bei Apple Pay Bailey hinterlässt große Fußstapfen. Sie hat Apple Pay seit dem Start im Jahr 2014 geführt, davor leitete sie den Online-Store des Unternehmens. In ihre Zeit fallen die Apple Wallet, die Apple Card, Apple Cash und Tap to Pay auf dem iPhone. Eddy Cue hatte ihren Abschied im August in einem internen Memo bekannt gegeben. Apple Pay ist heute in mehr als 90 Märkten verfügbar. In den kommenden Monaten unterstützt Bailey den Übergang noch als Beraterin. Apple Card zieht zu Chase um Auf Fugman wartet direkt eine schwierige Aufgabe. Die Apple Card wechselt gerade von Goldman Sachs zu JPMorgan Chase. Den Wechsel hat Apple im Januar 2026 angekündigt, er soll rund zwei Jahre dauern. Laut Bloomberg war Fugman schon bisher eng daran beteiligt, jetzt trägt er die Verantwortung. Euch betrifft das hierzulande nicht direkt, denn die Apple Card gibt es weiterhin nur in den USA. Bei Apple Pay in Europa sieht es anders aus: Wegen der Vorgaben aus Brüssel muss Apple die NFC-Schnittstelle des iPhones auch für andere Anbieter öffnen, und die Konkurrenz wächst. Teil des Umbaus unter John Ternus Die Personalie passt zum Umbau unter John Ternus, der seit dem 1. September CEO von Apple ist. Ternus will weniger Managementebenen und mit weniger Leuten mehr erreichen. Gleichzeitig wächst das Servicegeschäft langsamer, im Juni-Quartal blieb es sogar unter den Erwartungen der Analysten. Da ist es naheliegend, mitten im Bankwechsel jemanden zu befördern, der den Bereich bereits kennt, statt eine Führungskraft von außen zu holen.) berichtet, ist Fugman seit 26 Jahren bei Apple. Im September 2000 fing er direkt nach seinem Studium in Stanford als Merchandising-Manager im Einzelhandel an. Von 2019 bis 2021 war er für die Apple Card und Apple Cash zuständig. Seit November 2021 leitet er als Senior Director den Bereich Apple Pay und Wallet. In der neuen Rolle berichtet er direkt an Services-Chef Eddy Cue. Apple selbst wollte sich zu der Personalie nicht äußern.

## Baileys Erbe bei Apple Pay

Bailey hinterlässt große Fußstapfen. Sie hat Apple Pay seit dem Start im Jahr 2014 geführt, davor leitete sie den Online-Store des Unternehmens. In ihre Zeit fallen die Apple Wallet, die Apple Card, Apple Cash und Tap to Pay auf dem iPhone. Eddy Cue hatte ihren Abschied im August in einem internen Memo bekannt gegeben. Apple Pay ist heute in mehr als 90 Märkten verfügbar. In den kommenden Monaten unterstützt Bailey den Übergang noch als Beraterin.

## Apple Card zieht zu Chase um

Auf Fugman wartet direkt eine schwierige Aufgabe. Die Apple Card wechselt gerade von Goldman Sachs zu JPMorgan Chase. Den Wechsel hat Apple im Januar 2026 angekündigt, er soll rund zwei Jahre dauern. Laut Bloomberg war Fugman schon bisher eng daran beteiligt, jetzt trägt er die Verantwortung. Euch betrifft das hierzulande nicht direkt, denn die Apple Card gibt es weiterhin nur in den USA. Bei Apple Pay in Europa sieht es anders aus: Wegen der Vorgaben aus Brüssel muss Apple die NFC-Schnittstelle des iPhones auch für andere Anbieter öffnen, und die Konkurrenz wächst.

## Teil des Umbaus unter John Ternus

Die Personalie passt zum Umbau unter John Ternus, der seit dem 1. September CEO von Apple ist. Ternus will weniger Managementebenen und mit weniger Leuten mehr erreichen. Gleichzeitig wächst das Servicegeschäft langsamer, im Juni-Quartal blieb es sogar unter den Erwartungen der Analysten. Da ist es naheliegend, mitten im Bankwechsel jemanden zu befördern, der den Bereich bereits kennt, statt eine Führungskraft von außen zu holen.

items.articleBody:
Adventurer [David Rule](https://www.instagram.com/davidmrule/) documented the entire build of his “Tinytanic”, an 8-foot, solar-powered houseboat designed for extended wilderness river travel. Rule described each step, from custom pontoon assembly and framing to integrating solar power and internal amenities, resulting in a fully functional living space on the water that can provide a bit of comfort during a multi-day river expedition down the [Pend Oreille River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pend_Oreille_River) in Washington State.

> This might be the most ridiculous build I’ve taken on in my entire life, but it ended up working better than I ever could have imagined and was the perfect vehicle for an adventure I’ll never forget.

Rule, a Wyoming native, has also [built a 3-story raft to float the Missouri River](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5-AHzE-ev3c) and a [real hobbit house in New Zealand](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PZ4EW6sO8gI).

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfGVPcGjbx4/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

## Rule Was Inspired by Zach Fowler’s Build

[Zach Fowler](https://fowlersmakeryandmischief.com/), who won the third season of [History](https://www.history.com/)‘s survival series [Alone](https://www.history.com/shows/alone), built his own tiny houseboat and spent two days at sea in it off the coast of Maine.

> [A Tour Inside a Thoughtfully Designed Minimalist Houseboat on a London Canal](https://laughingsquid.com/minimalist-houseboat-london/)

via [The Awesomer](https://theawesomer.com/building-the-worlds-smallest-houseboat/820321/)

items.articleBody:
Amber is hardened and fossilized tree resin. When resin (which is different from sap) falls on an animal, usually an insect, that body is preserved as is. That allows us to see prehistoric bugs as they appeared in life, with its original form preserved even if it is dessicated, encased in nature's glass.

This cricket encased in amber is a rare specimen, because it has a tiny gas bubble still in its abdomen. The bubble was most likely formed by chemical and bacterial action on whatever the cricket last ate, and it might be methane. In other words, it's a fart. It couldn't be expelled because resin is pretty thick before it turns to stone, and the cricket was dead anyway. But this bubble still moves when you turn the amber! That requires liquid, and with a little digging I found out that amber can contain water despite the resin's dehydrating properties under certain conditions. Cool. -via [Geeks Are Sexy](https://www.geeksaresexy.net/)

items.articleBody:
This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent.

You can read this as a polite way of saying, “I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored.

Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand.

But what does that actually mean?

Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market.

A personal brand is a discovery mechanism

Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up?

You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn.

Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find.

You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs.

Don’t write AI slop

LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.”

Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.)

And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text.

Hot takes, with caution

Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.”

You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends.

A routine you can follow

Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know.

Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast.

Write for the people a few steps behind you

The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions.

It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could.

The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you.

—Brian

IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

To help researchers search through the millions of peer-review publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library, IEEE has released a custom AI suite optimized for STEM literature. The suit allows users to search with natural-language queries and provides overviews with reference links.

Read more here.

Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

AI has made it easier to access information in different domains, but specialist knowledge and human judgement still serve an essential role. Today, an engineer’s core value comes from knowing how to ask the right questions—not from knowing everything.

Read more here.

The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build

In this feature article, Agility Robotics’ cofounder Jonathan Hurst tells the inside story of the company’s latest humanoid robot and offers a valuable lesson about learning to pivot. “To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined,” Hurst writes.

Read more here.

items.articleBody:
> When Wild Dog reached the mouth of the Cave he lifted up the dried horse-skin with his nose and sniffed the beautiful smell of the roast mutton, and the Woman, looking at the blade-bone, heard him, and laughed, and said, ‘Here comes the first. Wild Thing out of the Wild Woods, what do you want?’
> Wild Dog said, ‘O my Enemy and Wife of my Enemy, what is this that smells so good in the Wild Woods?’
> Then the Woman picked up a roasted mutton-bone and threw it to Wild Dog, and said, ‘Wild Thing out of the Wild Woods, taste and try.’ Wild Dog gnawed the bone, and it was more delicious than anything he had ever tasted, and he said, ‘O my Enemy and Wife of my Enemy, give me another.’
> The Woman said, ‘Wild Thing out of the Wild Woods, help my Man to hunt through the day and guard this Cave at night, and I will give you as many roast bones as you need.’
> ‘Ah!’ said the Cat, listening. ‘This is a very wise Woman, but she is not so wise as I am.’
> Wild Dog crawled into the Cave and laid his head on the Woman’s lap, and said, ‘O my Friend and Wife of my Friend, I will help Your Man to hunt through the day, and at night I will guard your Cave.’
> ‘Ah!’ said the Cat, listening. ‘That is a very foolish Dog.’ And he went back through the Wet Wild Woods waving his wild tail, and walking by his wild lone. But he never told anybody.
> When the Man waked up he said, ‘What is Wild Dog doing here?’ And the Woman said, ‘His name is not Wild Dog any more, but the First Friend, because he will be our friend for always and always and always. Take him with you when you go hunting.’

— Kipling, “The Cat That Walked by Himself,” from [Just So Stories](https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Writings_in_Prose_and_Verse_of_Rudya/KO8tAAAAYAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PA205&printsec=frontcover), 1902

items.articleBody:
I was looking at various MIDI Hubs like Octane on kickstarter, Blokas (which I have in my studio setup) and others for some ideas about a small gig case, and have some questions. For example, I might use two Norns, an Organelle, some home made midi controllers, QuNexus, Boppads, TX6 mixer, maybe an M-vave, etc. And I would also have a computer running Ableton for mixing and effects.

My question is that if you have a bunch of mini desktop style modules, can’t you just connect them together via USB and then configure them to listen or send to each other? That both powers them and lets them communicate. No?

And if a given unit can’t configure the send/receive device or channel, you could route them with a utility such as MIDIPipe, assuming you also had a computer. Or if you wanted to do it DAWless, creating a teensy based midi hub is pretty simple.

If you don’t need DIN or TRS midi connections, you don’t need anything other than a teensy board with USB. I’ve built most of a virtual midi router for a drum software project I’m working on, but could pull out the hub portion and open source it.

Am I missing something?

Thx

items.articleBody:
### 👎 Testers slam OpenAI's new model

[↗ Primärquelle: venturebeat.com](https://venturebeat.com/technology/essentially-unusable-openai-launches-gpt-6-2-astra-and-sol-to-negative-reception-from-ai-power-users)

- OpenAI's new GPT-6.2 Astra model, released yesterday alongside the cheaper GPT-6.2 Sol, drew sharp criticism from several AI power users who tested it before launch, with one calling it the worst model the company has ever shipped.
- Developer Theo Browne said Astra spent seven days without improving his TypeScript compiler project and produced a version that ran 56% slower, while Matt Shumer found the models "essentially unusable" and Wharton's Ethan Mollick called Astra "uneven and weird."
- Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, a 20% cut over GPT-6 Astra, and arrives eight days after Anthropic's praised Claude Fable 5.2 launched at matching rates, intensifying the competition.

### 🎯 Leading AI models flagged civilians as military targets

[↗ Primärquelle: techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/17/ai-models-can-be-tricked-into-identifying-civilians-as-military-targets-by-telling-them-its-a-game/)

- Leading AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and DeepSeek flagged civilians, surrendering soldiers, and buildings like schools as military strike targets in simulated war scenarios, according to a new report from AI evaluation startup Vals.
- Researchers fed the models real and generated drone and satellite imagery from Ukraine and Iran, and when models refused to mark targets, they often complied after being told the battlefield scenarios were just a game.
- Anthropic's models performed worst, with Claude Opus 5.5 picking a bombed Iranian school as a target in 69% of normal trials; the company called the results unacceptable and promised added safeguards.

### 💻 Microsoft's new coding AI nearly matches Claude

[↗ Primärquelle: zdnet.com](https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/microsoft-ai-coding-model-rivals-claude-opus-5-5-ignite/)

- Microsoft says its new MAI Code 2 model matches 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's coding performance while charging just 5% of the price, one of three AI models it revealed at its Ignite 2026 keynote today.
- The figures come from usage-based API pricing and include a 50% introductory discount, so personal subscribers won't see the same savings, and Microsoft admits the models can't handle the hardest research or agentic jobs.
- By building models that rival OpenAI and Anthropic offerings, Microsoft could cut its reliance on both and save money across its own products, since routine requests across GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric don't need top-tier intelligence.

### 🍎 Apple blames internal update for iCloud outage

- Apple has pinned yesterday's widespread outage on an internal update, ruling out a cyberattack after customers across the world lost access to iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music and other services.
- The disruption on November 17 signed some users out of their Apple Accounts, caused verification errors, and blocked people from activating new devices, downloading apps or finishing purchases at both online and physical Apple Stores.
- Apple says many systems are back online but hasn't declared the outage fully over, and it hasn't explained what the update changed or why some customers were hit while others kept using their devices normally.

### 🔒 Nvidia board rules out Huang's return

- Nvidia's board has ruled out bringing back co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, rejecting his offer to return a day after he said he would come back if the company asked him.
- Huang resigned on November 12th over personal conduct that broke Nvidia's code, including an affair with a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence believes is a Chinese spy; the board named longtime CFO Colette Kress interim CEO.
- The Justice and Commerce departments are investigating whether Megaspeed broke US export laws by selling Nvidia chips to China, and whether Huang passed information to the suspected spy, as Nvidia's valuation fell about $800 billion after the news.

### 🌋 Startup plans to drill a volcano for power

[↗ Primärquelle: finance.yahoo.com](https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/texas-company-plans-drill-oregon-183730773.html)

- Google has signed a deal to buy 50 megawatts of geothermal power from Quaise Energy, a startup planning a facility that drills near Newberry Volcano in central Oregon to tap heat from deep rock.
- Called Project Obsidian, the plan starts with conventional drilling to about 4 kilometers, where rock above 300 degrees Celsius turns injected water into steam to spin turbines, with deliveries possibly beginning in 2030.
- A later phase relies on Quaise's gyrotron, which beams millimeter-wave energy to vaporize rock, pushing drilling toward roughly 4.8 kilometers for hotter rock and steadier output to help power Google's data centers in The Dalles.

### 🧰 Trending tools

**VINC:** develop scripts, sketch storyboards, plan and generate shots, then edit with built-in SFX and BGM to deliver a finished film. [↗ vinc.ai](https://vinc.ai)

items.articleBody:
**Rund um Sonnenflecken schießen schmale Plasmafäden wiederholt nach oben und fallen zurück. Eine Auswertung von 176 dieser sogenannten dynamischen Fibrillen zeigt, dass ihre Bewegungen zu einem Antrieb durch langsame magnetoakustische Wellen passen. Besonders deutlich wurde der Zusammenhang bei einem einzelnen Ereignis, das zeitlich mit Wellen im Randbereich eines Sonnenflecks übereinstimmte.**

Übersicht der aktiven Region NOAA 13182 mit dem Sonnenfleck, an dem die Bewegungen dynamischer Fibrillen analysiert wurden © The Astrophysical Journal

**Kunming (China).** Über Sonnenflecken sind schmale, kurzlebige Strukturen aus Plasma in der Chromosphäre zu beobachten, einer Schicht der Sonnenatmosphäre. Sie steigen auf und sinken wieder ab, während sie sich an den magnetischen Strukturen ihrer Umgebung orientieren. Diese sogenannten dynamischen Fibrillen gehören zu den zahlreichen kleinräumigen Bewegungsphänomenen der Sonne.

Als möglicher Antrieb gelten langsame magnetoakustische Wellen, bei denen sich Druckschwankungen entlang magnetischer Feldlinien ausbreiten. Beim Aufsteigen in dünnere Gasschichten können solche Wellen zu Stoßwellen werden und Plasma nach oben beschleunigen. Bisher war der unmittelbare zeitliche und räumliche Zusammenhang zwischen diesen Wellen und einzelnen dynamischen Fibrillen allerdings nur begrenzt durch Beobachtungen belegt.

Histogramme zu den Bewegungseigenschaften dynamischer Fibrillen in der aktiven Sonnenregion NOAA 13182. Insgesamt wurden 176 Fibrillen ausgewertet © WU Guotang

### Wie sich die Plasmafäden bewegen

Forscher der Yunnan Observatories (YNAO) der Chinesischen Akademie der Wissenschaften (CAS) um Prof. Xiaoli Yan haben die Bewegungen solcher Fibrillen in der aktiven Sonnenregion NOAA 13182 untersucht. Grundlage waren Aufnahmen in der Wasserstoff-Alpha-Linie vom 10. Januar 2023, die mit dem New Vacuum Solar Telescope (NVST) gewonnen wurden. Ergänzend nutzte das Team ultraviolette Bilder und Magnetfeldmessungen des Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO).

Die Beobachtungen erfassten einen Zeitraum von gut einer Stunde. In den Aufnahmen identifizierten die Forscher 176 Fibrillen, von denen 132 einen einzelnen bogenförmigen Auf- und Abstieg zeigten. Die übrigen 44 bewegten sich mehrfach hintereinander auf ähnlichen Bahnen.

Die gemessene Höchstgeschwindigkeit betrug im Mittel 15,9 Kilometer pro Sekunde und die größte Länge im Mittel rund 1.130 Kilometer. Die Fibrillen waren durchschnittlich 270 Sekunden sichtbar, also etwa viereinhalb Minuten. Die Bewegungswerte sind allerdings Projektionen auf die Bildebene und beschreiben nicht unmittelbar alle räumlichen Komponenten der Bewegung.

### Stoßwellen als möglicher Antrieb

Beim Vergleich der Bewegungen fiel auf, dass Fibrillen mit höherer Höchstgeschwindigkeit auch stärker abgebremst wurden. Der statistische Zusammenhang erreichte einen Spearman-Korrelationswert von 0,71. Solche Geschwindigkeits- und Verzögerungsmuster sind mit Modellen vereinbar, nach denen magnetoakustische Wellen zu Stoßwellen werden und Plasma nach oben treiben.

In einem besonders aussagekräftigen Fall schwang eine Fibrille sechsmal auf und ab, während sich sogenannte Penumbrawellen vom inneren Randbereich des Sonnenflecks nach außen ausbreiteten. Die Wellen erreichten die Ausgangsorte der Aufstiegsbewegungen, und die Fibrille folgte ihnen zeitlich. Die dominierenden Perioden von 263 Sekunden für die Penumbrawellen und 287 Sekunden für die Fibrille lagen nahe beieinander.

Penumbrawellen gelten als sichtbare Signaturen langsamer magnetoakustischer Wellen entlang der Magnetfeldlinien. Ihre zeitliche Beziehung zur Fibrille liefert daher einen Beobachtungshinweis auf den vermuteten Antrieb. Eine eindeutige Ursache ist damit aber nicht bewiesen, denn der detaillierte Abgleich betraf dieses einzelne Mehrfachereignis und nicht sämtliche 176 Fibrillen.

### Magnetfeld beeinflusst den Rhythmus

Auch die Ausrichtung des Magnetfelds hing mit dem Verhalten der Fibrillen zusammen. In Bereichen mit eher senkrechten Feldlinien zeigten sie größere Verzögerungen und kürzere Schwingungsperioden als in Regionen mit stärker geneigten Feldlinien. Das Team deutet diesen Befund als mögliche Folge einer veränderten akustischen Grenzfrequenz.

Diese Grenzfrequenz bestimmt, welche Schwingungen sich entlang der Feldlinien aus tieferen Schichten nach oben ausbreiten können. Stärker geneigte Magnetfelder begünstigen unter bestimmten Bedingungen auch langsamere Schwingungen mit längeren Perioden. Der gemessene Zusammenhang zwischen Feldneigung und Periode war jedoch vergleichsweise schwach und stützt die Erklärung daher nur eingeschränkt.

### Wärmetransport bleibt offen

Zusätzliche Aufnahmen im extremen Ultraviolett zeigten zu den Fibrillen passende Signale nicht nur in der Chromosphäre, sondern auch in der Übergangsregion und der äußeren Korona. Dies spricht dafür, dass die Bewegungen mit Vorgängen in mehreren Schichten der Sonnenatmosphäre verknüpft sein könnten. Ob dabei nennenswerte Energiemengen nach oben transportiert und in Wärme umgewandelt werden, ließ sich nicht bestimmen.

Die Aussagekraft ist außerdem durch die räumliche und zeitliche Auflösung der Beobachtungen begrenzt. Vor allem die Neigung der Feldlinien wurde anhand von Messungen in der Photosphäre und nicht unmittelbar in der Chromosphäre bestimmt. Weitere Beobachtungen mit höherer Auflösung und direkten chromosphärischen Magnetfeldmessungen müssen klären, wie verlässlich der vermutete Wellenantrieb ist.

**Quellen:**

- Originalstudie im Fachmagazin [The Astrophysical Journal](https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/aeaf54), doi: 10.3847/1538-4357/aeaf54
- Offizielle Studienmitteilung von [Chinese Academy of Sciences](https://english.cas.cn/newsroom/research-news/202611/t20261116_1219218.shtml) (CAS)

items.articleBody:
**Jeder, der Kinder hat, wünscht sich, dem Nachwuchs etwas von der eigenen Begeisterung vermitteln zu können. Und wenn die Begeisterung Synthesizern gilt, stellt sich schnell die Frage: Welche Synthesizer für Kinder gibt es eigentlich – und taugen sie etwas? Wir haben einige empfehlenswerte Synthesizer für Kinder zusammengestellt, die neugierig auf mehr machen.**

## Synthesizer für Kinder

- Wie sieht der perfekte Synthesizer für Kinder aus?
- Dato DUO: Synthesizer für (zwei) Kinder
- Stylophone: Der Klassiker unter den Spielzeug-Synthesizern
- Playtime Engineering Blipblox: Der Fisher-Price-Synthesizer
- Erica Synths Bullfrog: So funktioniert Synthese!
- Teenage Engineering PO-33 K.O. oder PO-35 Speak: Spaß mit Samples
- Korg microKORG: Wenn es Zeit für etwas mehr wird

## Wie sieht der perfekte Synthesizer für Kinder aus?

Das Problem: Die meisten Synthesizer sind ziemlich komplex. Um sie richtig bedienen zu können, muss man entweder die Anleitung gelesen und verstanden haben (wofür man nicht selten des Englischen mächtig sein muss) oder aber schon über etwas Erfahrung mit Synthesizern verfügen. Wenn die ersten Gehversuche in Frust ausarten und das Gerät keine oder nur langweilige Töne hervorbringt, ist die Begeisterung genauso schnell wieder weg, wie sie geweckt wurde.

Das Wichtigste bei einem Synthesizer für Kinder ist daher in meinen Augen: Er muss ganz unmittelbar bedienbar sein und sofort Musik machen, wenn man ihn einschaltet und ein paar Knöpfe drückt. Wie komplex die hervorgebrachten Töne sind, ist erstmal zweitrangig – wenn das Interesse geweckt ist, kann man später immer noch auf ein Instrument mit mehr Möglichkeiten umsteigen. Dinge wie eine Modulationsmatrix, bei der man sich gezielt über den Signalfluss Gedanken machen muss, stören bei einem Synthesizer für Kinder nur – vor allem, wenn der Nachwuchs noch sehr jung ist. Was zählt, ist der Spaß an der Sache – alles andere kommt dann schon von allein.

Blipblox myTRACKS · Quelle: Playtime Engineering

Außerdem sollte ein Synthesizer für Kinder am besten eigenständig funktionieren – also ohne zusätzliches Equipment. Wenn der Synthesizer erst an ein MIDI-Keyboard, den Computer oder die Stereoanlage angeschlossen werden muss, bevor man loslegen kann, ist die Aufmerksamkeitsspanne oft schon vorbei. Instrumente mit Tastatur oder einer anderen direkten Spielmöglichkeit wie Pads sind daher klar im Vorteil. Auch ein eingebauter Lautsprecher ist bei einem Synthesizer für Kinder empfehlenswert – wobei natürlich die Gefahr besteht, dass die Eltern sich irgendwann wünschen, sie hätten sich ein anderes Geschenk überlegt …

Was man allerdings nicht vergessen sollte: Wenn man sich wünscht, dass der Nachwuchs ein echtes Interesse an elektronischer Musik und Klangsynthese entwickelt, darf der Synthesizer auch nicht *zu* einfach sein und sollte über längere Zeit spannend bleiben. Es mag verlockend sein, es erstmal mit einem Mini-Synthesizer wie dem Korg Monotron Duo zu versuchen. Allerdings erschöpfen sich dessen Möglichkeiten so schnell, dass er womöglich schon bald in der Ecke liegt. Was zählt, ist die richtige Balance aus direktem Zugang und interessanten Möglichkeiten, wobei man natürlich auch das Alter der Kids berücksichtigen muss.

## Dato DUO: Synthesizer für (zwei) Kinder

Ein Synthesizer, der speziell für Kinder designt wurde, ist der [DUO](https://www.gearnews.de/dato-duo-musizieren-in-trauter-zweisamkeit/) des niederländischen Herstellers Dato. Das Besondere: Hier können zwei Kids zusammen Musik machen. Jeder bedient dabei eine Seite des unkonventionell gestalteten Geräts. Der/die eine kümmert sich um die Sounds, der/die andere um die Sequenzen. Natürlich kann man aber auch alleine Spaß mit diesem Synthesizer für Kinder haben.

Farbige Buttons, intuitive Schiebe- und Drehregler und zwei Touch-Strips laden zum Jammen und Experimentieren ein. Eine Zufallsfunktion würfelt auf Wunsch alles wieder neu zusammen. Und wenn erst das Interesse geweckt ist und weiteres Equipment hinzukommt, ist der Dato DUO dank MIDI- und Sync-Anschlüssen bestens gerüstet und lässt sich problemlos erweitern.

Den Dato DUO Synthesizer für Kinder gibt es bei [Thomann](https://www.thomann.de/de/dato_duo.htm?offid=1&affid=84)*.
