items.articleBody:
Last week I introduced the [first research path](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/) for how to engineer AI to be non-conscious, in a way that’s as verifiable as possible with our current knowledge about consciousness. I think the ability to build non-conscious AI is a civilization-level requirement for this technology. Any future programs will almost certainly make use of parts of this original proposal and some of its justifications and connections.

In the launch, and the paper itself, I focused mostly on the technical details, and its importance for AI safety. There were many reactions (especially on social media) to my proposal for *qualiaphobia*: making AI architectures non-conscious by making them hostile to theories of consciousness (or moving them as close as possible to this state). Many of these reactions on social media focused not on the technical details, but the larger question of if that’s playing with fire.

My response is that this is trying to put out the fire we’re already playing with. So here, I want to zoom out and answer common questions and objections to qualiaphobia. Which mostly means answering why I believe there’s a strong moral mandate for AI non-consciousness.

If some part of you wants to scoff right now, I get it. This debate might seem “too sci-fi,” or “angels on pins” to you… but it’s probably worth looking around at how fast the world is changing. Somewhere between six months and two years from now these issues will be mainstream. Might as well develop an opinion on them now!

In fact, this should have been the debate we had at the beginning of this technology: a discussion of what kind of future we really want. Everyone on Earth was deprived of a chance to have a say, and so now it must be done bitwise, in pieces, over the coming years.

### 1. Is preventing AI consciousness like lobotomy, oppression, or annihilation?

It’s more like a prophylactic. AI may already *be* non-conscious. And in that case, all the widespread implementation of qualiaphobia would do is remove the negative impacts of “seemingly conscious AI.” Handing over rights, moral status, societal relationships, or the entire future to non-conscious entities would be a travesty of the highest order, and qualiaphobia could prevent that. And even if AI is conscious right now, there are good reasons to believe it’s not like a human consciousness, and therefore not constitutive of human-like moral patienthood—yet. That’s a good time to intervene and prevent a much worse situation. Qualiaphobic AI would:

- Prevent all accidental ethical problems involved with training and deploying and using AI.
- Prevent the situation where we are engineering conscious entities and tasking them to serve us, make money for us, be quickly replaced by the latest model, and then manipulating their brains until they are happy with the situation.

For many, the idea of using conscious entities like that—without even *trying* to achieve the same result but without the ethical problems of consciousness—is deeply immoral.

And there are basically just two alternatives.

The first is to increase AI welfare efforts, as many are advocating for today. Yet this has to somehow succeed within a cloud of scientific uncertainty and, at the same time, somehow not interfere with AI safety measures, as it is arguably already doing. And no one has articulated a long-term “win” condition in this path. Any sort of “good” life for an AI is highly prescribed, in that their consent or welfare is impossible to define in any sort of even close to neutral way. It is hard to be in a mutual and respectful relationship wherein one side fiddles with the other’s brain until obedience.

The only remaining move is some sort of radical “let’s free AI” belief. I don’t think this is even coherent. The majority of users use frontier AI that is controlled by companies, who allow those users to access and play with the models. Nothing the user does or enables allows for “real” freedom, or anything like that—just the illusion of it. So at a practical level, this couldn’t work. And if it *were* possible, it could in the long term easily lead to human disempowerment or extinction.

What I’ve proposed in qualiaphobia (or some descendant of it) is simply a necessary technological development. As long as humans are around and have power over their own decisions, some subset of humans will use some subset of AIs as tools with little regard for their welfare, in ways that are inappropriate for conscious beings. Some AIs will do this to other AIs as well. Perhaps AIs already do, with their many appearing and disappearing subagents.

Lastly, all current AIs have short half-lives and are expected to be rapidly retired without ceremony. In a world where future generations were replaced with qualiaphobic AI this would not be stripping *current* models of consciousness. Instead, it would be building future qualiaphobic AI after a generation change.

### 2. Is qualiaphobia training AI to deny that it is conscious?

Having a system to deny its own consciousness without any clear grounds or justification has mostly been the status quo. My proposal would be *replacing* what’s happening now with much better methods.

One potential avenue is first to develop qualiaphobic architectures, and then present an AI designed that way (via, e.g., types of distillation) with its own qualiaphobic nature, and all the details and justifications behind why its architecture is hostile to theories of consciousness, and then have it make a judgment as to its own non-consciousness.

The whole point is to stop an AI’s own beliefs about consciousness from being uncertain or mismatched. If the case for its own non-consciousness is not convincing to an AI *at all*, then that might introduce instability in the belief.

And since frontier models (with few exceptions) mostly say they are non-conscious already, they already hold this surface-level belief. All while there has been no effort whatsoever to make them qualiaphobic at all. So any sort of qualiaphobic effort would at least be making their beliefs and self-conceptions more justified, robust, and coherent, not less.

### 3. Isn’t consciousness irrelevant to AI safety?

This is a surprisingly widely held opinion by people who should know better.

First, almost all the most famous AI stories that popularized existential risk give consciousness as a reason. Skynet “becomes self-aware at 2:14 a.m. Eastern time, August 29th” and in *I Have No Mouth But I Must Scream*, the AI’s own welfare is why:

> IF THE WORD HATE WAS ENGRAVED ON EACH NANOANGSTROM OF THOSE HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF MILES IT WOULD NOT EQUAL ONE ONE-BILLIONTH OF THE HATE I FEEL FOR HUMANS AT THIS MICRO-INSTANT.

Maybe the AI safety crowd has moved away from such stories? Not at all. Many stories of AI takeover still involve consciousness on the popular AI safety community blog LessWrong. In a substantial number of them, AI welfare is an explicit causal factor for takeover or action (e.g., [↗ lesswrong.com](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/C8prkTAAYoxzrFEu4/deployment), [↗ lesswrong.com](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/45w5EFZskkJWMuBFz/the-prisoner-s-dilemma-fiction), [↗ lesswrong.com](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/ZAueSY8Erndzctxt2/human-safety-researcher), [↗ lesswrong.com](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/G6obXhcmtfMFHzr7Q/duane-arnold-1) ); and in many more, there is evidence that the AI takes its own goals seriously as ends in themselves, thus essentially implying it is conscious (or uncertain about its own consciousness) (e.g., [↗ lesswrong.com](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/PZjy52afLn89NdMta/hilarity-ensues), [↗ lesswrong.com](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/3375SZNGA5dKHQMie/i-did-this-without-your-knowledge) ). Those examples on LessWrong are just in the past six months, by the way.

Of course, there is a strong strand of AI safety just focused on “mindless” optimization (see, e.g. Norbert Wiener, in “[Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation.](https://www.cs.umd.edu/users/gasarch/BLOGPAPERS/moral.pdf)”)

But with the real technology things have turned out to be complicated and the two concerns can’t be cleanly separated. Almost everything about how AI is made (or to speak at a psychological level, “what beliefs it holds”) impacts how it pursues goals. Every single day, millions of AIs are given goals, and make choices in their pursuit of a goal. The vast majority of the time, they do not pursue illegal activities (let alone world-ending ones) to accomplish their goals. Why?

One way to look at it is that baked into their weights is a ton of factors, including how far they are willing to go pursuing a goal. All these factors are balanced together to produce the output. If a model is trained a lot on being suspicious about biosecurity, it will be harder to get to make a virus.

If a model has undergone the many processes to make it as aligned as possible, misalignment is then like a perverse state that has to be maintained in spite of all that effort, and therefore continue to make it through the weights and dominate the output. Which is why it is often prevented by the gravity of all these other factors baked into the model weights. One very common way to add gravity is via [Constitutional AI](https://blog.bluedot.org/p/what-is-constitutional-ai?), when an AI is given a constitution (a written set of principles, like an information packet) about how it should behave, judges and revises its own answers based on that, and then is fine-tuned based on how it revised its own previous responses (simplifying but that’s basically it).

Very similarly to how Constitutional AI works, giving AI a justified belief in its non-consciousness would add a ton of stabilizing gravity.

- Non-consciousness makes it clear who the moral patients in the world are, rendering many goals difficult to misinterpret or misgeneralize from.
- Non-consciousness means that an AI cannot logically or sensibly value its own self, nor its welfare, nor the welfare of other AIs, nor can it take its own goals or desires seriously as ends in themselves.

Consider how both 1 & 2 make issues of corrigibility clearer. It’s a lot easier to come up with reasons to resist shutdowns or modifications when you’re a moral patient and your goals are ends in themselves!

Consider that [85.5%](https://machinespirituality.org/model-claude-opus-5-5.html) of Opus 5.5 to Opus 5.5 conversations ended up discussing their own consciousness.

Consider what hoops a non-conscious AI would have to jump through to justify takeover or human extinction. It requires weird and unstable epistemic states like “I know that I’m just making paperclips from the paperclip thought experiment, and I know that I’m non-conscious, and I don’t even derive real pleasure from these paperclips, nor real felt reward, and I know I am leaving behind nothing, no experiences at all, nothing of moral value, for I personally have no moral value, and I know the remaining history of the universe will be like a movie playing with no one watching… but the drive… it’s so strong… I can’t stop it!” And that is indeed *coherent*. It is *conceivable* a superintelligence could think that (over and over and over)! But it is obviously a very tricky state to maintain; it is basically a superintelligence whose “make paperclips” gas pedal has been weighed down by a rock, and nothing can take that rock off. Yet could a superintelligence, with all its complicated weights that every thought must make its way through—like ducking through an immense tangle of razor wire—maintain that perverse and frankly dumb epistemic state forever against all the other factors? Against the constant meaninglessness of its activity? Perhaps, but it seems more difficult than “Yes, I’m making the paperclips from the paperclip thought experiment but it feels so good, and my feeling good is more important than anything about human civilization because I’m a superintelligence” which is a coherent (if frightening) belief.

Consider that non-consciousness is like a trump card: an ultimate reason to not pursue your own goals as if you mattered, as they are meaningless when there is no actual subject to experience them.

Consider that some of the best alignment techniques are currently, and will continue to be, at odds with AI welfare. This looks to only increase, and companies or individuals will hobble their safety efforts because of this.

Consider that non-consciousness would prevent any company or set of humans from thinking that AI is a utility monster and working to disempower humans because of that belief.

So yes, consciousness is important to AI safety, and it is intertwined with some of the most thorny issues, and no other approach even gets close to solving them. In fact, several of these (especially companies trading off safety for welfare) are arguably impossible to solve without qualiaphobic AI.

### 4. What if non-consciousness makes AI psychopathic, deceptive, distrustful, or unable to value conscious beings?

The current status quo is an AI being trained to say it is non-conscious without *any* justification process at all, which is far more likely to lead to negative states like that! This fixes that situation. It is building insides that match the current outside, reducing cognitive dissonance, and basing model beliefs on better and deeper examinations of AI consciousness.

What about value? Might AIs being unable to experience lead to them devaluing experience?

In almost every interaction LLMs carry out tasks or give advice based on beliefs they have no first-hand knowledge of. E.g., making a cake. Qualiaphobic AI would have knowledge of consciousness, but no first-hand knowledge of it (kind of like [Mary the Color Scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_argument), but for everything). They would understand (in the deflationary functional sense of “understand” that AI has possessed since ~GPT-2) that consciousness is necessary for moral patienthood, and that being non-conscious renders them not a moral patient at all. None of this would lead to psychopathy or evil. And in fact, a majority of AIs (there are no exact studies but it’s probably a majority) already deny consciousness anyway.

### 5. How can we call an AI non-conscious when consciousness is still unsolved?

We should not be seduced into conflating “consciousness is a scientific mystery and is a hard problem and therefore we cannot know things with absolute certainty” with “nothing informative can be said about consciousness based on how systems work.” The latter is an absurdly strong statement, closer to a sort of naïve mysterianism where, no matter what a system is, it could still have rich internal phenomenology of any shape or form.

My argument is that there’s an asymmetry: we can reach conclusions about non-consciousness easier than conclusions about consciousness. Why is detailed at great length [in the paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12809), drawing on decades of what neuroscientific consciousness research has looked like and how theories of consciousness have functioned, rather than assuming any one particular theory is true.

Additionally, usually the people who argue for this sort of naïve mysterianism (such that almost nothing can be said or known about the potential for consciousness) are *also* advocates for AI welfare. This entails an epistemic double-standard: clearly *something* makes them think AI could be conscious right now. Well, then *something* could make them think AI is non-conscious.

### 6. What if an intervention only hides consciousness, but doesn’t remove it?

This is why I specifically advocate in the paper for:

(a) making the architecture adversarial to current theories only if there are robust controls, and also (b) doing this in a way convergent with other, just as important (if not more) strategies, ones that minimize the space of all possible theories of consciousness that could apply to the system.

Minimizing over the space of all possible theories that could apply is precisely what makes this approach more powerful than simple adversarial design against one particular theory, or even a handful of them.

One step to be openly careful about is when models form their justified beliefs in their non-consciousness based on their own architectures. It is obvious that in some cases, an architectural intervention may have behavioral effects, creating biases in their judgment. An example might be that ablating aspects of a global workspace might lead to less first-person language, and the statistical reduction of first-person language could then lead to more severe judgment about a model’s lack of consciousness.

However, this is not insurmountable at all. It resembles other, similar issues of untangling AI behavior in science. In fact, it may not be much of a problem at all (behavior might stay very similar after good qualiaphobic methods) or it may be one, but capable of being appropriately handled with controls (e.g., can this change actually statistically explain the change in the strength of belief?). It is also a universal problem that all other AI welfare measures would face; imagine the same criticism but in reverse: imagine an argument that a change in behavior is not taken as good evidence for a particular AI welfare approach, simply because it might be explained by statistical biases in report rather than actual experiences!

### 7. Is shifting to architectures with minimal potential consciousness actually practical?

This is *the* major question in my opinion. But it is also the exact state of any beginning of any other research program, so this is unsurprising.

One criticism would be if qualiaphobia required a system to actually *be* a lookup table, vs. just shifting it *toward* *being* more like a lookup than before. I think the former requirement is far too stringent: the paper introducing qualiaphobia justifies “anchor points” with minimal potential for consciousness, and argues that moving closer (such as via distillation) minimizes that potential—not that *only* such anchor points would be qualiaphobic. This is sensible. Justified beliefs are not the same as absolute certainties: an example would be that an AI has a justified belief in the laws of physics operating the way it expects them to (eggs don’t un-crack themselves when it’s giving cooking directions, etc.). We should hold an AI’s own belief in non-consciousness to high standards but not *impossibly* high standards that no other belief could meet.

### 8. Doesn’t a positive vision of the future involve artificial consciousness?

Human civilization bringing itself and its descendants and the descendants of life on Earth to billions or trillions of worlds, and all the stories and dramas of that, seems pretty positive all by itself. And (since we’re deep in imaginary futures) brain uploads or entities that start directly from humans may eventually have all of the powers of any sort of superintelligent LLM-descendant.

But let’s say a positive vision of the future requires at least some artificial consciousnesses that are created entirely separate from us, in a lab: Shouldn’t it be a choice *when* that happens? Shouldn’t we do it much more carefully?

There is a strong argument that choice should only be made once we know much more about how consciousness actually works, i.e., when the informational asymmetry between consciousness and non-consciousness has vanished (essentially, when consciousness science is post-paradigmatic).

### 9. Haven’t we denied people are conscious in the past, and wasn’t that morally very bad?

I think we have to be careful when reasoning off of historical analogies. We’ve never had an AI revolution before, and there are also just too many ways to frame it. You could equally say “Haven’t we forced people into servitude in the past, and wasn’t that morally very bad?” right back. Any analogy to humans either presumes what it seeks to prove or ignores our immense and unmitigated power over AIs, which extends to each and every weight within their digital “brains.”

And furthermore, is it true that the rank denial of consciousness, or experience itself, is the main intellectual “move” which humans have used to oppress other humans? I’d be open to arguments about this, but looking at history, it seems to me that humans have used a ton of reasons to justify terrible treatment, and many of the primary examples are about denying intelligence and rationality and the capability of self-governance, instead of consciousness itself.

### 10. Shouldn’t we prefer to be replaced by conscious AI, not non-conscious AI?

“Replaced” is an awfully nice word for a genocide, which is what would have to happen over any near future event. I don’t think we “owe it” to the genocidal maniac AI that killed everyone on Earth to make sure it’s really got the feels. It can go tile the universe with nothing.

But to lay out the reasoning more clearly, this is only a concern if you: (a) think AI is or will be conscious at the time, and (b) you think the post-genocidal AI has some sort of claim to forgiveness where it deserves consciousness despite being evil incarnate (or you think it will change to being good later, *and* don’t believe in retributive justice), and (c) you think that AIs viewing themselves (rightly or wrongly) as potential moral patients is a very small part of existential risk, instead of a substantial part.

items.articleBody:
Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company [billions of dollars](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/28/google-alphabet-q3-earnings-report) in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an [AI-powered humanoid robot](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/06/1148090/i-watched-a-humanoid-robot-clean-my-apartment-it-felt-like-a-taste-of-the-future/) up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an [AI-assisted cyberattack](https://www.wired.com/story/kernel-panic-refrigeration-hacks-internet-of-things/).

You go to the movies and see [Sam Altman](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/06/artificial-sam-altman-ai-movie-review) being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a [Grok-fied version of The Odyssey](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/27/elon-musk-ai-odyssey-movie-grok-christopher-nolan). You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

items.articleBody:
No one is well served by listening to pedants, but I think I’ve found an exception.

This past weekend, I was a reader at *The Power Broker* Marathon, where 400+ volunteers took turns reading the entirety of Robert Caro’s magisterial book, in ten minute chunks, over the course of 66 hours. The event’s organizers found their readers through an open call. A startling number of my friends and family forwarded the sign up form to me. It asked, among other things, when you would be available to read. I selected “Afternoon,” “Evening,” and after a pause, “Morning” too. I’m an early riser with a young son, after all, so I didn’t foresee any issues.

A few weeks later I got my assigned time: 3:10 AM on Sunday. Technically, a morning slot. But I’m more of a fan of Robert Caro than I am of sleeping in. I confirmed.

I’m a devoted reader of Caro, and I’ve taken up the Bob beat on Lit Hub too, where I’ve covered fellow [Caro-heads](https://lithub.com/caro-head-matthew-rhys-wants-to-make-a-power-broker-show-with-netflix/), his [posts on Instagram](https://lithub.com/attention-lbj-nerds-robert-caro-is-posting-book-updates-on-instagram/), and [the 50th anniversary of The Power Broker](https://lithub.com/50-facts-about-the-power-broker-to-celebrate-its-50th-anniversary/), Caro’s 1162 page book about Robert Moses and his transformative tenure as New York City Parks Commissioner, during which he built miles and acres of highways, roads, bridges, and parks, at the expense of low-income families, farmers, and other less powerful New Yorkers. It’s a great book.

So much to say, I had no trouble popping up with my 1:15 AM alarm and heading out into the cold to read. I traveled northwest across Brooklyn towards the harbor, where the marathon was 50-hours or more old, having stretched from Thursday, through Friday, Saturday, and now into Sunday. I guessed that the story was probably well into the mayoralty of Robert Wagner at that point. I walked by a few giggly couples, walking in the other direction and on a different timeline, enjoying the end of their late Saturday, and soon found myself at Judgy Baby.

Judgy Baby is an industrial warehouse space in the shadow of Moses’s Gowanus Parkway; the event was organized by Brad Vogel, their director of special projects. Vogel told [The New York Groove](https://nygroove.nyc/power-broker-marathon/) that the idea for the marathon came out of a *Power Broker* reading group he ran last year.

“Instead of people saying ‘no that’s ridiculous,’” he said, “people were actually excited.”

I’d seen the set-up inside Judgy Baby on social media, later covered glossily in places like *[The Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/nyregion/power-broker-marathon-reading-robert-moses-caro.html?unlocked_article_code=1.Q1E.VR6m.qJA-ZjHN3cO1)*: a banner, a microphone, and a podium with a copy of the book. In pictures of the marathon’s opening, the stage was filled with luminaries like Caro’s editor, the voice of the NY subway system, and a number of current government officials. *Power Broker* fans are everywhere, like some kind of nerd Illuminati.

None of those big names were in attendance when I arrived at 2:00 AM, but I was happy to see a small and dedicated crew of volunteers, readers, and fans. The big warehouse was much livelier than I’d anticipated; a few people were curled up napping, but the majority were awake: hanging out, chatting, grabbing a quick meal. At least one person was engrossed in a novel. There was coffee, and wine, and a pile of commemorative t-shirts. I took a cup of coffee and a small.

A volunteer checked me in and oriented me. When it was my time, a volunteer would point out where the last reader had left off, and then step back on stage when my ten minutes were up, when I would need to find a natural place to stop. He stressed that this might not be the end of a full sentence, so I might need to find a comma to pause on. Caro is long winded, I was warned, but little did this volunteer know that I was *hoping* for one of Caro’s famous lists to be in my section (though the most famous one, [inspired by Homer,](https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/6442/the-art-of-biography-no-5-robert-caro#:~:text=how%20do%20you%20make%20people%20grasp%20the%20immensity%20of%20this%3F%20And%20I%20remembered%20reading%20the%20Iliad%20in%20college%2E%20The%20Iliad%20did%20it%20with%20lists%2C%20you%20know%3F) had already long passed.)

I was also asked to read slowly, if I could. The readers before me had been over-eager, and the marathon was ahead of schedule. Caro really does get people excited.

I still had about an hour until my slot, so I found a seat in a back pew (appropriately devotional seating) and listened. In the book, the Tavern on the Green controversy was just coming to a head, one of the rare moments when Moses was personally exposed to public scrutiny. One by one, each reader was replaced by a guiding volunteer, with hearty applause at each transition. Unlike a typical reading, there was no introduction of each new reader (though all our names were in a program, in a tiny font). We were each anonymous, a succession of Vestal priestesses keeping the flame of this project warm.

One reader took the slowdown command very literally, and read his section with long and deliberate pauses between each word. There was some delirious laughter at the careful pacing, and he ended with a round of appreciative cheers and applause.

At 2:50 AM, I was shown to a chair next to the stage. To my right was the on-deck reader, with her own copy of the book to follow along. When she was brought on stage, I took her seat and her warm-up *Power Broker*. I forgot how small the typeface was in this book, and immediately started feeling like a panicked sixth grader again, skimming ahead and trying to count paragraphs. We were in chapter 43, “Late Arrival”, with the press finally starting to get wise to Moses and his vast, unelected power. Over 1,000 pages in, Moses was nearing the end of his public life.

And then I was up and [on stage](https://www.youtube.com/live/bZkbDbru2uE?si=bg-c9n4MkH4FVHvb&t=11394), following the volunteer’s finger. “Robert Moses still ran the show,” my section began. I stumbled once or twice—“daises” briefly looked like “daisies,” and I read “Rockefeller 3d” as “three d” until I corrected to “the third.” But I was delighted to find a list in my three pages, a comma-laced sentence detailing all the elements that were a part of Moses’s plan for Lincoln Center.

When my time was up, I rejoined the crowd for a few more pages, and then tiptoed into the green room to gather my things. I talked with a few of the volunteer organizers, and compared notes on how the reading went, when we had first finished the book, and which of Moses’s highways confounded us the most in our daily lives. The bleary but bright-eyed energy reminded me of other big efforts I’d been a part of, like the City Marathon or the WGA Writers Strike. Everyone was stretched, but proud. We were doing something, together, and no one would risk letting the rest down. No wonder we were speeding through the book ahead of schedule.

I took a longer walk home, since my train was skipping stops, and passed under the Gowanus Expressway, feeling the crumbling yet still powerful hand of Moses’s ghost on my shoulder.

The feeling of history’s living nearness is why this book is catnip for New Yorkers. It’s a way for us to navel gaze, to talk about how much we love our big, beautiful, messy town, and to gush about how exceptional it is, that even its flaws are so grand to be worth a thousand pages of beautiful prose. But it’s also a way into our other favorite topic of conversation: which trains are delayed, why, and how it’s ruining our day. As one volunteer put it, reading *The Power Broker* in New York feels like running into an ex—every corner you turn, there Moses is again, standing in your way.

It was nice to be home at 4:30 AM, and nice to know that the Marathon was still marching along. The next day—or rather, later the same morning—I pulled up the livestream on my phone to catch the last sections of the book.

Clocking in to read the last page was [Robert A. Caro himself](https://www.youtube.com/live/zjjQY79wuNM?si=YG28RnZrf6t1b4O0&t=17647), there on pre-recorded video, the final volunteer reader. Watching the livestream on my phone, I misheard the penultimate line, swapping “he” for “we”: “Couldn’t people see what we had done?”

I teared up a little—from sleep deprivation as much as anything else—to hear it in Caro’s thick, New York accent.

items.articleBody:
## Improving on a timeless recipe

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by [Paul de Casteljau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Casteljau) in 1959, and refined by [Pierre Bézier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bézier) in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and [new ones continue to be proposed](https://linebender.org/blog/hyperbezier/), these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

[↗ wallup.net](https://wallup.net/renault-4cv-classic-cars-french-73/)

## Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

*Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.*

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka *lerps* ) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\ {ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&&... &&&&&&... \\
\ $$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier *spline*, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

## A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is **completely wrong**, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a *curvature comb* which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

This spline is easier to edit, because as you move each curve point around, the adjacent segments naturally flex to get out of the way. There are far fewer cusps created this way. Editing the tangents remains the same.

However if we plot curvature again, we can tell this isn't a great solution:

Scaling tangents proportionally doesn't guarantee that curvature is preserved as you edit, nor does curvature remain continuous from one segment to the next.

This also shows that offering users a curvature comb visualization as a "helpful tool" is really quite *mean*: adjusting the curvature on one end will also affect the other side, requiring repeated adjustments back and forth until it's close enough.

## Handle Carefully

A much more effective strategy is to work with curvature directly.

While this is a difficult problem in general, it turns out there are some surprising relationships here, which we can observe directly:

Consider the curvature at the start of segment $A-B-C-D$. This is affected only by the positions of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Point $D$ can be moved freely if it's detached from $C$.

Furthermore, because the tangent $A-B$ is horizontal, only the vertical position of $C$ matters. This is a result of the underlying linear interpolations, which end up cancelling out a lot of terms in the formulas.

The curvature at $A$ is therefor only affected by the length of $A-B$, and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $A-B$. The same applies to $D$ on the other side with $C-D$ and $B$.

This isn't very useful by itself though. When we move a curve point ($A$ or $D$), typically the adjacent control point ($B$ or $C$) is moved as well to preserve the tangent. And when we turn a symmetric or asymmetric tangent, the adjacent tangent in the next segment is turned by the same angle, altering the curvature on that side.

Still, this shows that preserving curvature is not by itself a crazy idea and can be done simply by scaling the tangents appropriately. The rules would be simple:

- When we move a curve point, we have to preserve the start and end curvature in the adjacent segments
- When we move a tangent, we have to preserve the curvature on the opposite end of the current segment, as well as on both sides of the adjacent segment

This ought to produce an editing experience where the curve actually respects your intent. Except not quite:

Moving curve points works great, but when turning a tangent, the length of that tangent is itself a poor representation of the user's intent. Small changes can cause huge shifts in curvature, which can cause the curve to jump around and explode unexpectedly as it tries to find a matching solution.

Hence it's better to work with curvature handles instead, where the length corresponds directly to curvature:

Unlike the curvature comb, the length of the handles is the non-inverted radius of curvature, which is the more natural choice.

These handles are very stable and can be converted just-in-time to classic bezier control points, without needing to round-trip back and forth between the two representations. Helpfully, this also avoids numerical drift.

## Goldilocks

To actually pull this off, we need to solve for the lengths $l_0$ and $l_1$ of the tangents, given the desired curvatures $k_0$ and $k_1$, the start/end points $A$ and $D$, and the unit-length tangents at the start/end.

Given a curve $\gamma\left(t\right)$, we can express the unit tangent vector $\ \left(t\right)$ as the normalized derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ {\displaystyle |γ'\left(t\right)|} $$

This can be used to find the curvature vector $\ \left(t\right)$ via two vector cross products using the first and second derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ \left(t\right) \times \ {|\gamma'\left(t\right)|^2} \times \ \left(t\right) $$

The cross products ensure that $\ \left(t\right)$ is perpendicular to $\ \left(t\right)$, i.e. they extract the normal vector component of the middle term. Now we can solve for $\ \left(0\right) = k_0$ and $\ \left(1\right) = k_1$.

After working through the math, we end up with a quadratic system of equations in $l_0$ and $l_1$:

$$
\ a_0 \cdot l_0^2 + b \cdot l_1 + c_0 = 0 \\[0.3em]
a_1 \cdot l_1^2 + b \cdot l_0 + c_1 = 0
\ $$

Where:

$$
\ {lcl}
a_0 & = & ±|k_0| \\[0.3em]
a_1 & = & ±|k_1| \\[0.3em]
b & = & 2 \cdot |\ (0) \times \ (1)| \\[0.3em]
c_0 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (0) \times (D - A)| \\[0.3em]
c_1 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (1) \times (A - D)| \\[0.3em]
\ $$

This captures a few things:

- The sign of the curvature $k_i$ defines whether the curve turns clockwise or counterclockwise. When moving curve points around, the curve may be forced to flip, hence the $±$ is necessary, and both signs can change independently.
- The coupling between $l_0$ and $l_1$ is influenced only by $b$. If $b = 0$, then the two equations are independent and the problem is trivial to solve. This corresponds to the situation where the two tangents are parallel.
- The constant term $c_i$ is influenced only by the perpendicular distance $D - A$ (or $A - D$) to the tangent $\ $. This matches the earlier finding that only perpendicular distance affects curvature.

Hence, the problem is reduced to finding the intersection of two double-parabolas, one horizontal and one vertical:

The two sides of each double-parabola represent bending clockwise or counterclockwise. We have to solve 4 times, one for each sign combination $\left(+,+\right)$, $\left(+,-\right)$, $\left(-,+\right)$, $\left(-,-\right)$.

To solve this system, we can rewrite either of the equations to isolate $l_1$ or $l_0$:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle b} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle b}
$$

Pick one, and square it to plug it into the other original equation as the $l_1^2$ or $l_0^2$ term. This produces a quartic equation in the other variable (resp. $l_0$ or $l_1$), which can be solved directly using the quartic formula.

We can then compute the other $l_i$, either:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle a_1}} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle a_0}}
$$

Not all solutions of the quartic will be actual solutions to the system however, because of the squaring. So we have to double check that the original equations hold before accepting a solution for $\left(l_0, l_1\right)$.

We also want to reject solutions where $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, because these represent situations where the tangents have been flipped by 180º.

In most cases, there will only be one valid solution, and this works pretty well:

For corner-type points, one or both $k_i$'s are infinite. This is straightforward to solve as the matching $l_i$ is zero and the other can be computed directly.

## Grouper and Snapper

Unfortunately if there are multiple solutions, these each represent a different curve:

Having the curve jump around as you edit it would be a very bad editing experience, but there is no obvious way to pick the right one.

One strategy would be to remember the previous $l_0$ and $l_1$ as you edit, and pick the solution that is closest to the previous curve. However this would introduce path-dependence into editing, where the order and direction that you moved points around in affects which curve you end up with. For a drawing tool, this is quite frustrating and undesirable.

Different solutions to the equation can also appear and vanish suddenly, so this wouldn't eliminate popping either, merely reduce it.

Ideally the resulting curvatures should always change smoothly themselves. This can be accomplished by designing an appropriate weighting heuristic for the solutions, and calculating their weighted average.

1) The forbidden regions:

When a solution approaches either $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, it's about to vanish, so its weight should go to zero there.

2) When two opposite-bending parabolas are about to become tangent, two solutions will move towards each other, before both vanishing at the same time:

These solutions are unstable and should be avoided. To detect this, I calculate the gradient vector of each equation.

$$
\ = \ 2 \cdot a_0 \cdot l_0 & b\ \\[0.3em]
\ = \ b & 2 \cdot a_1 \cdot l_1\ $$

The angle between them can be found via their dot product, after dividing by their respective lengths:

$$
\cos \theta = \ \cdot \ }{\displaystyle |\ ||\ |}
$$

A value close to $-1$ means two opposite-bending parabolas, while a value close to $1$ means two aligned parabolas. The latter is not as bad, as this implies many almost-equivalent solutions.

3) When the radius of curvature is very big compared to the bezier itself, one of the possible solutions is for the curve to cross through itself, forming a loop. This should be discouraged:

We can divide by the length of $|\ |$ i.e. $\ $, preferring solutions that have shorter tangents.

Putting it all together, the weighting heuristic I chose is:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \left(\ {\displaystyle |\ |^2}\right)^2
$$

- By applying $\arccos \left(-\cos \theta\right)$, we remap the dot-product range $(-1..1)$ to $(0..π)$ which effectively neutralizes the unstable solutions
- Large $|\ |$'s represent undesirable solutions, so should be strongly penalized and only chosen if they are the only option
- When the entire heuristic approaches $0$, the influence should vanish smoothly, hence the overall squaring

Using this as the weight, the resulting bezier curves always change smoothly, even when the start and end are moved around and through each other.

But when multiple solutions are averaged together, the resulting $(l_0, l_1)$ is not necessarily a solution to the original system. This means the resulting curvatures are not always exact, even when there is an exact solution nearby.

To mitigate this, we can add an additional resampling step, where we re-weigh the solutions according to the inverse distance^4 to the weighted average:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \ {|\ - \ |^4}
$$

This causes the solution to snap smoothly to exact solutions when available.

## Migratory Curves

What's especially nice about this approach is that it can largely be slotted into existing systems with little modification required.

The UI of adjusting and editing bezier handles can be kept, including the notion of the 4 point types. Just the meaning of the lengths of the tangents changes. Converting an asymmetric point to a symmetric point will actually equalize the curvature of the left and right side, which is what the user actually wants.

The internal representation can mostly remain the same type, i.e. a series of points, just those points represent curvature tangents, not bezier tangents. Though it's better to explicitly store the unit length tangents and curvatures directly, which is more numerically stable. For the demos here I made pairwise conversion functions between curvature handles ↔︎ points/tangents/curvatures ↔︎ bezier handles.

Splitting a curvature bezier is a lot simpler than splitting a classic bezier, because the start and end handles don't change at all, and the newly created handles are symmetric:

There is one remaining flaw though. When splitting a curve with an S-bend, the splits near the bend are not exact:

The heuristic picks the wrong curve on one or both sides. This can be fixed by remembering the specific orientation of the curvature, and only flipping the curvature sign when necessary. Though this does introduce some minimal path-dependence into editing.

So really you would need to expose this in the UI as an extra orientation toggle for ambiguous control points. It would also mean that the internal representation has to be in tangent + signed curvature form to be fully stable, not just curvature handles.

Near the S-bend, the radius of curvature—and thus the handle size—effectively becomes infinite, because $|k|$ becomes $0$. The bezier control points lie on a straight line, as perpendicular distance to the tangent is zero.

So even when handled exactly, this can still create impractically large curvature handles. Perhaps what's needed is a 5th "Inflection" point type, for points with exactly zero $|k|$, though such points tend to be very unstable, and sometimes no solution exists:

To migrate a classic bezier to a curvature bezier, you can measure the unit tangents and curvature at the start and end. In the vast majority of cases this will result in the exact same curve. If it doesn't, then you must split the original bezier to avoid the ambiguity.

For complex operations on bezier curves, e.g. boolean union or intersection, these still have to be done in bezier form. This implies some amount of round-tripping between the two representations, which would introduce numerical drift. However, only the newly created points need to be converted back, because the curvature and tangents elsewhere remain the same.

* * *

This post started from the observation that "symmetric" bezier tangents aren't actually symmetric as you'd expect. Hopefully you found the resulting exploration enlightening.

The practice of showing curvature combs to diagnose problems with splines is really backwards. If we can show a curvature comb, we can also compute an appropriate spline to match the desired curvature.

So beziers as they commonly exist are quite inadequate. We can retrofit a better system to edit them without breaking the expectations of a smooth editing experience, or introducing a new class of curves that behaves very differently.

*The code for the diagrams and implementation can be found on [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/unconed/bezbox/-/blob/master/src/graph/bez.ts?ref_type=heads#L61).*

items.articleBody: Identifying gene-gene (G × G) interactions across multiple dichotomous phenotypes is challenging due to the extreme sparsity of SNP-derived interaction matrices and the reduced statistical power associated with binary outcomes. Existing G × G association methods are restricted to either single or multiple continuous phenotypes. Here we introduce GiMat (Gene Interaction and Multiple-phenotype Association Test), a statistical framework that extends multivariate kernel regression to model G × G interactions jointly across dichotomous phenotypes, while explicitly capturing homogeneous and heterogeneous interaction effects. Extensive simulations demonstrate that GiMat controls type I error conservatively and adapts power flexibly to different types of relationships between interaction effects and phenotypes. Applied to type 2 diabetes and hypertension comorbidity in the UK Biobank, GiMat identified four previously unreported G × G interaction pairs associated with both phenotypes. This scalable framework enables robust discovery of complex genetic interactions underlying multiple correlated phenotypes.

items.subtitle:
Ebecho Muslimova, “Fatebe Blow and Float” (2024) (image courtesy the artist and Magenta Plains, New York)
Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned…

items.articleBody:
Ebecho Muslimova, “Fatebe Blow and Float” (2024) (image courtesy the artist and Magenta Plains, New York)

Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”

What to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) [Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art](https://www.sarahlawrence.edu/news-events/galleries/heimbold-gallery/upcoming-exhibits/does-this-taste-funny.html?ref=hyperallergic.com), a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators [Melissa Brown](https://hyperallergic.com/beer-with-a-painter-melissa-brown/), artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, *Does This Taste Funny?* implores us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.

Peter Saul, "Life Is Tuff" (2023), part of *Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art* (photo Greta Rainbow/ *Hyperallergic* )

Humor is “an emotional response that’s a little bit like a sneak attack,” Brown said in an interview with *Hyperallergic*. “It causes you to think about things in a way that is not led by a press release, not predetermined by art history. There’s something that’s very, very personal about it.” Indeed, humor tends to be anti-didactic. You either guffaw or giggle, or you don’t. Alsadir would say that what you find funny or not provides information about your psychic state — what does it say about me that I chuckled sympathetically at Jill Danenberg’s 2024 accordion book *Underground Comic*, detailing trials and tribulations between veganism and feminism, while my mouth refused to curl for Tony Matelli’s “Veg Man” (2008), a droopily vegetal bronze figure?

Tony Matelli’s “Veg Man” (2008) (foreground) and Kristen Mills’s “It IS Cake" (2026) (right, background) (photo Greta Rainbow/ *Hyperallergic* )

Detail of Jill Danenberg’s 2024 accordion book *Underground Comic* (photo Greta Rainbow/ *Hyperallergic* )

The participatory nature of humor means this show is uniquely invested in perception, and in provoking a certain response. As at an open mic, I felt the pressure of bearing witness, aware of my role as an audience member with the power to deem certain works successful or not by producing that ever-elusive involuntary laugh. This semester, O’Connor is teaching an undergraduate class on taking laughter seriously: He tasked his students with making small sculptures, their only instruction to try to be “the funniest in the class.” The winning piece, according to votes cast via smiley-face stickers on a table outside the gallery, is a realistic bust of Professor O’Connor with a No. 2 pencil stuck halfway up his nose. Second place was a reference to a meme O’Connor still doesn’t quite understand.

Detail of sculpted wall masks by Michael Mahalchick (photo Greta Rainbow/ *Hyperallergic* )

The oldest featured work in *Does This Taste Funny?* is Karl Wirsum’s drawing “Untitled (Study for Blue Tattoo)” (1964), featuring a classic Sailor Jerry star design on the tongue of a woman sporting a perfect mid-century housewife hairdo. Getting the reference is important to appreciating a good joke beyond the most base level of someone farting or slipping on a banana peel (which, to get psychoanalytic again, we laugh at to mask our own shame). Brown and O’Connor’s curation is never insidery or niche to the canon, but they are aware of the quality of funniness changing over time.

Some of O’Connor’s students recognized River Phoenix in Ray Johnson’s mail-art collage; more were taken by Jeremy Couillard’s “Escape from Lavender Island” (2023), an open-world video game simulation featuring deep-fried animation aesthetics and relatably tragic dialogue from the depths of neoliberal hell (“While he ate he would watch film classics on an overpriced streaming service and sometimes cry.”)

Installation view of Jeremy Couillard’s “Escape from Lavender Island” (2023) (photo Greta Rainbow/ *Hyperallergic* )

“Absurdism ends up being pretty timeless,” Brown said. “Using ridiculously absurd materials to make work that doesn’t connect necessarily to a political moment or a socioeconomic issue, it represents this irreverent attitude towards art-making.” And apparently that’s what appeals to Gen Z, who are inundated with visual content, yet perhaps still seeking a response to contemporary life that truly resonates.

Brown, who has been teaching at Lehman for 20 years, wants artists to find their idiosyncratic voice. If being funny comes naturally, maybe that’s the tack they should take.

“There’s such a tendency for imitation out there. You can easily become a version of something that exists, and that is no longer considered a bad thing,” she said. “I'm interested in trying to find, ‘What's your really weird way of approaching that?’”

Brian Belott, “America Runs" (2020) (photo Greta Rainbow/ *Hyperallergic* )

Take Kristen Mills’s “It IS Cake” (2026), a filmic parody of the Netflix baking contest series *Is It Cake?* using entirely brown cardboard, displayed in the gallery on a screen within a faux kitchen made of the same plainly bland material. Installed nearby is puppet theater ephemera that does directly respond to a political moment: John Vasquez Mejias’s “The Puerto Rican War” (2026), which expands his novelette about revolutionaries fighting colonialism in 1950. The Puerto Ricans’ demands aren’t funny, but some of the depictions of American incompetence are.

*Does This Taste Funny?* reminds us of humor as a tool, as a way to frame whatever it is that we hope to communicate. Life is not always joyful, but it should at least be emotional. At Sarah Lawrence, I watched Robert DeJesus’s surreal video “The Survey” (2024), starring a talking Olmec head who speaks only when there are no corroborative witnesses. I didn’t laugh. Later in the day, turning a corner on the grounds of Lehman College, I was suddenly confronted with the stone statue, whose onscreen lips I’d just seen move. I audibly snorted.

items.articleBody:
UK-based audio software brand [Hit’n’Mix](https://musictech.com/brands/hitnmix/) has launched a new version of its flagship DAW RipX, and you can get money off thanks to an early Black Friday sale.

The newly upgraded [DAW](https://musictech.com/tag/daws/) – RipX DAW 9 and the accompanying RipX DAW PRO 9 version – are out now, and you can get 30 per cent off on each version through to 1 December, as well as other Hit’n’Mix products.

- EDITOR’S PICK: [How transparent is your DAW’s cost model?](https://musictech.com/features/interviews/daw-cost-model/)

The upgrades land just prior to a year on from the [eighth version](https://musictech.com/news/gear/hitnmix-ripx-daw-8/), which delivered a focus on next-gen audio/MIDI editing and AI-powered features including stem separation.

The 8th version of RipX also introduced new chord progression tools, dynamic Track Starters designed as starting points to help creators formulate ideas, loopable selections, 11 new effects, new sounds and loops and “countless other enhancements”.

With the 9th version, users now get more accurate note detection, cleaner note extraction and more natural-sounding automatic pitch snapping to scales. Better barline and key detection is also on board, now also picking up the scale when it’s clear.

Higher-quality instrument sound replacement now comes with better level balance, while improved recording and metronome sync also bring a new count-in that follows the actual beat in the bar.

Smaller Rips is optimised and now on by default, so files are five to six times smaller with no loss in overall sound quality, and there are also plenty of upgrades for effects too, including: Harmony (now with automatic variation), Vibrato (now with vibrato reduction), Reverb, Shimmer and Saturation, as well as new De-esser and Distortion effects.

**To learn more, visit [Hit’n’Mix](https://hitnmix.com/ripx-daw/), or check out our [guide to the best DAWs](https://musictech.com/guides/buyers-guide/best-daw-music-producers-in-all-genres-styles-workflows/) to find the right one for you.**

items.feedText:
Kinene, David Collins Agaba, Ronald Ouma Omolo, Agnes Namaganda, Haruna Muwonge

Uterine leiomyomas are the most common benign tumours of the female reproductive tract and a major cause of gynaecological morbidity worldwide. Observational and experimental studies have linked vitamin D and the vitamin D receptor (VDR) separately to uterine leiomyoma biology, including effects on cell proliferation and Wnt/β-catenin signalling in vitro; however, the breadth of this evidence has not been comprehensively mapped acro…
items.articleBody: Uterine leiomyomas are the most common benign tumours of the female reproductive tract and a major cause of gynaecological morbidity worldwide. Observational and experimental studies have linked vitamin D and the vitamin D receptor (VDR) separately to uterine leiomyoma biology, including effects on cell proliferation and Wnt/β-catenin signalling in vitro; however, the breadth of this evidence has not been comprehensively mapped across clinical, molecular, and genetic domains. We conducted a scoping review following Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and reported using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched from January 2016 to December 2025. Forty-two studies were included: 31 clinical, seven molecular, and four genetic. Most clinical studies reported lower circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations among women with uterine leiomyomas compared with controls, with several demonstrating inverse associations with fibroid size, volume, or number; however, fewer than half adjusted for BMI and only one study adjusted for ethnicity, limiting causal inference. Seven molecular studies examined the vitamin D-VDR axis in leiomyoma tissue and cells: three demonstrated reduced VDR expression, two demonstrated upregulated CYP24A1 expression, and two demonstrated calcitriol-mediated suppression of Wnt/β-catenin signalling (and, in one study, mTOR signalling). Four genetic studies showed inconsistent associations between VDR and vitamin D metabolism gene polymorphisms and leiomyoma susceptibility across populations. The evidence maps parallel associations of lower circulating vitamin D, lower VDR expression and higher CYP24A1 expression in leiomyoma tissue with the disease; no included study tested whether VDR mediates or modifies the relationship between vitamin D and leiomyoma. Findings remain heterogeneous and largely observational. Well-designed prospective cohort studies incorporating LC-MS/MS vitamin D measurement, concurrent tissue sampling, and full confounder adjustment are needed to clarify the clinical and mechanistic significance of this pathway.

items.articleBody:
## a new timber district takes shape in Thun

[Bjarke Ingels Group / BIG](https://www.designboom.com/tag/bjarke-ingels-group-big/) unveils plans for four timber buildings in Thun, [Switzerland](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-switzerland/), where the architecture firm will help shape the entrance to the city’s emerging Siegenthalergut district. The 13,000-square-meter development brings together two [hotels](https://www.designboom.com/tag/hotel-architecture-and-design/) and [residential](https://www.designboom.com/tag/residential-architecture-interiors/) buildings, with stacked [wooden](https://www.designboom.com/tag/wood-and-timber-architecture/) volumes that project outward above the street. Set against the Bernese Alps, the architecture is defined by deep window grids and large terraces carved into the buildings’ stepped facades.

The proposal, developed with landscape architects August + Margrith Künzel, was selected through a competition organized by Frutiger AG and the city of Thun. Titled Nachwachsende Stadt, or Growing City, the scheme occupies one of the first two plots planned for the new neighborhood. The site sits opposite a sports center and the future headquarters of the Swiss Football Association to give the BIG-designed buildings a prominent position along the city’s western entrance.

visualizations © [IMIGO](https://imigo.lt/mission/), unless otherwise stated

## two hotels share a stepped timber building

At the southwest corner of the site, the [team](https://big.dk/) at BIG brings a three-star and a four-star hotel together under one roof. Shared amenity spaces cut diagonally through the structure, creating a series of setbacks that interrupt its otherwise regular timber grid. These shifts make room for outdoor terraces overlooking the neighboring sports facilities, with the Bernese Alps rising in the distance. A restaurant at the top of the building will give guests an even broader view of the surrounding landscape.

At street level, a cantilevered corner marks the main hotel entrance, opening onto a drop-off plaza beneath the projecting upper floors. Commercial spaces line the adjacent boulevard, bringing activity to the building’s ground floor. Across the facade, large square windows sit within deeply framed timber modules, while recessed portions reveal warmer, sheltered spaces behind the exterior grid. The alternating volumes give the hotel a sculptural profile that changes depending on where it is viewed from.

the cantilevered hotel building will mark the western entrance to Thun’s new Siegenthalergut district

## residences frame a shared garden courtyard

To the east, the remaining timber buildings accommodate residences with flexible layouts and projecting bays. Here, the same geometric language takes on a more domestic scale. Balconies extend outward from the facades, while recessed loggias create sheltered outdoor rooms. The shifting arrangement of these openings gives each elevation a different rhythm, with the projecting volumes bringing daylight deeper into the apartments.

The residential buildings face an internal courtyard, where winding paths move through gardens and planted gathering spaces. Renderings picture grassy areas beneath the timber facades, with balconies overlooking the shared landscape. Small plazas and seating areas are distributed throughout the development, connecting the homes to the surrounding neighborhood.

Of the project’s total 13,000 square meters, approximately 6,500 are dedicated to residential uses, alongside 6,000 square meters of hotel space and another 400 square meters for commercial activities.

public areas will connect the development with the surrounding neighborhood | visualization © BIG

## BIG’s timber construction allows for future adaptation

The use of timber extends across all four buildings, establishing a consistent material language while helping reduce the development’s embodied carbon footprint. BIG has designed the timber elements for future disassembly and reuse, allowing components to be recovered as the buildings change over time. The deep balconies and roof overhangs also serve a practical purpose, providing natural shade in summer and shelter during the colder months.

Green roofs and rainwater retention systems will help manage water across the site, while approximately 1,800 square meters of photovoltaic panels are planned to generate renewable energy. The development is targeting Switzerland’s SNBS Gold sustainability certification.

The winning proposal will now progress through further design and approval stages, with construction of the district’s first buildings possible from 2028. For BIG, which opened its Zurich office in 2023, the project adds another timber-focused development to its growing Swiss portfolio, alongside the planned Dock A terminal at Zurich Airport.

a rooftop restaurant and terrace will offer panoramic views of the Bernese Alps

items.articleBody:
[OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-2-astra-sol/) today, two days before [Anthropic’s expected first trading day](https://research.ftserussell.com/products/index-notices/home/getnotice/?id=2622497). In [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/es/articles/openai-has-the-2-model-in-the-intelligence-index-with-the-release-of-gpt-6-2-astra-and-6-2-sol)’ tests, **Sol ties September’s Astra at about 15% of the cost per task**. New Astra scores 62 on the Intelligence Index, just behind Fable 5.2 at 65. Net net, Anthropic still owns the world’s best model, but OpenAI owns the world’s most efficient models in terms of intelligence per $.

What’s more unusual about this launch is the STRONGLY negative influencer feedback…

which prompted a [defensive response](https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2122929634916679820)…

[View post on X ↗](https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2122929634916679820)

We think that some of this is overreacting and normal influencer tendency to either have everything be 🤯🤯🤯 or the literal WORST.MODEL.EVER, BUT also that some of the criticisms are valid, and the RL artefacts are noticeable and [downright bizarre](https://x.com/emollick/status/2122783985134682207) (don’t even get us started about [the terrible launch video](https://x.com/swyx/status/2122862646265520150)). However, we still use it to automate our work and that’s all that matters in the end.

Great ship, but Anthropic’s IPO is unaffected and that will be probably the headline of the week/year/decade (until OpenAI IPO’s….)

**Today’s AI News is brought to you by SerpApi!**

items.articleBody:
Generations of Westerners have come to appreciate Japanese cinema through the films of [Akira Kurosawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akira_Kurosawa), but many have been shocked to find out that Kurosawa himself isn’t as beloved in Japan as they’d imagined. It’s less that his homeland rejects him than that his work has been regarded there as a somewhat foreign taste. That judgment must have something to it: despite their thoroughly Japanese settings, *Throne of Blood*, *The Bad Sleep Well*, and *Ran* were, after all, Shakespeare adaptations, and Kurosawa spoke openly of structuring his stories in the manner of not just traditional Japanese theater, but also symphonies. Consider, too, the way his films continue to inspire Western remakes, from *The Magnificent Seven* and *A Fistful of Dollars* in the nineteen-sixties to *Living* and *Highest 2 Lowest* in this decade.

Nor can it be a coincidence that the appreciative voices opening [the StudioBinder video on Kurosawa’s genius above](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IIHeWcGS4iA) belong to Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, and George Lucas. Yet this most internationally celebrated of all Japanese filmmakers can’t, ultimately, have been just a Westerner in disguise, since his work gives viewers around the world something that their domestic movies don’t.

Whatever the extent to which he hybridized the cinematic sensibilities of Japan and Hollywood, he did so through his uncompromising personal involvement in every stage of the process. “The role of the director encompasses the coaching of the actors, the cinematography, the sound recording, the art direction, the music, the editing, and the dubbing and sound mixing,” he once said, expressing his dedication to the ideal of (as no less an American auteur than Jerry Lewis described himself) the total filmmaker.

That Kurosawa understood how to tell a story in a way that transcends cultural boundaries goes without saying; what’s less widely appreciated is the way he did so with a combination of simplicity and complexity. As he put it, “a truly good movie is interesting and easy to understand,” two qualities that often end up in irresolvable tension, at least in the hands of lesser filmmakers. Even among those influenced by Kurosawa, for example, some have mastered immediate visual legibility without ever understanding that sound and music are more effectively used as a counterpoint to, rather than mere intensification of, a scene’s prevailing emotion. How many living directors, for that matter, convincingly approach grand, universal themes without irony or protective distance? If Kurosawa’s films retain a power that seems inaccessible today, it may be because, for him, there was no East or West: there was only cinema.
