items.articleBody:
Wie gelingt gute Wissenschaftskommunikation? Fünf Podcasts und ein Bonus-Tipp bieten praktische Anregungen, internationale Perspektiven und Einblicke in aktuelle Debatten.

Wissenschaftskommunikation ist längst mehr als das Vermitteln fertiger Forschungsergebnisse. Es geht um Verständlichkeit, Zielgruppen, Vertrauen, Unsicherheiten, Dialog und die Frage, wie Wissenschaft in gesellschaftlichen Debatten sichtbar wird. Wer in diesem Bereich arbeitet oder sich dafür interessiert, muss deshalb nicht nur die aktuelle Forschung im Blick behalten, sondern auch die eigene Kommunikationspraxis immer wieder reflektieren. Podcasts können dafür ein niedrigschwelliger Einstieg sein. Sie bieten Einblicke in praktische Erfahrungen, aktuelle Debatten, internationale Perspektiven und Forschung über Wissenschaftskommunikation selbst. Manche Formate liefern konkrete Tipps für Forschende und Kommunikator*innen, andere laden eher zum Nachdenken über Rolle, Wirkung und Verantwortung von Wissenschaftskommunikation ein.

Die folgende Auswahl stellt fünf Podcasts vor, die Wissenschaftskommunikation aus unterschiedlichen Perspektiven hörbar macht. Sie eignen sich für alle, die neue Impulse für ihre Arbeit suchen, sich fachlich weiterbilden oder einfach besser verstehen möchten, wie gute Wissenschaftskommunikation gelingen kann.

## SciComm Palaver

**für alle, die persönliche Perspektiven, Erfahrungswissen und reflektierte Gespräche aus der Wissenschaftskommunikation hören möchten**

Der Podcast „[SciComm Palaver](https://sabinegysi.ch/podcast/)“ fragt danach, warum Wissenschaftskommunikation gebraucht wird, was sie erreichen soll und wodurch sie wirkungsvoll werden kann. In jeder Folge spricht die Moderatorin Sabin Gysi mit Akteur*innen aus der Wissenschaftskommunikation über Erfahrungen, Herausforderungen und konkrete Fragen aus dem Feld.

Die Themen sind breit angelegt und reichen von Finanzierung und Zielgruppen, über Wissenschaftskompetenz bis hin zur Frage, wie Forschende in ihrer Rolle als Kommunikator*innen gestärkt werden können. Dadurch entsteht ein Format, das weniger auf schnelle Tipps setzt, sondern Wissenschaftskommunikation als Arbeitsfeld mit unterschiedlichen Perspektiven, Erwartungen und Rahmenbedingungen sichtbar macht.

Interessant ist „SciComm Palaver“ besonders durch den persönlichen Gesprächsansatz. Statt Wissenschaftskommunikation abstrakt zu erklären, kommen Menschen zu Wort, die dies praktisch gestalten, begleiten oder erforschen. So bietet der Podcast Einblicke in konkrete Projekte und macht zugleich deutlich, dass gute Wissenschaftskommunikation immer auch von Zielen, Ressourcen und Kontexten abhängt.

### Let’s Talk SciComm

**für** Forschende, Studierende und Kommunikator*innen, die internationale Perspektiven und praktische Tipps zur Wissenschaftskommunikation suchen

Der englischsprachige Podcast „[Let’s Talk SciComm](https://science.unimelb.edu.au/engage/lets-talk-scicomm-podcast)“ kommt aus dem Science Communication Teaching Program der University of Melbourne. Moderiert wird er von Associate Professor Jen Martin und Dr. Michael Wheeler. Im Mittelpunkt stehen Tipps, Interviews und Gespräche darüber, wie Wissenschaft wirksam, verständlich und ansprechend kommuniziert werden kann.

Der Podcast verbindet praktische Kommunikationsfragen mit Einblicken in unterschiedliche Arbeitsfelder der Wissenschaftskommunikation. In den Folgen geht es unter anderem um Forschungskommunikation, Karrierewege, Storytelling und vieles mehr. Dadurch ist der Podcast für alle, die Wissenschaftskommunikation als erlernbare Fähigkeit verstehen und sich konkrete Anregungen aus einem internationalen Kontext holen möchten interessant.

Der Podcast rückt Wissenschaftskommunikation als Handwerk in den Mittelpunkt: Wie wird aus Forschung eine verständliche Geschichte? Welche Rolle spielen Sprache, Format und Publikum? Und wie können Forschende lernen, ihre Themen sicherer zu kommunizieren?

### SciComm Conversations

**für alle, die Wissenschaftskommunikation stärker aus europäischer, forschungsnaher und internationaler Perspektive betrachten möchten**

Der englischsprachige Podcast „[SciComm Conversations](https://coalesceproject.eu/category/podcast/)“ ist die offizielle Podcastreihe des europäischen COALESCE-Projekts. Das Format widmet sich aktuellen Fragen der Wissenschaftskommunikation und bringt internationale Perspektiven aus Forschung und Praxis zusammen. In der ersten Staffel stand Wissenschaftskommunikation im Zeitalter künstlicher Intelligenz im Mittelpunkt; spätere Folgen greifen stärker aktuelle Forschung aus dem Feld auf.

Der Podcast betrachtet Wissenschaftskommunikation nicht nur als praktische Aufgabe, sondern auch als Forschungs- und Kompetenzfeld. Die Folgen behandeln etwa Public Engagement, Science Storytelling, KI in der Wissenschaftskommunikation oder die Frage, wie Forschende in der Öffentlichkeit sichtbar werden. Damit bietet das Format einen guten Einblick in internationale Debatten und Entwicklungen.

### The SciComm Collective

für Studierende, Nachwuchskommunikator*innen und alle, die Wissenschaftskommunikation aus einer jungen und internationalen Perspektive kennenlernen möchten

Der englischsprachige Podcast **„**[The SciComm Collective](https://thescicommcollective.com/podcast/)**“** wird von Studierenden der Wissenschaftskommunikation an der University of Western Australia gestaltet. Das Format verbindet Interviews, Diskussionen und persönliche Einblicke in Fragen rund um Science Storytelling, Kommunikationspraxis, Karrierewege und Theorien der Wissenschaftskommunikation.

Besonders überzeugt der Podcast durch seine Nachwuchsperspektive. Hier sprechen nicht nur etablierte Expert*innen über Wissenschaftskommunikation, sondern auch Studierende und junge Kommunikator*innen, die sich das Feld selbst erschließen. Dadurch wirkt das Format nahbar und offen: Es geht ums Ausprobieren, Lernen, Reflektieren und die Frage, wie Wissenschaftskommunikation in unterschiedlichen Kontexten praktisch gestaltet werden kann.

### Potluck der Perspektiven

für Kommunikator*innen, Forschende und alle, die sich mit Inklusion, Zugänglichkeit und gerechter Teilhabe in der Wissenschaftskommunikation beschäftigen möchten

Wie lässt sich Wissenschaftskommunikation inklusiver und gerechter gestalten? Dieser Frage widmet sich „[Potluck der Perspektiven](https://potluck-der-perspektiven.podigee.io/)“. Der Podcast beleuchtet, was inklusive Wissenschaftskommunikation bedeutet, welche Projekte und Strukturen es bereits gibt und welche Ressourcen nötig sind, um Veränderungen möglich zu machen.

Der Podcast ist erst im Juli 2026 gestartet und bietet bislang zwei Gespräche: über einfache Sprache und Inklusion mit Dr. Phyllis Mania sowie über Leichte-Bilder-Sprache mit Simone Fass. Die Auswahl ist damit noch überschaubar, macht aber neugierig auf weitere Perspektiven. Schon die ersten Folgen laden dazu ein, die eigene Kommunikationspraxis mit Blick auf Zugänglichkeit und Teilhabe zu reflektieren.

### Archivpodcast: ZEIT für WissKomm

Der Podcast „[ZEIT für WissKomm](https://zeit-fuer-wisskomm.podigee.io/)“ richtet sich an Menschen, die professionell mit Wissenschaftskommunikation, Wissenschaftsmarketing oder Wissenschafts-PR zu tun haben. Das Format bietet einen offenen Austausch über Themen, die Hochschul-, Forschungs- und Wissenschaftskommunikator*innen in ihrer Arbeit beschäftigen. Produziert wurde der Podcast von ZEIT Advise. Zwar werden inzwischen keine neuen Folgen mehr aufgenommen, das Archiv bietet aber weiterhin vielfältige Einblicke und Anregungen für die eigene Kommunikationsarbeit.

Im Mittelpunkt stehen Gespräche mit Expert*innen aus der Praxis. Die Folgen behandeln unterschiedliche Aspekte der Wissenschaftskommunikation, etwa Transfer, Public Engagement, Diversität, Branding, Nachwuchswissenschaftler*innen oder Wissenschaftskommunikation im ländlichen Raum. Dadurch eignet sich der Podcast besonders gut, um Einblick in aktuelle Arbeitsfelder, Herausforderungen und Perspektiven der professionellen Wisskomm zu erhalten.

items.articleBody:
The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, located in Cincinnati along the banks of the Ohio River makes a solemn statement about the lives that were lived enslaved in the early history of the United States, and the many heroic men and women who played important roles in the Underground Railroad movement, which helped to bring an end to African slavery in the United States.  Referred to as a "museum of conscience", The Freedom Center is dedicated to exploring the struggle to abolish human enslavement. During the era when the Underground Railroad was active, Cincinnati was a major gateway across the Ohio River where freedom seekers escaped from southern slave states to the northern states or Canada, making the Center's location rather significant.

Having opened its doors in 2004, the Freedom Center uses immersive exhibits across multiple floors to convey an account that is simultaneously rich in the cultural traditions of the enslaved, as well as steeped in the violence and tragedies that were endured.  The histories are told through a combination of permanent and traveling exhibits that utilize storytelling, film, artwork, hands-on activities and more.

Perhaps one of the most impressive and prominent displays at the center is an authentic, 19th-century reconstructed slave pen that was obtained from a farm in Kentucky. It stands as America's only remaining, pristinely preserved slave pen and stands as a stark reminder of the atrocious conditions that were endured.

The pen, originally built somewhere around 1830 by a wealthy Kentucky farmer, runaway slave catcher, and slave trader, was used as a holding facility for captured and purchased enslaved men, women and children. It was discovered, quite by accident in 1998 when a farmer, who was preparing to demolish an old barn on his property, discovered that the barn had been built up around this old pen, thus protecting and preserving (and hiding) the slave pen for more than 100 years.

During its unfortunate years of use, enslaved people would be kept in the pen, often for months, until the slave trader accumulated a large enough "stock" to march them further south to be sold. These forced marches would often cover upwards of 750 miles. Conditions in these pens would be brutal, offering no sanitation, lighting or warmth.  As many as 65 enslaved people would often be housed in this small pen.  Also very moving is the memorial room dedicated to the Transatlantic Slave Trade, as well as the Freedom's Eternal Flame Terrace which overlooks the Ohio River and the city skyline.

The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center is a beautiful and meaningful tribute to the human right for freedom, and to the brave men, women and children who stood up to the inhuman treatment of themselves and of others; and to those who continue to fight for the cause of freedom through out the world today.

items.title: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
items.subtitle: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age.
items.feedText: The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves seen in younger people.

Howdy, folks! Welcome to the future where science fiction becomes reality every day. Where AI-powered cyberattacks paralyze air travel one day and banks the next. Where shadowy billionaires make fortunes illicitly selling America’s enemies the technology to create artificial gods, while you slave away for $150 a day hoping to get half a day off. Where it seems like a new rare disease is [cured every week](https://www.ajmc.com/view/5-rare-diseases-that-now-have-their-first-fda-approved-treatments), even as [measles returns to America](https://abcnews.com/Health/us-officially-loses-measles-elimination-status-paho/story?id=138203543) thanks to an anti-science cult that somehow made it to the highest rungs of power. Where self-driving cars whizz past people hunched over dying of fentanyl in the street. I mean, look at this:

Or this:

Or this!

In such confusing times, it’s all your friendly neighborhood economics blogger can do to keep up with it all. But I’m trying my best, so that I can help you understand these crazy times just a little bit better.

Smith](https://braddelong.substack.com/p/live-with-brad-delong?utm_source=substack&utm_campaign=post_embed&utm_medium=web&embedding_publication_id=35345)

And here’s a conversation between me and the streamer Destiny, in which we talk about how liberalism can resist rightism and leftism at the same time:

Anyway, on to this week’s roundup.

#### 1. Good news on teen happiness

For years, we watched America’s young people — and young people throughout the world — become less and less happy. They told surveys they were unhappy. They attempted (and committed) suicide more. They were more socially isolated. They formed relationships less.

The most plausible candidate for a cause for all of this was [smartphone-enabled social media](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/honestly-its-probably-the-phones), which replaced in-person small-group interaction with impersonal arm’s-length interactions with huge numbers of potentially hostile strangers — something the human animal never evolved for.

But human beings are resilient and adaptable, and I always expected young people to find new ways to be happy in a hyper-connected world. Now, there are some signs that things are starting to turn around:

A word of caution: This is just one data source, the Youth Behavioral Risk Survey. Other sources, like the CDC, continue to show [high teen suicide rates](https://x.com/jtrothwell/status/2119885873735221719). It’s far too early to conclude that general teen happiness is on the upswing. But the YBRS data is a very positive sign.

If the trend is indeed turning around, what’s the cause? One possibility is that even as the online world became more all-consuming and alienating, the offline world was becoming kinder and gentler. Here’s [Rothwell again](https://x.com/jtrothwell/status/2061466828438966756):

Another possibility is that teens are [moving away](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/) from the toxic public platforms — X and Facebook — and moving toward either private discussions or passive video apps like TikTok:

Source: [Pew](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/)

Other surveys show that teens are [trying to cut back on social media use](https://thrive.psu.edu/blog/what-new-research-reveals-about-social-media-and-mental-health-are-teens-over-it/) in general, realizing that it’s bad for them.

This is why I’m a long-term techno-optimist. The downsides of technology can sometimes dominate in the short run, but eventually people figure out how to handle it and turn tech to their advantage.

#### 2. Is AI getting less bang for the buck?

As the Anthropic IPO approaches, various analysts are trying to figure out if the incredible rate of AI progress is going to slow down, speed up, or continue at a steady rate. A number of data sources show that progress has sped up recently, around either late last year or early this year:

Source: METR via [roon](https://x.com/tszzl/status/2122924317935898701)

One popular theory is that the speedup was due to the advent of AI coding tools. But economists [Luis Garicano and Alex Imas argue](https://www.siliconcontinent.com/p/are-we-approaching-an-intelligence) that what actually accelerated was spending on AI research. They show data showing a smooth deceleration in the amount of AI capability that each dollar of research spending buys:

Source: [Garicano and Imas](https://www.siliconcontinent.com/p/are-we-approaching-an-intelligence)

On the other hand, should we really think of a linear increase in the ECI as a linear increase in capability? [Some people argue](https://x.com/TomDavidsonX/status/2119415344745893963) that each point of increase in the ECI *multiplies* AI capabilities by a constant factor — like points on the Richter Scale.

Whether that’s true in any meaningful sense is hard to assess. But at the end of the day, what really matters is AI’s ability to generate *economic* returns. And [some people argue](https://x.com/ben_j_todd/status/2119784430348738647) that it’s here that we see the true acceleration, as AI hits critical thresholds for economic usefulness:

But it’s also possible that this increase in usefulness doesn’t cleanly map to increases in raw capabilities, and that human beings are simply finding new uses for AI capabilities that already exist.

So the jury is still out on whether AI progress is slowing down.

#### 3. The return of inflation

One of the great accomplishments of economic policy in the last few decades was [the conquest of the post-pandemic inflation](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/how-did-the-us-achieve-a-soft-landing). The Fed raised rates, and the economy didn’t tank, and inflation went down anyway. But that victory might prove ephemeral; inflation is creeping back up. Though there’s some volatility, most recent months have come in at around 5%:

Source: [Econvitals.org](https://econvitals.org/inflation/#underlying)

The rise in oil prices due to the Iran War is an obvious contributor, but in fact the new inflation is remarkably broad-based:

Source: [Mike Konczal](https://x.com/mtkonczal/status/2120149208338686137/photo/1)

It’s just not possible to play the old game of “Well, inflation is just X and Y and Z, so it’s not really a problem.” There are various possible causes of this broad-based price acceleration — budget deficits, Trump pressuring the Fed to be dovish, cost pressures from the data center buildout, and so on. Teasing these out deserves a longer post.

And just as basic economics would expect, a burst of unexpected inflation is causing real wages to go down:

Source: [Mike Konczal](https://x.com/mtkonczal/status/2120151986620215399)

In other words, Americans are getting poorer this year, because the cost of living is going up and their paychecks aren’t keeping up. It’s not as bad as it was in 2021, but it’s going to be enough to make a lot of Americans very angry at the people in power.

#### 4. Inclusionary zoning is bad

A lot of people mentally divide housing into two types: “luxury” or “market-rate” housing, and “affordable” housing — as if the price of a house or an apartment is built into its walls and floors. The assumption is that if developers aren’t forced to build “affordable” housing, normal people won’t be able to afford housing.

That assumption is [totally wrong](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/02/housing-crisis-rich-poor-building/686086/) — building market-rate housing drives rents down and makes housing more affordable. But because lots of people believe in the “luxury”/“affordable” distinction, they embrace policies that try to force developers to offer some units at below-market rates. These policies are called **inclusionary zoning**. Basically, inclusionary zoning says that some percent of the apartments in a new building have to be rented out for very cheap. The policy is attractive because it doesn’t have any direct fiscal costs — the cost of subsidizing cheap apartments comes out of the pocket of a corporation, rather than the taxpayer.

But this kind of policy ends up backfiring. Forcing developers to take a loss on some of their housing units simply makes it less financially possible to build new housing. And when they do build new housing, they end up raising rents for all the non-“affordable” units in order to try to recoup some of their losses. Here’s what [Kouchekinia (2026)](https://bpb-us-e2.wpmucdn.com/sites.uci.edu/dist/b/5302/files/2026/06/IZ_Kouchekinia.pdf) finds:

> In California, more than a third of localities have adopted [inclusionary zoning ordinances]. Mandatory inclusionary zoning acts as a tax on construction and, all else equal, reduces the overall supply of housing. This potentially reduces affordability in the aggregate…I find the typical inclusionary zoning ordinance reduces annual new residential construction by nearly a third (31.8%). Additionally, I find the policies relocate multi-family developments within jurisdictions to lower rent areas, where the policy is effectively less severe…I estimate the cost of generating an affordable unit with inclusionary zoning to be approximately $800,000 in “excess rents” paid by market rate renters as a result of the policy’s constraint on supply.

As Kouchekinia points out, making housing more scarce acts as a shadow tax on everyone in the area. Inclusionary zoning looks costless, but it’s actually extremely costly.

California cities and other places that use inclusionary zoning are [starting to realize](https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Inclusionary-Zoning-Los-Angeles-April-2024.pdf) that the policy doesn’t do what it’s supposed to do. Some have actually started cutting inclusionary zoning mandates:

Matt Yglesias also has [a good recent post](https://capitalcommonsense.com/p/end-inclusionary-zoning?r=d1s6&utm_medium=ios&triedRedirect=true) about inclusionary zoning in D.C., and why the District should scrap it.

Basically, it’s time for this policy to go. There’s really no salvaging it, it’s making our cities worse for no good reason, and we need to stop viewing it as just another inevitable cost of doing business.

#### 5. More on Cloud Laws

For years, [I’ve been arguing](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/a-golden-age-of-science-is-coming) that AI is going to cause a scientific revolution. My hypothesis is that there are a bunch of “laws of nature” — i.e., exploitable stable causal relationships — that are too complex and diffuse for the human mind to comprehend, but which AI can learn and exploit on our behalf. I call these “cloud laws”, because I envision them as diffuse clouds of weak but densely interrelated causal effects — the kind of thing that human minds will never be able to either grasp in their entirety or bite off into little separable chunks.

Well, here’s a little bit of evidence that cloud laws exist…in the clouds. [Yohan Iddawela writes](https://x.com/yohaniddawela/status/2046557831902417264) about Google DeepMind’s new weather forecasting AI model:

> A single GPU can now calculate hundreds of global weather scenarios in under 60 seconds. The exact same task requires a supercomputer and hours of brute-force physics.
> Google DeepMind recently released WeatherNext 2. The model beats the previous state-of-the-art system on 99.9% of weather variables across a 15-day forecast window. It achieves this massive jump in accuracy using a new modelling approach called a Functional Generative Network.
> Meteorologists categorise weather data into two buckets:
> 1. Marginals are isolated data points, like the precise temperature at a specific location or the wind speed at a certain altitude.
> 2. Joints are the massive, interconnected systems that form when all those individual elements interact.
> The researchers hid the joint systems from the model during training. They only taught it the isolated marginals. When they turned it on, the model skillfully predicted the massive, complex systems anyway…The model gives forecasters a full 24-hour advantage in tropical cyclone tracking compared to the previous leading system. It maps extreme wind speeds and heatwaves with unprecedented precision.
> We’re watching a pretty big shift in predictive capabilities. The machine is deducing the structural reality of planetary weather from isolated fragments of data.

Normal weather forecasting is reductionist. We take the basic physical laws of motion, model the atmosphere as a bunch of little chunks of air that sort of behave like independent units, and apply the laws of motion to those units. [What Google is doing](https://deepmind.google/blog/weathernext-ai-model-achieves-breakthrough-in-forecasting-cyclones/) is something else; it’s letting an AI model look at a bunch of weather data and then predict how the whole system is going to behave.

The AI approach ends up working better than the typical reductionist brute-force approach. Why? My guess is that weather has cloud laws — principles that no human could ever intuit from staring at masses of weather data, and which could never be explained in any graduate textbook, but which AI can just *grasp* holistically.1

What other phenomena might we be able to predict and control with AI this way? Patrick Collison has a fun list:

We know these effects have some sort of regular causes, but reductionist science has so far been unable to characterize any of them very effectively. But perhaps AI will, because they might be governed by cloud laws.

If so, we’re in for the most rapid and dramatic scientific revolution in our entire history.

#### 6. Paying people to have kids works (just not enough)

Plummeting fertility is a problem, and [nobody knows how to fix it](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/nobody-knows-how-to-stop-humanity). There are a few people who deny this obvious and disheartening truth. One of those is Lyman Stone, whose [own research](https://ifstudies.org/blog/pro-natal-policies-work-but-they-come-with-a-hefty-price-tag) has cast doubt on the efficacy of paying people to have kids, but who [stubbornly insists](https://ifstudies.org/blog/how-to-reverse-population-decline-the-crowbar-model) that such pronatal policies can act as a “crowbar” with which to pry open the door of child-rearing.

Well, they probably can’t do that. Here are Hartley and Jaros, evaluating a Michigan “baby bonus” program that paid people to have kids:

> This paper studies the fertility effects of the Rx Kids program, the first baby bonus introduced in the United States. Beginning in 2024, the program was launched in Flint, Michigan and subsequently expanded to additional municipalities across Michigan, creating staggered variation in treatment timing across places….[W]e estimate the effect of Rx Kids on birth outcomes. We find that live birth growth rates increase in treated municipalities…We find that Flint’s $7,500 baby bonus generates a small but statistically significant fertility response: actual 2024 births exceeded a three-year pre-treatment baseline by roughly 7.5%, implying $107,000 in program spending per induced birth. These results provide the first U.S. evidence that direct cash transfers tied to childbirth can measurably affect fertility behavior.

The issue isn’t that these programs don’t work. They do. The problem is that *their effects aren’t very large*. The United States’ current total fertility rate (TFR) is about 1.6 children per woman; replacement level is between 2.0 and 2.1. That would require at least a 25% increase in fertility rates. The program Hartman and Jaros study resulted in only a 7.5% increase, and was forced to spend $107,000 per child on that paltry increase. That’s not nearly enough, but you can bet that if it were scaled up to the national level, you’d hear a lot of anger directed at the “welfare queens” who benefited from the policy.

And if it’s not nearly enough for the U.S., it’s utterly, laughably inadequate for a country like South Korea, which has a TFR of 0.8. To increase that to replacement level would require *a 150% increase* — 20 times the size of the increase generated by Michigan’s extremely generous program.

In other words, we’re not going to buy our way out of the baby bust by paying people to have kids. I still think paying people to have kids is a good idea, but the main thrust of effective pronatal policy will have to be something else.

#### 7. Democrats can’t be the Second Party of Tax Cuts

When I was a kid, everyone knew that Democrats were the party that wanted to raise your taxes to spend more on the poor, while Republicans wanted to cut your taxes and spend less. Those days are long gone. America now has two parties who are both dedicated to cutting taxes on the vast majority of Americans — including most wealthy and high-earning Americans — and raising spending at the same time.

This is a big problem for the country, because there will be no getting out of our debt problem until this political equilibrium changes. When I was a kid in 1992, all the presidential candidates were stumbling over themselves to tell America how they were going to fix the deficit, so I know a different equilibrium is possible. We just have to figure out how to get there.

But Democrats’ fiscal profligacy is also a political problem for them. Higher deficits and debt contribute to faster inflation; we’ve already had both Biden and Trump be punished for failing to tame inflation, and Democrats are deluding themselves if they think it can’t happen to them again.

[Eric Levitz writes](https://www.vox.com/politics/510291/democrats-agenda-taxes-midterms) about how the incoming Democrats’ economic policy program is incoherent:

> To seize this historic opening, Democrats will need to formulate a platform that effectively advances their core goals. Unfortunately, this will be harder than it sounds — because the party’s current economic priorities appear incompatible with each other…During the midterm campaign, Democrats promised to:
> [Bring down inflation](https://archive.ph/o/tDWyP/https://www.knba.org/news/2026-05-11/peltola-unveils-affordability-campaign-as-she-challenges-incumbent-us-sen-dan-sullivan) and [interest rates](https://archive.ph/o/tDWyP/https://www.denvergazette.com/2026/08/27/troops-taxes-war-dominate-colorados-5th-cd-debate-between-jeff-crank-jessica-killin).
> [Dramatically](https://archive.ph/o/tDWyP/https://abdulforsenate.com/priority/medicare-for-all-the-path-to-a-healthier-america/) expand the [welfare state](https://archive.ph/o/tDWyP/https://maineaflcio.org/news/jackson-delivered-affordable-child-care-pledges-create-universal-child-care).
> Raise taxes on [the very wealthy](https://archive.ph/o/tDWyP/https://www.facebook.com/reel/2145426779730927/) — but [no one else](https://archive.ph/o/tDWyP/https://ginafortexas.com/priority/an-affordable-texas-that-works-for-everyone/) — while [cutting](https://archive.ph/o/tDWyP/https://jamestalarico.com/issue/taxes-cost-of-living/) [taxes](https://archive.ph/o/tDWyP/https://jamestalarico.com/issue/taxes-cost-of-living/) for millions of Americans…
> Democrats’ goals…aren’t necessarily coherent.[I]t probably won’t be possible to create large new social programs, avoid tax hikes on anyone but the rich, and drive down inflation and interest rates…
> The party’s congressional leaders have signaled support for a social welfare agenda at least as ambitious as President Joe Biden’s unpassed Build Back Better Act, which [contained $4.73 trillion of new spending](https://archive.ph/o/tDWyP/https://www.crfb.org/blogs/cbo-estimates-permanent-build-back-better)…Add up the estimated fiscal costs of all these programs and the bill comes out to nearly $5 trillion…Critically, America is already on track to run an [average annual deficit of $2.4 trillion](https://archive.ph/o/tDWyP/https://www.cbo.gov/publication/62105) over the coming decade…[A] greater than $2 trillion deficit will put upward pressure on interest rates and prices.

Democrats do want to raise *some* taxes, but only on the ultra-mega-super-duper-giga-rich. [I’ve written](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/californias-billionaire-tax-is-the) that this approach of “just tax the billionaires” is insufficient to fund all the other economic policies that Democrats want. Levitz concurs.

In time, fear of the deficit will grow to a level that enables the kind of fiscal hawk equilibrium that obtained in 1992. Until then, Democrats need a more modest economic agenda. The American people can be satisfied with an anti-corruption drive, tariff repeal, and policies to spread the wealth generated by AI. They don’t need infinite government largesse in order to be satisfied. Democrats need to stop chasing the Bernie Sanders dream, at least for a while.

Subscribe now

[Share](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/roundup-91-rocketing-into-the-technofuture?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

1

Also note that the model Google used here wasn’t an LLM. This suggests that AI is more general than the specific techniques the frontier labs are currently focusing on.

## Enshittifiers groom us for scammers (permalink)

[↗ Primärquelle: pluralistic.net](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/18/malice-v-incompetence/#porque-no-los-dos)

We live in a scam economy: there's a presidential memecoin, a public health system run by a supplement peddler (who sold his trademark for "MAHA" to a pal before taking the job), and Spacex got to debut into the NASDAQ 100 and turn your retirement savings into exit liquidity for Musk's Emirati and tech oligarch cronies:

[https://prospect.org/2026/06/10/elon-musk-spacex-ipo-retirement-savings-index-funds-stock-market/#:~:text=The%20upcoming%20SpaceX,rake%20in%20millions.](https://prospect.org/2026/06/10/elon-musk-spacex-ipo-retirement-savings-index-funds-stock-market/#:~:text=The%20upcoming%20SpaceX,rake%20in%20millions.)

Then there's AI: voice cloning, deepfakes, and image-genned documents (including convincing IDs) have ushered in a golden age of account takeovers, identity theft and good, old-fashioned impersonation:

[https://www.404media.co/the-confessions-of-an-ai-fraud-kingpin-onlyfake-owner-nazarenko/](https://www.404media.co/the-confessions-of-an-ai-fraud-kingpin-onlyfake-owner-nazarenko/)

AI summarization is a priceless gift to fraudsters, who can comb through otherwise intractable mountains of breach data to customize precision-targeted spear-phishing campaigns for millions of potential victims at once. These summarization tools have a *lot* to summarize, thanks to a string of catastrophic breaches that saw (for example) the escape of the credit histories of nearly every person in America:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Equifax_data_breach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Equifax_data_breach)

The companies involved in those breaches were not meaningfully punished. Quite the contrary, they were allowed to buy up and merge more of their competitors, combining these new divisions' creaking servers with their own spit-and-baling-wire frankensystems, even as they fired the people who had built and maintained those systems (in the name of "efficiency").

The commercial surveillance sector has repeatedly proven itself to be more interested in profits than security or accuracy, and yet we continue to entrust them with crucial public functions, including purging electoral rolls:

[https://mississippitoday.org/2026/11/10/u-s-senate-election-mississippi-andrew-goodman/](https://mississippitoday.org/2026/11/10/u-s-senate-election-mississippi-andrew-goodman/)

For margin-obsessed corporate leadership, IT cuts represent a unique hazard. When a manager fires the person who maintains the assembly line, the shop-floor quickly seizes up. But managers who fire IT staff inherit software that keeps chugging along long after the people who built it are gone…until it stops, and the company no longer knows how to restart it. This is one of the unique challenges of unionizing tech workers: when the tech workers go on strike, the scab software they wrote crosses the picket line on them:

[https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook)

Tech debt has a long maturity: you can incur a *lot* of tech debt before the margin call comes and you find yourself in technological bankruptcy. Corporate management has spent decades playing IT Jenga, removing every available block, leaving behind a skeletal skyline of teetering towers that now routinely collapse:

[https://www.404media.co/breaking-everything/](https://www.404media.co/breaking-everything/)

The entire IT system is grossly overleveraged and technological bankruptcies are everywhere. This is very bad, because the USA hasn't had a new consumer privacy law since 1988 (when Congress banned disclosure of your VHS rental history), which means that these eggshell-thin servers are *jammed* with the most sensitive data imaginable about everyone, everywhere:

[https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/02/agony-verification/#great-turnbulls-ghost](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/02/agony-verification/#great-turnbulls-ghost)

Far from breaking this cycle of overaccumulation and breach of sensitive data, the AI sector is accelerating it, claiming that a single person's "consent" to use pervert glasses, always-on mics, or other surveillance equipment can stand in for the consent of everyone they meet, see, or converse with:

[https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/tech-companies-are-trying-shift-entire-concept-privacy-again](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/tech-companies-are-trying-shift-entire-concept-privacy-again)

This is the new normal: everything is broken, everything is breached. It's completely normal to wake up and read panicked headlines advising companies to shut off their servers until the latest showstopper bug can be patched. Half the email you get is from companies announcing new security protocols in the wake of a fresh data breach (the other half is from companies announcing changes to their terms of service to allow them to collect even *more* of your data, and to ban *you* from suing them when that data leaks):

[https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/26/abandon-hope/#all-ye-who-enter-here](https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/26/abandon-hope/#all-ye-who-enter-here)

So it's also normal to get phone calls, emails and texts from your bank, employer, insurer and broker asking you to verify a transaction or requiring you to sign up for a new two-factor authentication system. What's more, it's normal for these entities to insist that you *immediately* install a new app or go through a new authentication process that is totally unlike any of the other ones you're already using.

It's normal to log in to a service you use every day and be confronted with an entirely different login flow – a CAPTCHA unlike any you've ever seen, a requirement to visit a third-party site to complete an authentication step (which may involve taking selfies and transmitting copies of sensitive ID documents using an app from a company you've never heard of), an embedded widget that only works if you disable your browser's advanced privacy settings that prevent cross-site scripting and other horrors.

We're told to hang up on anyone who calls us from our bank or credit-card issuer and to call them back using the number on the back of our cards. But when we call our banks, we get shunted to AI chatbots that "hallucinate" nonsensical advice for accessing our accounts. If we try to reach a human, we're stuck in lengthy hold queues whose soundtrack is a looping announcement scolding us for not using a faulty chatbot or the company's broken website to solve our problems. When a human *does* come on the line, they often seem to be improvising a new security protocol that was created five minutes before to deal with the latest state of exception.

This is the security storm: a world of zero visibility, shifting gale-force winds, and blockages that impede your usual route and force you down unfamiliar paths every time you venture forth.

It is the *perfect* environment for fraudsters.

It's not just that fraudsters can impersonate anyone with AI voice-cloning or generate undetectable document forgeries: it's *also* the fact that your bank, HR department, insurer, credit card company and government have groomed you to expect a chaotic process that requires you to do something different every time you try to access a service.

They've groomed you to turn off your browser's advanced protections. They've groomed you to ignore your carefully created, carefully saved random passwords in favor of clicking on links that get texted or emailed to you by third-party services you've never heard of. They've groomed you to expect cold-calls from outsource fraud prevention companies that don't know how to pronounce your bank's name.

This isn't new. As far back as 2009, the cryptographer Ben Laurie was railing against "Verified by Visa," which required you to enter sensitive data into a page hosted on a domain that was separate from both your bank *and* the merchant you were paying, which Laurie called "Phished by Visa":

[https://web.archive.org/web/20090331094020/http://www.links.org/?p=591](https://web.archive.org/web/20090331094020/http://www.links.org/?p=591)

No one listened to Laurie. Instead, the banks got *worse*. I've been a customer of HSBC subsidiary Firstdirect for nearly 20 years, and in that time, I've been told to make note of a "customer ID number," a "telephone passcode", *eight* password recovery answers, a "web username", a web password, a "digital secure key password", a "digital secure key PIN", and a regular PIN.

Despite all this, I haven't been able to access my bank account for two months, ever since they "upgraded" their system to block app log-ins on mobile devices running the open, secure Android fork Graphene (Firstdirect doesn't use a standard two-factor authenticator; you have to use its app to generate a one-time PIN in addition to all those other authentication details every time you log in, even via a browser).

When I spoke to Firstdirect about why they'd blocked Graphene, they told me that they "considered open source to be insecure." Talk about grooming for fraudsters: telling your customers that they should only trust systems that *can't* be independently inspected and validated is grossly irresponsible.

(Don't worry, we're going to use the UK's excellent open banking system to switch back to the Co-Op Bank, which we left after it was mismanaged to the brink of bankruptcy and flogged to private equity; it's since been restructured as a co-op again:)

[https://www.banktrack.org/success/the_cooperative_bank_bought_back_into_mutual_ownership](https://www.banktrack.org/success/the_cooperative_bank_bought_back_into_mutual_ownership)

The perfect mark is someone who thinks they can't get scammed. The more technologically savvy and security conscious you are, the more you've encountered the incoherence of the official system and the less surprised you'll be when you're told to do something *obviously* insecure in order to complete a transaction: *Boy, that stupid, dangerous requirement is even stupider and more dangerous than all the other stupid, dangerous things I've been forced to do this year.*

That's the story of Uri Bram, a technological sophisticate who edits Atoms vs Bits and nearly got scammed trying to buy an Amtrak ticket:

[https://www.atvbt.com/expected-incompetence-enables-fraud/](https://www.atvbt.com/expected-incompetence-enables-fraud/)

Bram tried to buy his Amtrak ticket on the web but found himself on a nonfunctional site that put him through a bizarre stopgap process that required him to enter his email address, click a link, log in to his Paypal account… Each step was more out-of-place than the last, but all of them had the eerie ring of plausibility, given the dysfunction of Bram's other interactions with giant, creaking companies like Amtrak. As Bram puts it: "Expected incompetence enables fraud."

The corollary is that technological excellence makes fraud easier to spot and harder to pull off. Most of our anti-fraud measures demand that *you* be more vigilant and more discerning. We'd be much better off if we insisted that our official institutions invest in coherent, orderly practices that are thoughtfully designed, well maintained, and staffed by easily reached experts who can guide us through our problems. It's much harder to impersonate a system where you can get through to a thoroughly trained, in-house customer service rep in a few minutes than it is to impersonate a system that's typically *worse* than the fraudster's vibe-coded scam website, whose "customer service" has been replaced by broken chatbots.

The ongoing collapse of all of our technology has created a permanent state of exception in which fraudsters' demands are no weirder than the ad-libbing our own essential institutions engage in every time we deal with them. The answer can't be to demand superhuman fraud-detection skills from the public: rather, we must demand excellence from our institutions:

[https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/07/mayor-mamdani-launches–public-interest-technology–pit–crew–t](https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/07/mayor-mamdani-launches--public-interest-technology--pit--crew--t)

By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role.

items.articleBody:
## Researchers Paid Students To Sleep More and Their Grades Quickly Improved

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/sleep-study-students/)

How much sleep do you get each night? According to the [National Center for Health Statistics](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db559.htm), one-third of American adults sleep less than seven hours a night—the amount of shuteye recommended by health authorities. Recognizing that many people, particularly students, struggle to get the rest they need, researchers recently explored whether offering small, financial rewards could encourage students to improve their sleeping habits.

The study, [published in July 2026,](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/740221) was conducted by Osea Giuntella, associate professor of economics at the University of Pittsburgh; Sally Sadoff, professor of economics and strategy at the University of California, San Diego; and Silvia Saccardo, professor of social and decision sciences at Carnegie Mellon University.

The researchers gave more than 1,100 undergraduates at University of Pittsburgh a Fitbit, a wearable activity tracker that recorded how much they slept, and an app that sent bedtime reminders and morning feedback. They randomly chose 468 freshman students and paid them around $5 for every night they slept at least seven hours over the course of four weeks.

Before the study, students at the University of Pittsburgh were getting an average of just 6.6 hours of sleep a night. “Half were going to bed after 1 a.m. on average—a quarter after 2 a.m,” [reveal](https://www.good.is/paying-students-to-sleep/) the researchers. “They also did not know how much sleep they were getting. Two-thirds told us they usually slept seven hours—the trackers showed only about one-third of students slept that much on even three nights out of five.”

Students offered money for getting enough sleep reached the seven hour target on 26% more nights than those who weren’t paid. They also got an extra 19 minutes of sleep each school night—about the difference between closing your laptop at 11:40 p.m. instead of midnight. Getting more sleep seemed to pay off in the classroom, too. Students who received the incentives saw their GPA rise by around 0.08 points that semester. The boost to grades didn’t last forever though, and lowered after two semesters.

The researchers also learned that students who were paid nightly slept more than those who received a lump sum at the end of the semester. Interestingly, bedtime reminders alone made little difference. Students already wanted more sleep—they just needed a little extra incentive to make it happen.

“Very few universities or students treat sleep as part of an investment in education, or ask whether the schedules and incentives schools create make adequate sleep harder,” say the researchers. “Our results suggest they should.”

#### Source: We paid college students about $5 a night to sleep at least 7 hours – and their grades quickly improved

items.subtitle: I’m teaching at the Inkhaven blogging fellowship again this month.

items.articleBody:
I’m teaching at the [Inkhaven blogging fellowship](https://www.inkhaven.blog/fall-26) again this month. In my first class, I showed off terribly-written sentences and made the fellows analyze and improve them. Some were my own miscreations, some were [Lyttle Lytton winners](https://adamcadre.ac/lyttle/), and some came from the darkest abysses of the Internet. The audience’s favorite was overwrought description of women’s breasts from erotica (one person pointed out that my PDF reader’s Recent History tab helpfully displayed porn story titles while I presented on screen - why does a PDF reader even have a Recent History tab? - so I hope my humiliation helped educate you).

But I hear that [Naomi Kanakia](https://www.woman-of-letters.com/)’s class was even spicier. She taught a course on “discourseposting”, which naturally descended into fiery discourse ([Naomi Kanakia, you are WRONG about Discourseposting!!!](https://wadapan.substack.com/p/naomi-kanakia-discourseposting), [Inkhaven Fight Club](https://www.oblomovka.com/wp/2026/11/13/inkhaven-fight-club-me-machiavelli-and-a-dog-beater-vs-naomi-kanakia-wadapan-and-the-discourse/)). I didn’t get a chance to listen, so in the grand tradition of discourseposting, I’ll argue about it without having seen the source material.

Sticking to our porn theme, and in the spirit of [The Last Psychiatrist](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/book-review-sadly-porn): one way to classify sex is through its external manifestations: positions, toys, fetishes. But another is through which psychological need it fulfills. The need to feel wanted. The need to feel valuable. The need to dominate. The need to lose yourself. The need to reenact a traumatic childhood, only this time, the Other really loves you. In the same way, we can supplement our superficial categorizations of discourseposting with the types of writer-audience dynamic that make each post exist.

In an ideal world, writers would write to convince others, and audiences would read to learn something and change their minds. But few people enjoy trying to convince others, and even fewer enjoy reading with an open mind and letting themselves be convinced. The conjunction of the two is like that murder case where the guy with the getting-eaten-by-cannibals fetish was dating the guy with the cannibalism fetish and they both, uh, achieved gains from trade. There’s nothing physically impossible about it. It just requires the conjunction of two rare types of people. Sometimes you get this in the blogosphere, and it’s great. But you wouldn’t want to sustain a national publication off of it.

I usually support taking things at face value - better underpsychologize than overpsychologize - but some of the norms and genre conventions divide more naturally by guilty motive than innocent appearance, so we can go over these in more depth. Your best bet will be to keep track of who the intended audience is (rarely the person it’s addressed to!) and what it’s doing for them.

**The Voxsplainer.** Your audience is people who already agree with you, or who are overdetermined to agree with you once they know that the issue exists (e.g. anti-corporate leftists, being informed that some new corporation is also bad). Their psychological need is for a smart-sounding person to validate their opinion and tell them that it is factually based. You’ll know you fulfilled it because they’ll say something like “I always knew something like this was true, but you put it into words so eloquently.”

**The Brutal Takedown.** The same as the Voxsplainer, except appealing to the id instead of the superego. A smart-sounding person reassures their audience that their hatred is completely valid. Nobody has ever been so hateable as their enemies. “You thought Skub supporters were slimy, but you don’t know the half of it! The latest news shows that they’re death cultists who want you to undergo constant humiliation rituals as the price of living in America.”

The Brutal Takedown combines the comfort of black-and-white certainty, with the group bonding of sharing a common enemy, with the frisson that maybe some Skub supporter is reading along, feeling angry and triggered and ashamed. It carries an apocalyptic promise that it’s *just a couple of days* before the preference cascade starts, and all right-thinking people band together to exile Skub supporters from society forever and accord you high status for being so right about this.

**The Marching Orders:** Your audience is people who are less cool than you. Their psychological need is to learn what position the cool and powerful people support, so that they can be sure to hold it, and not end up in the scary position of taking the opposite side from cool powerful people.

They wouldn’t put it in these terms, exactly. But they forgot to develop the brain lobe that distinguishes “cool, powerful position” from “correct position”, so they need a little help figuring out what position is coolrect.

**The Virtue Signal:** Your psychological need is to signal that you’re a good person. You can’t take a genuinely controversial position wouldn’t help, because then the people who disagreed with you wouldn’t know you were good. But you can’t take an obviously popular position either, because nobody will applaud you for saying “People shouldn’t be murdered” or some similar pablum. So you need to find a position which feels controversial, but in fact is popular. Common solutions include attacking an obsolete position on its way out (“Some people say that homosexuality is evil, but I think it should be tolerated!”) a position which is popular in communities far away from yours (“Some people say we should institute sharia law, but I’m against that!”), or a position which is technically true but has such terrible vibes that nobody wants to stand up for it (“Some people say that intelligence matters a lot in life, but I believe it’s creativity which is really important!”)

Your audience is people with the same psychological need, who are less good at finding seemingly-controversial-but-actually-popular positions, and are happy to mooch off your work by agreeing that you are so, *so* brave.

**The Revenge Killing:** Your psychological need is that somebody else has insulted you, probably incidentally while trying one of the maneuvers above. Your goal is to retaliate by proving they are more wrong than anyone has ever been before. Your audience’s psychological need is to get vicarious pleasure out of your victory, same as they would if their hometown sports team beat their bitter rival.

**The One-Level-Higher-Than-You:** Some people claim to be anti-Skub. Little do they know that anti-Skubness, as it currently exists, is *itself* a form of Skub, a loyal opposition created to distract people from the true points at issue. Here are 86,000 words that will give you a completely new worldview which lets you transcend the Skub/Anti-Skub dichotomy and confront the people who are *really* in charge.

Your psychological need is to look smarter than everyone else. Your audience’s psychological need is to feel smarter than everyone else. Taking one side or the other of a two-sided issue feels conformist, boring, unsophisticated. Going One Level Higher annoys everyone equally, which is almost as good as not being annoying at all!

**The Slatepitch:** Courtesy of [Matt Yglesias](https://www.slowboring.com/p/slatepitch). The Slatepitch is something unpopular yet trivial, like “Why owning a pet makes you a bad person”, or “Adultery is good, actually”. Your psychological need, as the writer, is to get clicks. Your audience’s psychological need is that they get to feel superior to it - no matter their actual station in life, they are, briefly, an Ordinary Red-Blooded American who gets to puncture the ridiculous pretensions of the elites. I [previously parodied these](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/sources-say-bay-area-house-party) with the fake publication ‘ Giving Middle-Aged Women Who Have Ruined Their Lives With Terrible Relationship Decisions A Platform To Recommend Those Decisions To Others, And People Obviously Notice The Contradiction And Post About It To Dunk On Us, But Actually They’re Only Taking Us Viral And In Fact That Was Our Strategy All Along, Ha Ha!’ *Magazine.* Yglesias is less long-winded than I am, and just name-dropped *Slate*.

**The True Contrarian:** Your psychological need is that for some reason, you hold a belief which it satisfies everyone else’s psychological needs to beat up. On the receiving end, you get a +5 bonus to Insight, letting you easily discern all the unvirtuous and non-epistemic motives of your attackers. You have thoughts like “If only I would state my beliefs clearly and unapologetically, people would stop using me as a punching bag and take me seriously.”

Your audience is everyone else whose psychological need it is to beat you up, because now they finally have a concrete target. The virtue signaler can *prove* that they’re not just falsely laundering a universally-popular belief as controversial. The Voxsplainer can eloquently tell people why you are wrong. The Brutal Takedown writer can grant their readers catharsis by turning you into the scapegoat for everything wrong with the world. The Slatepitcher can use you as camouflage and pretend they’re a true contrarian too. Everyone is happy, except that your “if only I would state my beliefs…people would stop using me as a punching bag” thesis gets proven more wrong than anything has ever been before.

**The Inkhaven Post:** The writer’s psychological need is that they have to write 500 words per day or get kicked out. Your audience’s psychological need is that they are your writing teacher who gets paid to read your work. The content is underdetermined by this relationship, and can be anything at all. Try to stay entertaining!

items.articleBody:
arXiv:2611.21682v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. Although responses generally demonstrated strong problem comprehension, they scored lower in factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, indicating that correct answers were not necessarily supported by technically sound justifications. Response clarity was also weakly indicative of technical quality. Furthermore, longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting that reasoning length may reflect question difficulty rather than improved problem-solving performance. Reasoning-token consumption may therefore provide an additional signal for identifying potentially unreliable responses. NEBench R1 establishes a benchmark for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning quality, providing a foundation for assessing the domain competence and reliability of LLMs in nuclear engineering.

items.articleBody:
“A construction can remain standing while losing its place in the everyday experience of the city. Its address remains, but its presence no longer draws attention. In this sense, disappearance can begin before demolition,” says a statement about a recent collaboration between [Alexandre Farto](https://vhils.com/) (a.k.a. [Vhils](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/vhils/)) and [Marcelo Cidade](https://www.instagram.com/cidade/).

The monumental project at Rua Cardeal Arcoverde, 2878 in Pinheiros, São Paulo, is a meditation on this sentiment as it considers how architecture and the seemingly mundane fixtures of city life shape our understanding of a place. Titled “2878,” the site-specific installation envelops a colonial-style building in silver thermal blankets typically used in emergencies. A cornstarch glue binds the utilitarian material to the structure’s facade, revealing the arched windows and ornate patterns in relief.

Photo by Henrique Cabral

Both drawing attention to the building and masking its real condition, the metallic blankets prompt questions about how we care for places and spaces. As passersby walk past, the installation mirrors their silhouettes as faint reflections, while the surface’s color and light shift depending on the time of day.

The collaborative intervention also evokes Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s “[Wrapped Reichstag](https://christojeanneclaude.net/artworks/wrapped-reichstag/)” and the early years of [Andy Warhol’s Factory](https://revolverwarholgallery.com/about-andy-warhol/the-factory/), in which silver paint and tin foil covered the walls of the artist’s New York studio. Warhol was interested in transience and the attention that comes with fame, concerns we see echoed and translated into broader conversations about public space, collective memory, and urban life in “2878.”

Find more from [Vhils](https://www.instagram.com/vhils/) and [Cidade](https://www.instagram.com/cidade/) on their Instagrams.

items.articleBody: Intracranial aneurysm (IA) is a focal dilation of the cerebral artery wall whose rupture causes aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage with approximately 40% case fatality. No intervention exists at the initiation stage because clinical imaging cannot resolve the cellular events that precede overt morphological change. We propose that pericyte dysfunction at the cerebral microcirculation barrier is the upstream event linking abnormal hemodynamics to IA initiation. Under physiological laminar shear, Piezo1–Notch mechanosensing and basal TGFβ–ALK5 signaling maintain the pericyte-supported microcirculation barrier; under disturbed flow, pericytes undergo HK2-driven glycolytic reprogramming, pro-inflammatory conversion, and contractile gain, causing focal barrier leakage. Leaked inflammatory mediators and plasma macromolecules are conveyed by cerebrospinal-fluid convection through the perivascular space to the adventitia of adjacent circle-of-Willis arteries, driving smooth muscle cell (SMC) shift toward a dedifferentiated, synthetic phenotype, expansion of POSTN+ perivascular fibroblasts, matrix degradation, internal elastic lamina destruction, and decompensated fibrosis culminating in saccular aneurysm. This cascade repositions aneurysm-wall fibrosis as an early event, opening a preventive window. We outline stage-matched interventions (HK2 metabolic axis, TGFβ/POSTN fibrosis axis, senolysis) and decisive experiments, including in vivo two-photon tracing of microcirculation-to-large-artery signaling through the perivascular space, with the evidence for each link explicitly graded.

items.articleBody: As human life expectancy increases, understanding the physiological changes that accompany aging becomes increasingly important. Gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is common with age, and age-related changes in the enteric nervous system (ENS), which regulates GI motility, may contribute to this decline in function. Studies of the aging ENS have reported contradicting results, potentially reflecting the substantial regional heterogeneity of the ENS and the fact that most studies focus on only one or two areas of the GI tract. Neurons in the myenteric plexus, which regulate intestinal contractions and motility, are organized into ganglia that form circumferential stripes along the length of the gut. Here, we systematically compare neuronal and glial density and organization across all five regions of the small and large intestine in young (3-4 month-old) and aged (22-26 month-old) mice. We find that neuronal density remains unchanged with age across all regions, despite localized changes in ganglia organization. Although the overall stripe-like arrangement is preserved, ganglia are less aligned with stripes in the duodenum and ileum, while those in the ileum and distal colon are smaller, contain fewer neurons, and have a greater proportion of neurons located outside the ganglia. Glial cell numbers vary regionally with age, increasing in the duodenum and distal colon but decreasing in the proximal colon. The proportion of Calretinin+ neurons, meanwhile, remains stable across the small intestine. Together, these findings reveal that aging is associated with selective, region-specific remodeling of myenteric plexus cytoarchitecture rather than uniform structural decline across the GI tract. This comprehensive regional analysis may help reconcile conflicting reports of age-related changes in the ENS.

items.articleBody:
*What tracks get Dave Seaman moving? We asked him.*

Dave Seaman has been a fixture of dance music for close to 40 years. As one half of Brothers in Rhythm he co-wrote and produced Kylie Minogue's 'Confide in Me', the record that marked her break from Stock Aitken Waterman pop, and his remix and production credits take in Pet Shop Boys, New Order, Michael Jackson and David Bowie. Alongside that sits a long DJ career built on Global Underground mixes, his *Back to Mine* compilation and Selador, the label he co-runs with Steve Parry.

Remarkably, he has never released a solo studio album until now. [Mirrorball Sleaze](https://found.ee/MirrorballSleaze) landed on Selador on 13 November. With the album now out, we put our Top Tracks questions to him.

### What's the first album you ever bought?

Blondie – [Parallel Lines](https://www.beatport.com/release/parallel-lines/5216975?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c). If you were a ten-year-old boy in 1978, Debbie Harry was particularly alluring.

### The first time you remember hearing electronic music?

Tubeway Army – ['Are "Friends" Electric?'](https://www.beatport.com/track/are-friends-electric/13256328?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c). Gary Numan had a huge impact on me and started a lifelong obsession with synth music.

### Your favourite ever album?

That's a tough one, but if pushed, I'd probably have to say Prince – [Sign o' the Times](https://www.beatport.com/release/sign-o-the-times/6752625?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The guaranteed floor-filler?

Donna Summer – ['I Feel Love'](https://www.beatport.com/track/i-feel-love/15739558?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c). Unbelievably, it's 50 years old next year!

### The best tune from last year?

From 2025? DJ Koze – ['Buschtaxi'](https://www.beatport.com/track/buschtaxi/20017608?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The guilty pleasure?

Olivia Rodrigo.

### The last track of the night?

That very much depends on the context. Too many variables. Early night or late night? Where and with whom? The occasion?

### The best chillout record?

The remit for my *Back to Mine* compilation was literally to collate some of my favourite chillout tracks, all mixed together on one album, so…

### The record everyone loves, but you hate?

Robin S – ['Show Me Love'](https://www.beatport.com/track/show-me-love/1051600?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The best record for a family party?

Earth, Wind & Fire – ['September'](https://www.beatport.com/track/september/11758082?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The soundtrack to a lazy Sunday afternoon?

Sade – ['Pearls'](https://www.beatport.com/track/pearls/4789376?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c), poolside at Pikes Ibiza.

### The worst record you've ever heard?

I try to banish those from my mind as soon as I've heard them.

### The record you're proudest of?

Kylie Minogue – ['Confide in Me'](https://www.beatport.com/release/confide-in-me/5832405?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The future classic?

DJ Koze – ['Buschtaxi'](https://www.beatport.com/track/buschtaxi/20017608?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

**Find Dave Seaman on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/daveseamandj/?hl=en) and [Soundcloud.](https://soundcloud.com/daveseaman)**

**Dave Seaman's Mirrorball Sleaze is out on Selador**.**[Listen and buy here](https://www.beatport.com/release/mirrorball-sleaze/7618002?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).**

items.articleBody: ContextThe cerebral substrates of fatigue in patients with Multiple Sclerosis (pwMS) remain incompletely understood. This study aims at exploring the functional brain substrates of fatigue in pwMS with a recent disease history.MethodsSixteen pwMS (disease history < 5 years) and 17 matched Healthy Controls (HC) performed a N-Back task with three difficulty levels during functional MRI (fMRI) acquisitions following high vs. low cognitive fatigue induction. Measures of subjective trait and state fatigue were also recorded. Behavioral performance at the N-Back task and evolution of subjective fatigue states were analyzed by means of Bayesian repeated measures analyses of variance. fMRI data were analyzed to determine between-group differences (1) in task-related brain activity, independently of trait fatigue score; (2) in the association between trait fatigue and brain activity.ResultsEvidence toward a similar trajectory in the two groups was observed for subjective and task-related measures of fatigue following fatigue induction. No between-group difference was observed in brain activity unrelated to fatigue score. However, negative associations between trait fatigue score and brain activity were observed in pwMS, while the associations are positive in HC. Specifically, opposite associations (positive in HC and negative in pwMS) were observed in regions belonging to the Striato-Thalamo-Cortical (STC) network and the fronto-parietal cortex.ConclusionSlightly different patterns of brain activity related to fatigue were observed in pwMS and HC in the STC circuitry, despite similar behavioral performance and subjective fatigue level. This is consistent with the implication of the STC loops in fatigue pathophysiology, occurring from the early stages of the disease.

items.articleBody:
Photograph by Darren James.

In the early seventies, Helen Garner and her two-year-old daughter moved into a communal house of mostly single mothers in the inner suburbs of Melbourne, the first of several share homes they would live in during that decade. The house was noisy and chaotic but offered Garner a creative freedom that she hadn’t found in her first marriage. While her daughter played with the other children, Garner read Proust and Tolstoy, wrote in her diary, and began a passionate love affair with a man who was addicted to heroin. As the relationship went on, she began to see her experiences as a narrative. “Story is a chunk of life with a bend in it, and I could feel this one coming,” Garner tells Thessaly La Force in **[The Art of Fiction No. 255](https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/7929/the-art-of-fiction-no-255-helen-garner)**, published in issue no. 241. “I suddenly thought, Maybe I could write about this while it’s still happening, as it’s coming into its bend.”

The resulting novel, Garner’s debut, *Monkey Grip* (1977), created a rupture in the landscape of Australian literature, winning Garner first prize in the National Book Council Awards while also provoking consternation among critics for its depictions of unconventional domestic life, sex, and female desire. Some accused Garner of merely publishing her journal—which is, in fact, more or less what she had done. In an essay published in 2002, she asked why this should be a bad thing. “As if there were no work involved in keeping a diary in the first place,” she wrote. “It’s as if a diary wrote itself, as if it poured out in a sludgy, involuntary, self-indulgent stream.” (Her extraordinary diaries have been published in three volumes spanning from 1978 to 1998.)

Garner was born in 1942 in the coastal city of Geelong, Victoria, the eldest of six. “In a big family you’ve got to find a way of getting away from everybody to a place where you can quietly exist, and that’s what reading was for me,” she tells La Force. “It was my way of being absent. I used to kneel by the side of my bed so I could keep reading even while I was pulling my clothes on.” The family unit—particularly under strain or in free fall—has frequently been a subject of her novels, including *The Children’s Bach* (1984), in which the circumscribed lives of a couple are upturned by a visit from an old friend’s bohemian family, and *The Spare Room* (2008), in which the narrator hosts an old friend who is undergoing alternative treatment for cancer, and which deals with the frustrations of care with brutal honesty.

Family has been central, too, in Garner’s nonfiction, most notably in two books about her experience of following murder trials: *Joe Cinque’s Consolation* (2004), about a young woman who killed her boyfriend, and *This House of Grief* (2014), about a father who drove himself and his three children into a dam, killing the children. “The thing is, despite being told that my concerns were too domestic, I’ve always known that the family is where everything is played out,” Garner tells La Force.

Over the past five decades, in her fiction, journalism, and essays, Garner has continually brought the fullness of her self to bear on the page: her scrupulous honesty, emotional intelligence, clarity, and imagination. She has been awarded the Windham-Campbell Prize, the Melbourne Prize for Literature, and the Walkley Award, and has been inducted into the Victorian Honour Roll of Women. We are delighted to add to this list the Hadada, our award for lifetime achievement, which has previously been awarded to writers including John Ashbery, Anne Carson, Deborah Eisenberg, Jamaica Kincaid, N. Scott Momaday, Edward P. Jones, and James Salter. We are tremendously excited to present Garner with the Hadada on **[April 6](https://www.theparisreview.org/revel)** at the Spring Revel, our annual gathering of writers, artists, and friends to celebrate and raise funds for the *Review*, which is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Tickets are now available, and all proceeds from the event will help us continue to seek out the best new work and share it with readers in print and online. We hope you’ll **[join](https://www.theparisreview.org/revel)** us.
