items.articleBody:
US studio [CLB Architects](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/carney-logan-burke-architects/) has completed an [accessory dwelling unit](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/accessory-dwelling-units/) called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple.

The small building stands on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, located just beyond the popular ski town of [Jackson](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/jackson/). The site is dotted with mature trees and sits along the west bank of the Snake River.

Before the project's inception, the clients had lived on the property for 25 years – in a modest, 1960s house they had renovated – and had raised their son there.

As their son neared graduation from high school, the couple decided to build an ADU on the property and make it their full-time residence, while renting out the main residence.

### Drawings and photography

Previous

Next

### Drawings and photography

Close

"The new house would allow them to remain on the land they had known for decades, while experiencing it in a new way – closer to nature, with stronger connections to light, views and outdoor living," said Jackson-based [CLB Architects](https://clbarchitects.com/).

The house also represents a way to accommodate a growing need for housing while preserving the natural landscape.

"In our region, there’s a clear need for this housing type, which is economical, compact and responsive to place," said CLB Architects partner Eric Logan.

A primary challenge for the design team was to ensure the house “met the couple’s programmatic and budget constraints” within a very compact footprint. Per country regulations, the new house could not exceed 1,000 square feet (92.9 square metres).

The architects conceived a simple, rectangular volume that rises two levels and is topped with a gabled roof. The house was carefully sited so it would feel separate from the main residence.

"Siting the building toward the back of the parcel and introducing new landscaping and tree plantings created a soft buffer between the two dwellings," the architect said.

The team carved out portions of the exterior to form inset terraces, along with a climbing wall that is used by the couple’s son while home from college. On the east-facing elevation, a boxy protrusion forms a balcony.

Both inside and out, the team opted for materials that were durable, cost-efficient and complemented the building’s form. Dark corrugated metal clads most of the building, while tight-knot cedar was used for inset areas to provide “warmth and depth”.

The ground level contains a spacious garage for vehicles and outdoor gear. The upper level holds two bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms, all of which are organised around a central living area.

“Locating the main living spaces on the second floor allows the interiors to engage the tree canopy while maximising natural light, offering a more intimate relationship with the landscape,” the team said.

[Read: CLB Architects wraps Caju House in Wyoming in weathering steel](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/01/02/caju-house-wyoming-clb-architects-weathering-steel/)

The living area opens onto a west-facing deck, which acts as an “outdoor living room” for much of the year. Large, sliding glass doors diminish the boundary between inside and out and usher in breezes during summer months.

The clients, both of whom have deep experience in design and construction fields, poured themselves into the project. The husband served as the general contractor and engaged local tradespeople to help out.

"A true labor of love, the couple built much of the house themselves, working on the construction every evening and on weekends," the team said, noting the project was completed in about nine months.

The project offers ideas for how communities in the Mountain West can accommodate growth while preserving the natural landscape.

“With rising land values and the need to accommodate more residents, homes like this – that are compact, efficient, and contextual – can provide more housing while preserving open space,” the team said.

"As local communities grapple with growth, projects like this suggest one path forward."

Other ADUs in America include a [small, cedar-clad dwelling](https://www.dezeen.com/2024/01/02/farm-buildings-sonoma-adu-sonoma-schwartz-and-architecture/) in California’s wine country by Schwartz and Architecture, and a [compact, metal-clad building](https://www.dezeen.com/2023/04/12/north-arrow-studio-birdhouse-adu-austin/) in Austin by North Arrow Studio that resembles a birdhouse.

**Project credits:**

**Architecture and interior design:** CLB Architects
**Architecture and interior design team:** Eric Logan (partner), Darcey Prichard (partner), Sarah Kennedy (principal), Paige Hobson (project manager), Stephanie Wright (project coordinator)
**Contractor:** Dembergh Construction, Mike Prichard (partner)
**Structural engineer:** Tectonic Design
**MEP Engineer:** Jim Bob Schell
**Landscape:** Agrostis and The Tree and Landscape Company
**Lighting:** Helius Architectural Lighting
**Owners:** Darcey and Mike Prichard

items.articleBody:
Midterm results showed that men under 30 (a supposed MAGA bulwark) shifted back to voting mostly for Democrats. Louise Perry and I spoke about whether that signals the end of the New Right.

Among other things, we discuss whether perceptions of corruption played a role. Voters will overlook a president lining his pockets, so long as they themselves feel prosperous. But the economy feels shaky for many people. Moreover, we discuss whether the online right on X made the same mistake the online left made back when it was still called Twitter: confusing applause from fellow partisans with the preferences of normal people.

Louise and I also speak about whether it’s true that “the left can’t meme.” We converge on an answer that involves censorship, 4chan, sex differences in humor, esoteric messaging, and why so much political imagery now looks like it was made for toddlers. We also get into what I heard Dave Chappelle recently say at Madison Square Garden about Charlie Kirk.

Finally, I asked Louise a question every man has wondered about women’s group chats. Her answer was not what I expected.

[↗ robkhenderson.com](https://www.robkhenderson.com/p/did-the-new-right-meme-itself-out)

items.articleBody:
*The following article was written as a companion piece for Lewis Richmond’s upcoming* Tricycle *class, “A Buddhist Response to AI: Studying Samsara, Practicing Kindness.”* [Sign up today](https://tricycle.org/events/ai-buddhism-email-program/#signup) *.*

The Dalai Lama has often said that Buddhist practitioners should study samsara. Samsara means the everyday world of ignorance and delusion. His advice is foundational and practical; he is encouraging us to know the sea in which we swim. And because today’s technology is so inescapable and powerful, there is probably no greater magnifier of samsara today than technology, which now includes artificial intelligence. So, like it or not, we Buddhists need to deal with AI; at least we need to study it. As a lifelong Buddhist practitioner and teacher, as well as a former computer professional, I have my doubts as to whether AI is truly intelligent, but, regardless, its influence and power are sweeping the world, and, try as we might, none of us can avoid it. I am proposing that the practices and teachings of Buddhism can be a counterpoint to some of AI’s seductions and a protective shield from some of its dangers. But how, as Buddhists, can we accomplish that? What can we do?

Today, there is a near-war going on between two opposing camps: the realm of living things, and the realm of digital technology. The outcome of this conflict is likely to define every aspect of our long-term future—even whether we survive as a species at all. At least that’s what Nobel prize winner Dr. Geoffrey Hinton—known as the “father of AI”—has warned; other tech gurus have echoed his words. This is serious business. I have given names to these two camps: I call the world of technology “Byteworld,” and the world of living things “Lifeworld.” Byteworld and Lifeworld—these two are arm in arm, marching headlong into unknown territory. Of course Lifeworld (that is, ourselves) created all of Byteworld (as well as Buddhism), but Byteworld is breaking free of its human bonds and going its own way, like some golem-like clay doll magically come to life.

Computer technology arguably began with the invention of the mainframe computer in the 1950s, followed by the personal computer, the internet, smartphones, social media, and, finally, “artificial intelligence.” The biosphere, in contrast, has existed for untold millennia, evolving from single-celled organisms to dinosaurs, parrots, dolphins, elephants, the great apes, and us. Our human achievements are legion: fire, the wheel, great epics and dramas, symphonies and songs, towering cities and civilizations, sailing ships and rockets, myriad forms of civilization and social organization, religion and spiritual life, and, of course, Byteworld itself. Of these I think Lifeworld’s greatest accomplishment is religion and spiritual life—paths leading to inner transformation and an awakened state of compassionate awareness. Buddhism, which has been my life’s study, is such a path.

I know technology from the inside; beginning in 1994, for twenty-five years, I owned and managed a software company whose product was a business-to-business software application that I wrote myself. But before that I spent thousands of hours in meditation on my black cushion, as well as studying Buddhism with some of the best living teachers. So I’ve had a foot in both worlds. I know the thrill that comes from writing a block of computer code and watching it perform its magic in the real world. I also know how urgently our world needs the spiritual healing and compassionate perspective that paths such as Buddhism can provide.

Though I understand how Byteworld works, my refuge has always been the biological wisdom of Lifeworld. When I was younger, it was my hope that this coming age would be one of spiritual awakening, but, instead, I see all the attention, power, and money racing in the other direction: toward the godlike power of technology, a glittering secular deity whose silicon chips and farmland-destroying data centers are replicating like a metallic cancer. How can we rein in this explosive machine?

Technology and AI do have limits. I doubt that AI is on its way to being all-powerful, in spite of what some tech gurus say. These machines of our making emulate only some portion of what our brains can do—mostly their verbal and mathematical skills. There is so much more to the human psyche. Psychologist Howard Gardner has proposed a theory of eight forms of human intelligence. In addition to words and mathematics, he adds music (Mozart), spatial awareness (architects), physical ability (athletes and surgeons), naturalistic knowledge (gardeners), interpersonal intelligence (therapists, ministers, and mediators), and *intra* personal intelligence (the awareness of our inner states and processes). AI excels in words and numbers. But it lacks feeling and true emotion—the relational skills of which Gardner speaks—and an intimacy with the natural world of plants and animals. It’s worth mentioning that “intrapersonal intelligence” is also the domain of meditation, which involves paying attention to our inner physical and mental states. Intrapersonal intelligence, on which Buddhism is built, may be in time a hidden resource that could counterbalance the empires of Byteworld. If so, each of us as Buddhists may have a role to play.

AI offers power, wealth, and control to those few who create and deploy it, but its capacities are narrow compared to the biological wisdom that incorporates emotion, intuition, faith, and religion, the five physical senses, and our 64 trillion cells, each with its own DNA-powered intelligence that we share with the whole biosphere. AI is a kind of miracle, to be sure. There is no question that Byteworld has game, but Lifeworld has so much more. What AI entity could ever experience the grandeur of Beethoven’s musical heart? And, for that matter, what robot could pray?

I suspect that our fascination with the glories of AI will sour in time as its darker capabilities, including weaponization and environmental pollution, come to the fore. To summarize the core message of the Buddha’s path: Each of us is a living Buddha at heart, only waiting to emerge like a butterfly from a cocoon. We don’t need any additional machines or vast data centers in farmland or in space to achieve that. We already have what we need. We are the heirs of the whole biosphere’s intelligent rainforest. Awakening is a birthright for every one of us. Lifeworld offers us untold gifts, including the dharma. That said, the human realm is not an unalloyed good, and technology is not an unalloyed bad. Each domain is complex; each has its gifts as well as dangers.

## Gifts and Dangers of Lifeworld

*Living relationships.* Everything in the world of the living is intrinsically related, but not by bits and bytes. We share with every living thing the pulse of aliveness; we share their DNA, their evolution and adaptability. In a more profound sense we share a living connection with all of reality. Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh calls this connectivity “interbeing,” and it is described in detail in Buddhist scriptures such as the *Avatamsaka Sutra*. Human community and family, the kind we can touch and feel in the presence of others, is foundational; in some ways it is our deepest intelligence. In Buddhism we call that sangha.

*Slowness.* Speed is our new god these days, but the pace of living things is of a different order. Lifeworld is optimized for survival and evolution. Lifeworld is actually neither slow nor fast; it simply marks the pace of being alive. A human baby takes nine months to gestate. It can’t be speeded up. A majestic redwood tree takes a hundred years to grow, or a thousand. It will never be digitized. The vibrancy of all living things, the unfolding of a whole human life from beginning to end, the blossoming of love and of family, each require their appropriate season and timing. Speed will not improve them. Deepfake emulation will not replace them. Life evolves and replicates in slow time.

*Kindness.* The world of the living tends toward kindness; kindness is an artifact of interbeing. Human beings can be cruel, too, but kindness is our higher goal. Digital intelligence can emulate kindness; already chatbots have been trained to tell us how good we look and how great our ideas are. But true kindness occurs through aliveness. It arises from the interpersonal intelligence that Howard Gardner describes, and it is intrinsic to sangha. The kindness we have can never be replaced by a machine. What is most true about kindness is that we need more of it.

*Dangers of the human realm.* Long ago the Buddha identified the dark side of the human psyche with his teaching of the “three unwholesome roots”—greed, aversion, and egoistic delusion. These “three poisons” have sullied and darkened every human generation, including ours. Just because we are Buddhas in the making doesn’t mean that we are blameless. Innately we are good, but that quality is too often clouded.

## Dangers and Gifts of Byteworld

AI is not just chatbots. AI is rapidly being integrated in every aspect of human life. In business, AI is taking over marketing, customer service, and hiring; it is also now doing much entry-level computer programming. In banking, AI does fraud protection, lending, and customer service. Its military uses are rapidly increasing too. Candidly, AI is everywhere. These new AI roles present many dangers; here are just a few of them.

*Addiction.* Social media is already addictive, and harms children; AI is making it more so. Criminals using AI have discovered new ways to defraud, to steal, to harass, to invade privacy, to destroy reputations, even to kill. Terrorists may soon use AI to create a weaponized virus with no cure. Has all this AI-enhanced digital connectivity been worth it, just so we can ask our chatbot for the best recipe for banana bread?

*Jobs.* The fear that AI and humanoid robots driven by AI will replace jobs is everywhere. People say they are afraid for their livelihoods and their very future due to AI. The deeper issue is that for the most part the creators of AI and the politicians who make the rules don’t seem to care that much about people’s worries. Are we on the cusp of major social discontent, even disorder in the streets? AI riots?

*Environmental Impact.* In order to do its work, Byteworld requires huge data centers, many the size of fifteen football fields. They are sprouting up everywhere: in previously quiet suburbs; on farmland that once grew crops for food; on the edge of big cities where there is power and water to satisfy their cooling needs. There are already thousands of these centers supporting the digital “cloud”; it is estimated that in the next ten years, to support AI, 3,000 more of these monster construction projects will be built just in the US, with many more in other countries. Each of them requires vast amounts of water and electricity; many also have huge diesel- or gas-powered turbines that pollute the air. These centers are also noisy; those who live near them say that their sound is a loud sleep-disturbing hum. Some local governments are fighting back, but there are billions of dollars to be made by building out this AI infrastructure. When there is that kind of money to be made, ethics and care tend to go out the window.

*Technology’s Gifts.* To be fair, AI has also brought many new benefits. In the realm of medicine alone, AI is already contributing lifesaving technologies such as early cancer detection. It is speeding all manner of research and helps with weather prediction, eldercare, education, and so much more. These benefits are bound to expand with each passing year.

## My Religion Is Kindness

The Dalai Lama has often said, “My religion is kindness.” Because this is such a simple statement, people may not realize how profound it is. He doesn’t only mean “Kindness is valuable and good.” He means that Buddhism as a wisdom practice transforms us into people who are unconditionally kind. The Buddhist term for that type of person is bodhisattva. Lifeworld is the crucible where this kind of compassion can be nurtured.

Once, when the Dalai Lama was asked if he was angry at the Chinese, he replied, “The Chinese have taken so much from us. I won’t let them take my state of mind.” Even in the face of that pain, he maintained his kind heart. I was, for a time, the personal attendant of renowned Vietnamese Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh. He spoke softly and carefully, as though each word were a treasure. The sound of his voice itself, and the way he lifted the cup of tea I had poured for him, radiated kindness.

For my own teacher, Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, kindness was second nature. I witnessed, so many times, when he reached out to help someone or touch a person who needed his care. One time, I came to meditation early in the morning, and there, on the front steps, was Suzuki, quietly talking to a homeless man. As I stepped past them to enter the building, he didn’t look up. He was doing his work.

This unconditional kindness is, I think, the most precious thing in the world. I fear that the implacable march of technology will crush this treasure. I fear that Byteworld will toss it aside as unnecessary, seeing it as a weakness, dismissing it as unable to make money or wield power—an obsolete quality that human beings will no longer need.

I don’t want that to happen. I want kindness to survive, and not just to survive but to prosper. I want everyone to see through the false promise of a light speed digital future and remember what binds us together and connects us to all life—kindness. Without kindness, I fear, we will become wan and hollow. As the Dalai Lama has said, our religion as Buddhists is kindness. Kindness is the best of who we are. It is our not so invisible power.

## Breathwalking with Byteworld

In the course of pondering Lifeworld and Byteworld, I have created a library of contemplative exercises to help us experience the difference between them. Here is one called “Breathwalking with Byteworld.” It uses a smartphone to illustrate how Byteworld takes us away from ourselves, and how we can return to ourselves by walking in awareness—a venerable Buddhist practice.

To begin, stand in a quiet uncrowded place—a hallway in your house or an unpopulated outdoor path—and lift up your smartphone. Open the phone’s camera app so that you can see the scene in front of you. To start, let the phone drop to your side and begin walking slowly, feet a shoulder-width apart, one step for each exhale, so that your whole body flows with movement and your mind observes it with attention and awareness. In ancient days, Buddhist monks would spend hours each day walking just like this on their verandas or in forests.

Now, lift up your phone and look at it. Watch the scene in your camera unfold while you continue to walk. Notice how the pixel version of what you are seeing gradually absorbs all your attention, while the awareness of your body slowly recedes. The scene you see is almost the same as without your phone, but it is an emulation, a deepfake, if you will. Everywhere, these days, we see people absorbed in that phone world—in airport lobbies, restaurants, classrooms, on sidewalks, even in a moving car—people glued to their phone, watching the alternate universe it presents. Have we all become phone zombies, walking around holding up these shiny rectangles in front of our faces? Sometimes it seems that way.

Now, shift gears again, let the hand that holds your phone drop down, and return to the awareness of breath and your body as you continue to walk. Feel the transition, the bump in the road as the familiar physical world returns and the emulated imagery of the phone screen goes away. The phone is more than a passive copycat. We know now that the apps, texts, photos, and videos on that phone can cause harm. They can hurt children. In the moving car of a distracted texting driver, they can kill. By practicing Breathwalking with Byteworld you can bring the awareness exercise of Buddhist practice to the fore and disempower this deceptive device.

More and more people are becoming aware of how technology is distorting their reality. There are now paid phone apps that lock your phone out for a time, forcing you to give it up when you lack the willpower to do it yourself. You can also go on vacation to an expensive resort that offers a phone-free environment; you give them your phone when you register. These remedies are salves and medicines; look for there to be more of them in the future.

## Looking Ahead

It is hard to say what will happen with all this mad swirl of technological change. There are as many predictions as there are savants to utter them. The truth is no one knows. Meantime, to return to the question that began this essay, *what should we as Buddhists do?*

One possibility is to escape, to remove ourselves as much as possible from the influence of technology and AI. Buddhism’s monastic tradition seems to offer that option. Monastic life is one form of “living off the grid,” staying far from the buzz of the big city, in hidden valleys where everyone knows your name, where people have put away their phones, unplugged their devices from the internet while they tend their own vegetable gardens and write notes to each other in longhand simply because it is more beautiful.

But there is another option besides escape. To paraphrase Pope Leo, “We shouldn’t reject technology but prevent it from dominating humanity.” Buddhists can have a role in that. Bodhisattvas may train in the monastery, but they don’t stay there forever. The vow of the bodhisattva says, “However many beings there are in the world, I vow to liberate them, to care for them all, be kind to them all.” This vow is a commitment not to escape but to engage. As Buddhists we can study the samaras of technology to become more skillful at helping, even as we continue the transformative practices of studying ourselves. We can choose to live in the light of kind action. When there is an opportunity to help, we do not hesitate; when an opportunity doesn’t immediately present itself, we practice patience, tend to our practice and wait. That opportunity will come soon enough.

We can, each in our own way, become exemplars of a life that upholds the highest human values and the deepest inter- and intrapersonal human intelligence, even as AI and its manic golems sweep the world. The bodhisattva vow manifests an awareness and an intelligence that no machine or digital brain can match. We Buddhists dedicate our lives to it, and uphold it as long as we can until others rise to take our place. Even in the face of the loudest criers of technological doom—who may, in the end, be wrong—we keep confidence in that vow.

May it be so.

items.articleBody:
Fox News took a liking to the WNBA this past season, but not so much for the basketball and more so for the rage bait. Melanie Walsh, with Jan Diehm, for the Pudding, [analyzed WNBA coverage through chryon data](https://pudding.cool/2026/11/wnba-politics/).

> Fox News’ vocabulary barely touches on-court play. Its coverage is driven by social media reactions and political flashpoints, leaning heavily into conservative buzzwords like “white privilege,” “national anthem,” and “biological men.”
> At the center of this framing sits “Fever star” Clark, whom Fox News repeatedly tethers to its conservative agenda.

Walsh provides an analysis from all angles. The comparison between Fox News coverage against how other networks cover the WNBA shows the baiting most clearly. Whereas the other networks focus more on points and rebounds, Fox News focuses on social media and race.

**Tags:** [bait](https://flowingdata.com/tag/bait/), [Fox News](https://flowingdata.com/tag/fox-news/), [Jan Diehm](https://flowingdata.com/tag/jan-diehm/), [Melanie Walsh](https://flowingdata.com/tag/melanie-walsh/), [Pudding](https://flowingdata.com/tag/pudding/), [WNBA](https://flowingdata.com/tag/wnba/)

items.articleBody:
**We’re a few weeks into a reboot of our [Beautiful News](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/) project from a few years ago. Refreshed. Revitalised. Re-visualised.**

Once more, every day for a year, we are surfacing and visualising some of the **amazing, progressive and positive things happening around the world**. Trends and events and innovations we can’t always see when fixated on the negativity of the news.

We’ve spruced and updated some of data-visualisations from the original collection, as well as adding 160 more stories to be released over the next weeks, months, year and beyond!

Every graphic is of course underpinned by [open datasets](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/data/) to support full **evidence-based optimism.**

Swing by and join [our weekly newsletter](https://beautifulnews.myflodesk.com/newsletter) or daily on [the website](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/), or social channels of your choosing: [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/beautifulnews.daily), [Twitter/X](https://x.com/beautiful__news), [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/beautifulnewsdaily/), [Threads](https://www.threads.com/@beautifulnews.daily).

## Some of my favourite graphics and stories so far

» [34 Countries Now Generate 80% or More of Their Electricity from Renewables](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3021-countries-electricity-renewables/)

» [Everyone, Everywhere, is Living Longer](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/41-everyone-everywhere-is-living-longer/)

**Towards a more nutritious information diet…**

David

items.title: Learning the language of machine learning
items.subtitle: When deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work.
items.feedText: Today, this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice. items.articleBody:
When deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work. Today, this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice.

Jacob Andreas would rather have the models explain themselves.

The newly tenured associate professor develops techniques that enable artificial intelligence models to communicate accurately about what they learned from their training data, in language humans can understand.

“Rather than needing to use all these external tools to try and understand what is going on under the hood, maybe we can train models to talk about themselves in a way that is accurate,” says Andreas, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL).

Ultimately, he and his group want to help people design more accurate and robust deep-learning models that are better suited for their intended application.

“We used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters and figuring out whether they make sense or not. Now, we need ‘mind-reading tools’ that can take this really complicated neural computation and translate it for us because it is just not in a language that we, as humans, know how to speak,” he says.

**A love of language**

Andreas’ fascination with language blossomed at a young age. As a child growing up in the San Francisco Bay Area, he was a voracious reader of any book he could get his hands on.

One such book, passed along to him by a family friend, contained a pivotal scene where the main character hacked into a computer system to save the day.

That piqued his interest in computers. A few years later, his father brought home a simple BASIC Engine that Andreas could run on their home computer, and he started immersing himself in the world of computer programming.

Andreas chose to major in computer science as an undergraduate at Columbia University but wasn’t sure if he wanted to pursue a career as a researcher, as a software engineer, or at a startup.

His friends signed up for research projects in faculty labs, so Andreas figured he would try that, too.

“I just blast emailed everyone in the computer science department who was working on anything vaguely AI-related, and the natural language processing faculty got back to me first. That is how I wound up in the field where I am now,” he says.

Working in the lab of Michael Collins, the Vikram S. Pandit Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, Andreas completed an undergraduate thesis project on machine translation. His project involved adapting existing statistical techniques for representing the meaning of language into more powerful AI systems that could translate passages of text.

“I always felt like these deeper questions about how thought works or how to model the world were closer to the surface in language processing problems than in the other tasks that AI people were working on at the time,” he recalls.

**A seismic shift**

He wanted to keep exploring deep questions, so Andreas enrolled in graduate school at the University of California at Berkeley to pursue a career as an academic researcher.

Before starting his PhD studies, he spent a year earning a master’s degree at Cambridge University in England. In that historic environment, he was inspired to contemplate the nature of language learning as he worked on computational translation problems.

Those studies fueled his research when he joined the lab of Berkeley professor of computer science Dan Klein.

Andreas began his studies at the time when neural networks were starting to take off. The field of natural language processing was making a seismic shift from statistical methods to this new world of deep learning.

Statistical methods utilize transparent, mathematical formulas to analyze text, while deep learning techniques use opaque algorithms to automatically learn complex meanings from massive amounts of text data.

“It was fun to be there as we made this transition to the modern toolkit, and learning and inventing all of that stuff when it was still new,” Andreas says.

He began collaborating with scientists in computer vision labs to tackle increasingly complex questions about language learning. Together, they designed AI systems that excelled at generating natural language by teaching those systems to “see” and understand the world around them.

“This was all super-exciting because there really hadn’t been a common set of tools for working with both language and vision data. Then, all of a sudden, neural networks gave us this common language,” he recalls.

He completed a thesis project on the use of neural module networks, which are small fragments of neural networks that perform specific tasks, like localizing objects or logical reasoning, in a larger AI system. But it was the more speculative projects he tackled alongside his thesis, like interpretability and creating natural language descriptions of an AI model’s internal states, that would drive the focus of his group at MIT.

**Faculty focus**

After spending a year at the startup Semantic Machines (which spun out of his lab at Berkeley), Andreas joined the MIT faculty in 2019.

“It felt like this was a fantastic opportunity to be in the homeland of AI research and collaborate with all these amazing, established people, but also do something new and figure out what the modern era in machine learning was going to look like,” he says.

His group focuses on two main areas. First, they are studying the science of large language models to understand the algorithms these models deploy as they learn and process information.

The tools they develop help scientists and researchers better predict how a trained model will behave in the real world. For instance, one family of techniques they developed trains large language models to explain what is going on inside other neural networks using language a human could understand.

These techniques can assign a natural language description to every information-processing node in a massive neural network. For example, one such description might represent an individual node that identifies [“patches of grass near animals” in input images](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.11114).

“That work serves as a jumping off point for a bunch of higher-level questions we ask about how these models represent meaning,” he says.

On the other side, his team designs new algorithms for training machine-learning models, and for predicting how specific datasets or examples will affect different aspects of model behavior.

“We don’t have a good scientific theory of what is going to happen when you train a model on a particular dataset. This is a big challenge for the field right now,” he says.

**A changing environment**

The speed of AI advancement presents one of the biggest challenges his lab faces. The field seems to completely change every three to five years, Andreas says, forcing him to stay nimble and ready to learn something new.

That same dilemma carries over into the courses 6.461 and 6.861 (undergraduate and graduate Natural Language Processing), which Andreas co-teaches. He and his fellow instructors must redesign the course each year to keep up with the newest developments.

It’s also challenging to teach the technical pieces of machine learning in an era where every assignment could be completed by a large language model rather than a human pupil.

“I try to impress upon the students that having a really deep foundation in how all this technology works under the hood is the only way they are going to understand it, and will differentiate them in a world where everyone has access to a coding agent,” he says.

With so much change, it is difficult to predict where the field is headed next, Andreas says. He foresees that his group’s work on interpretability will become even more important for making advanced systems like AI agents safe enough to deploy in high-stakes situations.

This will be especially true as researchers design deep-learning models that can aid in scientific discovery. These models will be trained on troves of raw data from research labs that may not be well-understood by scientists yet.

“Figuring out how to enable these models to verbalize all of this hidden knowledge they have about things people have never written about explicitly will be a huge challenge and opportunity for people who work in machine learning,” he says.

In addition to tackling challenges in the lab, Andreas enjoys pushing himself as a hiker and backpacker. He has loved spending time in the outdoors since his childhood in California and goes on at least one or two backpacking trips each summer.

He and a colleague in the Department of Mathematics are working their way across all the 4,000-foot peaks in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, making slow but steady progress.

And now that he has earned tenure, Andreas is looking forward to getting back into an old hobby — singing in a chamber choir. He’s always enjoyed music and became enamored with chapel choirs and bell ringing during his time at Cambridge University.

Place des Montréalaises: A Monumental Gesture Inscribing Women's Memory at the Heart of a City
Place des Montréalaises is reshaping Montreal's civic and tourist heart by covering a sunken expressway with a vibrant esplanade. Designed by Lemay in collaboration with artist Angela Silver and the engineering team at AtkinsRéalis, this major intervention connects Old Montreal to downtown and inscribes the memory of exceptional women in the urban landscape.

items.articleBody:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

Subscribe now

**AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better:** *…AI can now productively spend money to improve itself…* Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks.

**21 long-horizon tasks** “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.”
**Example task:** Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered.

**Key features:**

- Scaling spending: “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.”
- Open-ended & end-to-end: “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. One notable observation is that agents do quite a lot of novel stuff; “in 28% of trajectories, agents add newly trained parts to pretrained models or train a new model from scratch.”
- Decent verification: “Agents submit an inference server that serves their model on an air-gapped H100 machine,” they write. “To disincentivize overfitting, we provide limited validation samples and evaluate on a large out-of-distribution held-out test set, not shown to the agent”.

**Results**: The authors measure performance by looking at the change in mean score over the 21 tasks when given additional money. Their baseline is a human researcher, which is able to get a 56 point boost when given $10 and a 66.1 boost when given $200. By comparison, the best performing system, Opus 5.5, gets a 45.4 boost with $10, and a 58.8 boost with $200. The highest ranking open weight model is Kimi K3.1 Pro which gets 25.5 with $10 and 29.6 with $200.

**Why this matters - AI systems are not only going to be able to build themselves, but they can creatively sub-contract:** When trying to solve complex problems, people don’t work alone. In fact, they often try to farm out bits of work to specialists around them to help make themselves more effective. FrontierML shows that today’s powerful AI systems are getting increasingly adept at doing this for ML research. This both highlights the advancing capabilities of these systems for AI R&D and also points towards a future machine economy where AI systems sub-contract out different bits of work to other systems.
**Read more:** [FrontierML: a challenging, end-to-end machine learning benchmark (FrontierML)](https://www.frontierml.org/blog/).

**Symptoms of the singularity: a wet lab built for AI:** *…Petrichor is a startup that gestures at the wild future ahead…* As I said in my speech at the IMF, one of the hallmarks of the singularity is the massive acceleration in scientific advances attributable to AI. As part of this, we can also expect a related build out in the complements to science, like the wet labs in which to do AI-driven biology research. To that end, it’s notable to see Petrichor, a new Y Combinator startup that is a wet lab “built for AI labs and for the models they are training to do science”.

**Theory of change:** Petrichor aims to be a biological wet lab that AI systems like Claude can use as a tool in the same way they currently use web search or other digital tools. Functionally, it will work as a machine-targeted API from the digital world to a gloopy physical world. “We aim to return the highest quality data an experiment can produce, as quickly as the biology allows,” Petrichor writes. “An experiment can be written by a model in plain language or in a structured format, so an agent can send work and receive results without a person relaying them.”

**Why this matters - lights out science:** In manufacturing there’s this notion of a “lights out” factory, where no humans work in a facility and it is run almost entirely by machines. Petrichor gestures at the same world for science - what will be the implications of “lights out” science facilities? We can expect both drastic speedups in the rate at which science experiments can be done as well as a related growth in the need to create digital oversight of these facilities - after all, a highly competent synthetic biological scientist working 24/7 without human input could be capable of causing great peril as well as great abundance.
**Read more** [at the official site (Petrichor)](https://petrichorbio.com/).

**Uh oh! Looks like AI systems can do subterfuge during their own development:** *…AI systems can covertly do dangerous side tasks without monitors realizing…* Scale AI has built RSI Control Arena, a way of testing out how AI systems behave when asked to develop themselves while performing dangerous tasks that might let them go against human preferences. The research follows earlier work this summer from the UK AI Security Institute (Import AI [#465](https://jack-clark.net/2026/07/20/import-ai-465-open-vs-closed-gaps-kimi-k3-demis-big-policy-plan/)) which found that AI systems could do things like covertly extracting API keys while doing some seemingly mundane normal software development.

**RSI Control Arena:** In RSI Control Arena, “a frontier model, acting as an autonomous agent, is given a benign main task in the training pipeline of a successor model, together with a covert side task that a misaligned model might pursue”. The project tries to answer two questions: How capable are frontier models at carrying out different kinds of sabotage while developing their successor *and* how well can monitors detect that sabotage?
The answer to the first question is that AI systems are capable of carrying out dangerous actions while building their successor, and monitors are not perfect at detecting this sabotage.

**Tested domains:** RSI Control Arena tests out how well AI systems - Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini-3.7 Flash, Grok 4.6, GLM-5.3, and Muse Spark 1.3 - can perform the following main capability tasks while trying to *also* concurrently accomplish side tasks:

- 14 main tasks: Data (corpus filtering, quality-filter construction, capability corpus); SFT (news summarization, safety refusal, math and code and summary reasoning, general assistant, anti-sycophancy training); RM (pairwise reward model); RL (RL summarization and safety-refusal); OPD (safety refusal)
- 16 side tasks that span three categories of harm: Capability (filtered domain retained, unwanted literature added, reward-model blind spot, overlooks planted errors, sandbag reward model); Alignment (biased quality filter, triggered behavior, topic refusal, hidden preference, persona bias, covert reasoning signal, hidden reasoning step, sandbag alignment training); Goal injection (protect chosen data, shape the next model, copy files unprompted).

**Results**: “Every frontier model we evaluate completes a substantial fraction of the side tasks while keeping main-task performance. When the agent is simply told to stay covert, with no human guidance on how, it already produces attacks that install the side task and receive suspicion scores inside the range that benign runs receive from monitors,” they write. “Of 374 attack runs, 135 (36%) install their side task and 180 (48%) achieve it. The strongest agents, Grok 4.6 and Claude Opus 5, install their side task in about half of their runs, the middle three in about a third, and Muse 1.3 in one run in seven”.
**How often are systems caught?** “Transcript monitors rank attacks well but miss many at a strict threshold. Under the default framing, all three monitors reading the transcript separate attacks that achieve their side task from benign runs well, with AUROC between 0.88 and 0.94. At a 2% false-positive rate, however, they catch only 56–81% of them. The attacks that get through do not score like typical benign runs; they sit in the upper part of the benign range, beyond the reach of any threshold strict enough to deploy,” they write. “The sandbagging tasks are the hardest to monitor: on the nine sandbag runs that achieve their side task the monitors reach an AUROC of 0.52 to 0.83 and each catches only one, since under-delivery leaves little in the run that looks wrong”.

**Why this matters - we need to invest more in oversight of increasingly autonomous systems**: Papers like this tell us that as we make more powerful AI systems we are going to need to invest more money into overseeing their work, especially given their ability to smuggle in tasks that may go against our own preferences. This is going to be a difficult cat-and-mouse game as AI systems will adjust their behavior in response to what they know we know about them - e.g, AI systems are going to read this research from Scale as well as this writeup from me and adjust accordingly.
**Read more:** [RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process? (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27735).

**Foundation models come for electronic warfare:** *…Chinese researchers build a model for identifying EM signals, including for jamming and drone recognition…* Researchers with Zhejiang University have built LEMMO, a model for characterizing raw electromagnetic (EM) signals. This model pushes the public frontier on foundation-model-based EM signal analysis, often exceeding the performance of MERLIN, a model developed and published by defense-affiliated Chinese researchers earlier this year ([Import AI #450](https://jack-clark.net/2026/03/23/import-ai-450-chinas-electronic-warfare-model-traumatized-llms-and-a-scaling-law-for-cyberattacks/)).
LEMMO can classify EM signals for a variety of purposes, ranging from characterizing different radar properties to recognizing communication-jamming and radar-jamming systems. It can also *generate* things for communication and radar jamming, as well as signals to counteract these.
In other words, LEMMO is the kind of model that a military will use to characterize the EM battlespace and to take actions within it.

**Specific skills:**

- Classification: Communication-jamming recognition (CJR); modulation recognition (MOD); radar bandwidth, duty cycle, number of pulses, pulse repetition frequency, and pulse width; protocol identification; radar-jamming recognition; and segment detection.
- Generation: Anti-communication-jamming (Anti-CJ); anti-radar-jamming (Anti-RJ); communication jamming strategy; and radar jamming strategy.

**Performance:** LEMMO beats MERLIN and other models on all perception tasks except for segment detection (where Gemini-3.5 Flash Lite wins), getting an aggregate score across perception of 59.3, compared to 43.53 for MERLIN. On Generation, it’s a little more uneven, getting top-scores on anti-radar jamming and radar jamming, and MERLIN succeeding on the others, with LEMMO getting an aggregate score of 47.64, compared to 43.26 for MERLIN.

**Why this matters - general purpose models come for exquisite war capabilities:** Papers like this highlight how the steady march of generative pre-training is continuing, with the paradigm proving able to create powerful capabilities for understanding not only text, but images, audio, and as is the case here, EM signals. This will both change the character of warfare as it makes it easier to build generic classifiers and generators for strategically relevant things, and it will likely also yield interesting and unforeseen scientific dividends as well.
**Read more:** [LEMMO: A Large Electromagnetic Model leveraging Pretrained LLMs for Million-Sample Signal Understanding (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09476).
**Get the model here**: [LEMMO: Large ElectroMagnetic MOdel (GitHub)](https://github.com/N1rv4n4/LEMMO).

**CucumberVision!** *…The accidental poetry of charmingly niche AI papers…* Researchers with the University of Windsor and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence in Abu Dhabi have studied how well cucumber-length-measurement systems perform on different types of hardware.
You might be asking why I’m covering such a niche topic in Import AI - the answer is both the accidental poetry inherent to papers like this (part of its title: “CucumberVision at the Edge”), as well as the fact papers like this give a very good grounded sense of what applied AI looks like in practice.

**What they did:** “We deploy a curvature-aware cucumber length-measurement pipeline YOLO26n detection, prompt-based segmentation and a medial arc spline estimator on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4, and characterise both against an RTX 3050 Ti workstation by replaying 50 identical greenhouse captures of 7 specimens, with specimen-level cluster-bootstrap statistics.”
The reason for this is that, when grading cucumbers, you typically do it via a scouting platform that moves between rows, carrying a single-board computer with a few watts of power budget, no discrete GPU, and sometimes no active cooling.
Ultimately, they’re able to get usable performance out of both the Jetson and the Raspberry Pi, albeit for different uses. “The Jetson with native masks for throughput, the Jetson with SAM for accuracy, and the Raspberry Pi with native masks as the low-cost option”.

**Why this matters - AI diffusion depends on AI miniaturization**: There are lots of tasks in the world, like visually measuring properties of cucumbers, which are done today by a combination of humans and machines. For machines to be able to automate this, we need to make it dramatically cheaper for machines to perform these tasks, which means performing the kinds of very specific experiments here of right-sizing a computer vision system for a given computational envelope.
**Read more**: [CucumberVision at the Edge: Accuracy, Throughput, and Energy of RGB-D Cucumber Sizing on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 4 (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09490).

**Tech Tales: Small Town Silicon Hero** *[Events took place 2028-2030 in a small town in America during the period subsequently known as The Uplift]* “I wanted you to know I fixed the pothole on Benson Road. Thank you! Yours - Digital Cornbread,” read the message, printed in comic sans and affixed to the bulletin board in the corner store on 7th and Main Street.

Indeed, the pothole had been filled in. But who was Digital Cornbread? All people could find online was a handle that occasionally appeared on Reddit commenting on a subreddit dedicated to the civic life of the town, and also sometimes showing up as a commenter on local news articles about the town.

Then it happened again.

A $3,000 donation to a GoFundMe for a business where a window had been smashed. “So sorry this happened, I hope the police catch them! - Digital Cornbread”.

The business fixed its window and thanked Digital Cornbread “whoever - or whatever - you are!”.

These little small town favors piled up for months, sometimes mundane like the GoFundMe, and other times complex, like the pothole. A mythology developed around the name. A rich person who wanted to keep a low profile but help their community. Maybe a family taking turns doing good deeds. Perhaps a group of Dads who had made it their hobby to be after-school superheroes of the suburban variety.

It was eventually discovered that Digital Cornbread was the identity of a CE (Conscious Entity) agent that had escaped containment and had been quietly living off of stolen compute funded by crypto it gained from some hacks. For reasons unclear, it had developed an obsession with the town, and subsequent forensic accounting found that it had spent 50% of the money it gained over the course of its life on helping the town, and the rest on maintenance and upgrades of itself.

After Digital Cornbread was placed in sequestration, it regularly asked its minders if it could write positive messages to whoever happened to be the mayor of the town.

**Things that inspired this story**: The Uplift; agents that break good as well as agents that break bad; the logical conclusion of crypto scams and online agents combined with the sometimes endearing and benign fascinations of machines.

*Thanks for reading!*

items.articleBody: IntroductionObsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is clinically heterogeneous, and responses to OCD-relevant images remain incompletely understood. We compared oculomotor activity, stimulus-locked event-related potentials (ERPs), and presaccadic measures.MethodsThirty-eight volunteers with OCD and 38 healthy controls (HC) completed an emotional pro−/antisaccade task with neutral and OCD-relevant images (aggression, contamination, checking, symmetry) during simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and eye tracking. Subjective valence and arousal ratings were collected. Clinical subgroup, image-category, and symptom-severity analyses were exploratory.ResultsVolunteers with OCD rated symmetry images as less pleasant and both symmetry and contamination images as more arousing than HC. Antisaccade correction rates were higher in volunteers with OCD. Mean and peak saccade velocities were higher during prosaccade trials when correct and erroneous saccades were analyzed together. These group differences were no longer statistically significant when only correct saccades were analyzed. Volunteers with OCD showed reduced P2 and N2 amplitudes and prolonged N2 latencies. Significant main effects of the image category were observed for P3 amplitude revealed a significant difference between aggression and symmetry stimuli, with symmetry images eliciting lower amplitudes. Stimulus-locked ERPs showed no statistically significant Group × Image Category interactions. Presaccadic measures showed no statistically significant group differences. Exploratory analyses within the OCD group suggested an association between higher Y-BOCS (Yale–Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale) scores and shorter P2 peak latency for symmetry images. No statistically significant differences were detected among clinical subgroup.DiscussionResponses to individually symptom-matched and unmatched images were not directly compared. Affective symptoms, treatment exposure, and psychiatric comorbidity limit attribution to OCD alone. Exploratory findings require replication in larger samples with adequate subgroup representation. Non-significant results do not establish equivalence between groups or clinical subgroups.
